label: verify:Davidson & Associates v. Jung (Blizzard v. bnetd), 42
actual_description: The official slip opinion PDF of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, No. 04-3654, Davidson & Associates d/b/a Blizzard Entertainment and Vivendi Universal Games v. Jung, Crittenden, Combs and Internet Gateway. It is the bnetd / Battle.net emulator case, reported at 422 F.3d 630 (8th Cir. 2005). I fetched it and read all 20 pages. It was submitted June 20, 2005 and filed September 1, 2005. The panel was Murphy, Bye and Smith; Judge Smith wrote the opinion. It is an appeal from the Eastern District of Missouri (Judge Charles A. Shaw), and it affirms summary judgment for Blizzard and Vivendi. The claim's description is accurate, with the nuances listed under key_facts.
license: none/unknown (US federal court opinion; public domain under the government edicts doctrine)
how_to_use:
Reference-only legal authority for the project's LEGAL.md / risk analysis. Nothing in it can be ported. It is the main US precedent against game-server emulators and reverse engineering done under a clickwrap agreement. What it means for the LOTRO project:
(a) Anyone who clicked through the LOTRO/SSG EULA or ToS has probably given up, by contract, the right to reverse engineer the client, at least in the 8th Circuit. Contributors who disassemble the official client therefore carry personal contract risk. Prefer clean-room work: one group documents formats and protocols from files and observed behavior, and a separate group implements from that documentation. Have non-party or EU-based specification writers where you can. EU Software Directive Art. 6 interoperability rights cannot be overridden by contract, unlike the US position here.
(b) The DMCA part of the ruling hinged on bnetd skipping the CD-key handshake, which let pirated copies play. The project must never bypass, stub out or "always-OK" any authentication or access control, or anything that resembles one. Any server or emulator component must not help unlicensed copies, and the client should only load user-supplied, legitimately obtained .dat files.
(c) The §1201(f) interoperability exemption needs all four elements. Element (4), that the circumvention is not infringement, is the one that failed here. Structure the project so it does not depend on circumventing technical protection measures (TPMs) at all.
Caveats: this is an 8th Circuit, conflict-preemption-only ruling that has been widely criticized. Compare Vault v. Quaid (5th Cir.), Sega v. Accolade (9th Cir., reverse engineering as fair use), and Lexmark (6th Cir.). Have a lawyer confirm before relying on any of this.
key_facts:
Verified from the PDF itself (application/pdf, 144.9KB, 20 pages):
- Caption: Davidson & Associates d/b/a Blizzard Entertainment, Inc.; Vivendi Universal, Inc. v. Tim Jung; Rob Crittenden; Internet Gateway. The caption says "Tim Jung" but the body says "Jim Jung", and Ross Combs is also named in the body. Games at issue: StarCraft, Brood War, WarCraft II BNE, Diablo, Diablo II LoD.
- Facts: the defendants reverse engineered the protocol using tcpdump, "Nextray" and a "ripper" tool that unpacked client archive files to learn the ad-banner format. Combs tried to disassemble a game. Crittenden made an unauthorized copy of a game for testing. The BNS utility redirected games to bnetd. Most importantly (p.10), the bnetd server "always sends the game an 'okay' reply regardless of whether the CD Key is valid or currently in use", so unauthorized copies were played on it.
- EULA (fn 4) forbids "reverse engineer... disassemble, decompile". TOU (fn 5) forbids reverse engineering, emulating or redirecting Battle.net protocols, and "server emulators".
- Preemption (Part II.A, pp.13-15): at oral argument the appellants dropped express preemption (fn 9), so only conflict preemption was decided, specifically conflict with the §1201(f) interoperability exception. The court distinguished Vault v. Quaid and relied on Bowers v. Baystate (Fed. Cir.) and Nat'l Car Rental. Key quotes: "private parties are free to contractually forego the limited ability to reverse engineer" and "By signing the TOUs and EULAs, Appellants expressly relinquished their rights to reverse engineer." So the claim's "not preempted" is accurate only in this narrow conflict-preemption sense.
- §1201(a)(1) circumvention: the CD-key "secret handshake" is a technological measure that effectively controls access to Battle.net mode. The court distinguished Lexmark v. Static Control.
- §1201(a)(2) trafficking: bnetd had "limited commercial purpose because its sole purpose was to avoid the limitations of Battle.net."
- §1201(f) four-element test (p.19), quoted verbatim in the claim's sense: (1) lawfully obtained the right to use a copy of the program; (2) the information was not previously readily available; (3) the sole purpose was to identify and analyze the elements needed for interoperability of an independently created program; (4) the circumvention did not constitute infringement. The court held "Appellants's circumvention in this case constitutes infringement" because unauthorized copies were freely played on bnetd servers that did not check CD keys. The claim's summary of why the defense failed is accurate.
- The district court also found the defendants waived fair use and that the agreements were not copyright misuse. The appeal affirmed on all points.
last_activity: Opinion filed 2005-09-01; PDF still live on ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov as of 2026-10-03

label: verify:Directive 2009/24/EC on EUR-Lex
canonical_url: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/24/oj (equivalent CELEX link: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32009L0024). A readable mirror that this environment can fetch: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2009/24/contents (UK retained-law snapshot of the text as first adopted).
actual_description:
Directive 2009/24/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 April 2009 on the legal protection of computer programs (Codified version). Published in OJ L 111, 5.5.2009, pp. 16-22. It codifies Council Directive 91/250/EEC, the "Software Directive". It has 12 articles: 1 Object of protection, 2 Authorship, 3 Beneficiaries, 4 Restricted acts, 5 Exceptions, 6 Decompilation, 7 Special measures of protection, 8 Continued application of other legal provisions, 9 Communication, 10 Repeal, 11 Entry into force, 12 Addressees. It also has Annexes I and II.

Verification: I fetched the claimed EUR-Lex URL plus the /TXT/HTML/ and ELI variants. All three came back with an empty body to the fetcher, which matches the claim's own note (EUR-Lex appears to block non-browser clients). Search results confirm the identifiers: CELEX 32009L0024, the ELI eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/24/oj, and OJ L 111 of 5.5.2009. I took the article texts below verbatim from the legislation.gov.uk mirror, which fetched without problems. That mirror says its version is the text "as it stood when it was first adopted in the EU" and that no amendments have been applied since IP completion day (31 Dec 2020). The directive has not been amended, so the mirror text should match EUR-Lex. Confidence: verified (resource exists and the claim is accurate). The "provides" note in the claim is also accurate.
license: none/unknown (official EU legislative text. Under Commission Decision 2011/833/EU, EUR-Lex content can be reused with attribution. The legislation.gov.uk mirror is under the UK Open Government Licence v3.0. Neither licence was re-checked in this session.)
how_to_use:
Use as a reference only. It is the main EU legal basis for the project's clean-room and interoperability policy, so cite it in LEGAL.md / CONTRIBUTING.md. Link the EUR-Lex ELI as the authoritative source and quote from the legislation.gov.uk mirror, because EUR-Lex blocks scripted fetches.

What it allows:
- Studying the behaviour of a lawfully owned LOTRO client while running it (Art 5(3)).
- Treating file formats, interfaces and protocol ideas as not protected by copyright (Art 1(2)).
- Decompiling, only when it is indispensable for interoperability and only for the parts needed (Art 6(1)).
- Contract terms in the EULA/ToS that override Art 5(3) or Art 6 are void (Art 8).

What it limits:
- Information obtained by decompiling may only be used for interoperability.
- It must not be shared except as needed for interoperability.
- It must never be used to build a program "substantially similar in its expression" (Art 6(2)(c)).

Project rules that follow from this:
1. Keep two roles apart. Reverse engineers write prose/spec documents describing formats and behaviour. Implementers write code only from those specs. Never copy decompiled code, symbol names or code structure into the repo.
2. Prefer observing behaviour (Art 5(3)), such as parsing .dat files and capturing traffic from one's own client, over decompiling. Note that the "not previously readily available" condition in Art 6(1)(b) may fail where public docs already exist (for example LotroCompanion/DATUnpacker-derived format knowledge). Decompile only to fill gaps.
3. Ship no means whose sole intended purpose is circumventing technical protection (Art 7(1)(c)). Do not distribute DRM/anti-cheat bypass tooling or the client's encryption keys.
4. Art 8 says the directive does not affect trade-mark or unfair-competition law. Do not use the "LOTRO" / "Lord of the Rings" marks or Standing Stone Games / Middle-earth Enterprises branding as the project name or logo.

Limits of this source:
- It is EU-only, so pair it with US sources (17 U.S.C. §1201(f), Sega v. Accolade, Sony v. Connectix) and with the CJEU ruling SAS Institute v WPL (C-406/10), which applies Art 1(2)/5(3) to functionality and file formats. I did not verify those here.
- It does not cover server emulation or connecting to the official servers, which are ToS/contract and unfair-competition questions. Get real legal advice.
key_facts:
Text verified verbatim from legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2009/24/article/{1,5,6,7,8}:

- Art 1(2): "Protection ... shall apply to the expression in any form of a computer program. Ideas and principles which underlie any element of a computer program, including those which underlie its interfaces, are not protected by copyright under this Directive."
- Art 1(3): a program is protected if it is "the author's own intellectual creation".
- Art 5(1): loading, running and error correction by a lawful acquirer are allowed "in the absence of specific contractual provisions". A contract CAN override this paragraph.
- Art 5(2): making a back-up copy cannot be prevented by contract.
- Art 5(3): "The person having a right to use a copy of a computer program shall be entitled, without the authorisation of the rightholder, to observe, study or test the functioning of the program in order to determine the ideas and principles which underlie any element of the program if he does so while performing any of the acts of loading, displaying, running, transmitting or storing the program which he is entitled to do."
- Art 6(1): reproduction and translation of code (decompilation) do not need authorisation when "indispensable to obtain the information necessary to achieve the interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs". All three conditions apply:
  - (a) it is done by the licensee or another person with a right to use the copy, or on their behalf;
  - (b) the information "has not previously been readily available";
  - (c) it is "confined to the parts of the original program which are necessary in order to achieve interoperability".
- Art 6(2): information obtained this way may NOT be:
  - (a) used for goals other than interoperability;
  - (b) given to others except when necessary for interoperability;
  - (c) used "for the development, production or marketing of a computer program substantially similar in its expression, or for any other act which infringes copyright".
- Art 6(3): Berne three-step test. Art 6 may not be applied in a way that "unreasonably prejudices the rightholder's legitimate interests or conflicts with a normal exploitation of the computer program".
- Art 7(1)(c): remedies against "putting into circulation, or the possession for commercial purposes of, any means the sole intended purpose of which is to facilitate the unauthorised removal or circumvention of any technical device which may have been applied to protect a computer program".
- Art 8, para 1: the directive is "without prejudice to ... patent rights, trade-marks, unfair competition, trade secrets ... or the law of contract".
- Art 8, para 2: "Any contractual provisions contrary to Article 6 or to the exceptions provided for in Article 5(2) and (3) shall be null and void." So EULA anti-reverse-engineering clauses cannot override Art 5(3) or Art 6 in the EU.

Identifiers and access:
- Identifiers: CELEX 32009L0024; ELI http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/24/oj; OJ L 111, 5.5.2009, p.16-22. It is a codified version of 91/250/EEC.
- Access issue: eur-lex.europa.eu returned empty bodies to WebFetch for the /TXT/?uri=, /TXT/HTML/?uri= and /eli/ URLs. Use the legislation.gov.uk mirror (/eudr/2009/24/article/N) for automated retrieval.
- Mirror caveat: legislation.gov.uk shows the text as adopted, frozen at 31 Dec 2020. It is UK retained law, not the live EU consolidated text.
language: n/a (legal text, English; official in all EU languages)
last_activity: Adopted 23 April 2009, published OJ L 111 5.5.2009; no amendments applied (per legislation.gov.uk note, unchanged since IP completion day 31 Dec 2020); still in force as the EU Software Directive.

label: verify:ACEmulator/ACE
actual_description: ACEmulator: an open-source C# server emulator for Asheron's Call (Turbine's earlier MMO), backed by MySQL/MariaDB. The solution includes ACE.DatLoader (a netstandard2.0 reader for AC's portal/cell/language/highres .dat files), ACE.DatLoader.Tests, ACE.Server (which has a large Physics/ tree: BSP, Collision, Animation, Transition, SpherePath, PhysicsObj, Particles), ACE.Database, ACE.Entity, ACE.Common and ACE.Adapter. Every part of the claim checked out. I verified it with a shallow clone; the README says it is a "completely from-scratch open source server implementation for Asheron's Call".
license: AGPL-3.0
language: C# (ACE.Server targets net10.0; ACE.DatLoader targets netstandard2.0)
last_activity: 2026-09-23 (latest master commit 47edade, an automated update to ServerBuildInfo_Dynamic.cs). The project is under active maintenance.
key_facts:
Read directly from the source:
- **Dat header:** at file offset 0x140 (`DAT_HEADER_OFFSET` in DatDatabase.cs). The class `DatDatabaseHeader` is commented as "DiskFileInfo_t in the client". Fields, all u32 unless noted: FileType, BlockSize, FileSize, DataSet (1=Portal, 2=Cell, 3=Language, 4=HighRes), DataSubset, FreeHead, FreeTail, FreeCount, BTree (root directory offset), NewLRU, OldLRU, UseLRU, MasterMapID, EnginePackVersion, GamePackVersion, VersionMajor (16 bytes), VersionMinor.
- **Directory B-tree node** (`DatDirectoryHeader`): 0x3E u32 branch offsets, then a u32 EntryCount, then up to 0x3D entries.
- **Entry** (`DatFile`, 24 bytes): BitFlags, ObjectId, FileOffset, FileSize, Date, Iteration.
- **File data** (`DatReader`): stored as a chain of BlockSize sectors. The first 4 bytes of each sector hold the next sector's offset (0 ends the chain), so each sector carries BlockSize-4 bytes of payload.
- **FileTypes/:** 53 parsers, including GfxObj, SetupModel, Animation, MotionTable, EnvCell, Environment (BSP), CellLandblock, LandblockInfo, RegionDesc, Surface, SurfaceTexture, RenderTexture, Texture, Palette, PaletteSet, ParticleEmitterInfo, PhysicsScript, SoundTable, Wave, Font, LayoutDesc, StringTable, LanguageString, MasterProperty, DbProperty, EnumMapper, DidMapper. DxtUtil.cs handles DXT decompression.
- **Physics provenance:** comments in ACE.Server/Physics point to the retail client, e.g. Polygon.cs:406 "The client decompile has this branch of code as well", PhysicsObj.cs:3365 "acclient might have a bug here", and similar notes in WeenieObject.cs and ObjCell.cs. So the claim's legal caution is justified: the physics code is closely derived from a decompiled acclient.exe.
- **Tests:** ACE.DatLoader.Tests/DatTests.cs needs real client_cell_1.dat, client_portal.dat and client_local_English.dat under DAT_PATH. This is a useful pattern for tests that depend on user-supplied data.

Note for LOTRO: these are Asheron's Call formats. LOTRO's dat files (client_general.dat and so on) come from the same Turbine lineage and use a related but different, versioned format (different header and directory layout, compression, 64-bit-style DIDs in newer clients). Treat ACE as a reference for the family's concepts (sector chains, B-tree directory, DID ranges by file type), not as a LOTRO-compatible parser.
how_to_use:
Use as a reference only: read it for concepts and learn the format by studying it, but do not copy code. Don't take it as a dependency and don't port it.

1. **License:** AGPL-3.0 is strong copyleft. Copying or porting any ACE code would force our client under AGPL, and we have not chosen that license.
2. **Legal risk:** ACE.Server/Physics openly says it mirrors the retail client's decompiled code. Porting it would weaken our clean-room position. Contributors writing physics or collision code should not study it line by line.
3. **Different game:** it covers Asheron's Call, not LOTRO. Its formats are only ancestors of LOTRO's, so nothing will load LOTRO data without changes.

What we can use:
- The overall dat design (header at 0x140, a sector-chained block store, a B-tree directory of 24-byte entries, file types chosen by ID range) as a starting hypothesis to test against LOTRO dat files. Write our own independent spec of it.
- The names and structure of the asset kinds (GfxObj, Setup, EnvCell, Surface, MotionTable, etc.) as a vocabulary, since LOTRO keeps many of these concepts.
- The test pattern that skips tests when the user hasn't supplied dat files.

Record any fact we take from it in a clean-room spec document, written by someone who does not then write the implementation.

label: verify:ACEmulator/ACViewer
actual_description: The claim checks out. ACViewer is a work-in-progress viewer for Asheron's Call DAT files, not LOTRO ones. It is a WPF desktop app that hosts MonoGame (WindowsDX, through MonoGame.Framework.WpfInterop) and targets net8.0-windows. It has separate viewers for models, textures, particles, maps, the world and world objects (ModelViewer.cs, TextureViewer.cs, ParticleViewer.cs, MapViewer.cs, WorldViewer.cs, WorldObjectViewer.cs). It reads DATs through the ACE.DatLoader library, which comes in as a git submodule of ACEmulator/ACE. It also bundles parts of ACE.Server's physics and world-object code. The README states that DAT editing and WorldBuilder-like features are future goals.
license: GPL-3.0-only (LICENSE file is GNU GPL v3). The ACE submodule it depends on (ACE.DatLoader, ACE.Server and others) is AGPL-3.0.
how_to_use: Use it as reference only, for architecture and design patterns. It is not a dependency to take on. (1) It is Windows-only (WPF, DirectX MonoGame) and C#. (2) It is GPL-3.0 and pulls in AGPL-3.0 ACE code, so copying code into our project would force its license on us. Only do that if the project deliberately chooses GPL/AGPL-compatible licensing. Otherwise read it to understand ideas and write our own code. (3) It reads the Asheron's Call DAT format and AC object types. LOTRO's engine descends from the same Turbine engine, so the concepts carry over: GfxObj, Setup, Surface, SurfaceTexture, Palette, EnvCell, Landblock, ParticleEmitterInfo, PhysicsScript and MotionTable. The actual LOTRO DAT container (version 0x200+), its compression and its file-ID ranges are different, so none of its parsers will read LOTRO data unchanged. The most useful lessons for our renderer and dev tools are: caching shared objects by DAT ID and applying per-instance texture/palette changes; instanced draw batches (InstanceBatch, ParticleBatch, TerrainBatch, TextureAtlas); and a separate viewer per asset type, which is a good model for an asset-browser tool. Also a clean-room note: ACViewer itself avoids original client code because it builds on ACE's emulator-side reimplementation, which is the same legal stance we want. It does not, however, address any LOTRO-specific legal question.
key_facts:
- The repo exists. HEAD is c5c54fb on master, last commit 2026-07-07: "Add weenie name/text search linking ace_world data to dat assets (#93)". There is also a branch named updatesubmod20260813. The project is active.
- Packages in the csproj: MonoGame.Framework.WindowsDX 3.8.0.1641, MonoGame.Content.Builder.Task, MonoGame.Framework.WpfInterop 1.9.2, AssimpNet 5.0.0-beta1, UkooLabs.FbxSharpie 1.0.99 and Newtonsoft.Json. It sets UseWPF=true and TargetFramework net8.0-windows7.0.
- Project references: ACE.Common, ACE.Database, ACE.DatLoader and ACE.Entity, all from the ACE submodule (https://github.com/ACEmulator/ACE.git).
- Caches: Model/GfxObjCache.cs and SetupCache.cs are static Dictionary<uint, T> keyed by DAT file ID. Render/TextureCache.cs is keyed by TextureChanges, with Get(fileID, textureChanges, paletteChanges). Per-instance texture/palette swaps follow AC's ObjDesc / PaletteChanges / PartChange model.
- Instancing: GfxObjInstance_Shared and ParticleBatchDraw bind two vertex buffers, one with the shared mesh and one with a per-instance buffer at step rate 1, then call GraphicsDevice.DrawInstancedPrimitives. Particles are drawn as billboard quads (a triangle strip of 2 primitives).
- Other render classes: TerrainBatch, TextureAtlas / TextureAtlasChain, R_Landblock, R_EnvCell, R_Environment, R_PartArray and R_PhysicsObj. The shaders are texture.fx and texture_clamp.fx, compiled with MGCB.
- Export (FileExport.cs): ExportModel_Assimp builds an Assimp.Scene from Setup parts plus motion data, with animation. It saves FBX via FileFormat.FBX7700Binary and also uses FbxSharpie. It writes OBJ with an MTL file whose map_Kd points to textures saved as {surfaceID:X8}.png.
- FileTypes/ has one viewer/exporter wrapper per AC DAT type: GfxObj, Setup, Surface, SurfaceTexture, Texture, Palette, PaletteSet, EnvCell, Environment, CellLandblock, LandblockInfo, Region, Scene, Animation, MotionTable, ParticleEmitterInfo, PhysicsScript(Table), Sound(Table), StringTable, SpellTable, CharGen and others. Physics/ includes BSP, Collision and Animation, ported from ACE.Server.
last_activity: 2026-07-07 (latest commit c5c54fb on master); branch updatesubmod20260813 suggests activity in August 2026

label: verify:ACEmulator/aclog
actual_description: An Asheron's Call 1 and 2 packet logger (C++, Windows DLL, written by tfarley). It builds a proxy 'msxml4.dll' that acclient.exe and ac2client.exe load from their own folder. The DLL patches the client's IAT entries for winsock recvfrom/sendto and wraps both calls, so it logs packets before encryption and framing are applied above the socket layer. It writes standard .pcap files with fake Ethernet/IP/UDP headers (the local address is always 127.0.0.1:12345), plus a timestamped _desc.txt that holds a user-written description. It also opens a small Win32 UI window that shows statistics and has start/stop controls. It only targets the AC1/AC2 client builds as of Jan 6, 2017. The claim's wording ("automatic packet capture tool attached to AC client") is accurate. Its "kind: tool" and C++ are correct.
license: none/unknown
how_to_use: Use as a reference only. Do not copy code. There is no LICENSE file, so all rights are reserved by default. The code is also bound to fixed AC1/AC2 addresses and does nothing for LOTRO. It is useful only as an idea for a clean-room capture tool: hook the client's winsock sendto/recvfrom through a proxy/side-loaded DLL or an IAT patch, then dump the traffic to pcap with a short description file alongside, for later analysis in Wireshark. For our project, pcap capture of the real LOTRO client should use our own tool (Wireshark/npcap, or a small self-written hook/proxy) and run only on accounts and setups where the user is allowed to do so. Hooking the live LOTRO client may break the SSG ToS, so the project should document that risk and keep the tool separate from the reimplementation.
key_facts: Verified via git ls-remote and a shallow clone. HEAD 5a8947be (refs/heads/master and tag 1.0.0) is the only commit: "Initial Commit" by tfarley, 2017-01-07. The GitHub page shows the repo as Archived, with 4 stars and 1 fork. No LICENSE file exists and the source has no license or copyright headers. The pcap global header is magic 0xA1B2C3D4 with linktype 1 (Ethernet). Each packet gets fake Ethernet MACs (00:24:B2:01:02:03 / 08:00:27:01:02:03) and hand-built IPv4/UDP headers. Packet capture is cut off at MAX_PACKETDATA_SIZE 8192. Timestamps come from a QueryPerformanceCounter offset added to the time() value at log start. The desc .txt is binary: u32 ts_sec, u32 ts_usec, u16 length, then the text. Nothing in it is specific to LOTRO. The pcap output format matches what ACE-era tools such as aclogview consume.

All from reading the source of the shallow clone:
- PacketHeaders.cs, ProtoHeader (20 bytes, little-endian): u32 seqID, u32 header (bitmask of optional headers present), u32 checksum (CRC), u16 recID (recipient/stream id), u16 interval (time since last packet received), u16 datalen (payload length excluding the header), u16 iteration (table/logical grouping).
- COptionalHeader flags: Disposable=1<<0, Exclusive=1<<1, NotConn=1<<2, TimeSensitive=1<<3, ShouldPiggyBack=1<<4, HighPriority=1<<5, CountsAsTouch=1<<6, Encrypted=1<<29, Signed=1<<30.
- Optional header masks: CServerSwitchStruct = 0x100 (u32 seqNo, u32 type); LogonServerAddr = 0x200 (followed by a sockaddr_in: i16 family, u16 port, 4-byte address, 8 bytes padding); BlobFragments present = 0x4 ("See SharedNet::SplitPacketData").
- PCapReader.cs: accepts pcap magic 0xA1B2C3D4 or 0xD4C3B2A1, plus pcapng. Classifies a packet as client-to-server if the UDP destination port is in 9000-10013, and server-to-client if the source port is in that range; it skips all other packets. Fragments (BlobFrag) are sorted by fragment number, de-duplicated, and checked for completeness before concatenation.
- The internal names (SharedNet::SplitPacketData, COptionalHeader, CServerSwitchStruct, RegisterOptionalHeaderType) mirror Turbine's own AC client symbol names. That shared Turbine lineage is why this is a useful model for LOTRO, but none of these values have been checked against LOTRO traffic.
- changelog.md mentions DDD messages (Evt_DDD__Interrogation / BeginDDD / Data / EndDDD / RequestData), described as the in-protocol mechanism for patching and versioning dat files. That is relevant as a concept for a Turbine-family client's dat versioning.

label: verify:CERTCC Kaiju (includes OOAnalyzer Ghidra importer)
actual_description: CERT Kaiju is a binary analysis framework for Ghidra, released as a Ghidra extension by the CERT Executable Code Analysis Team at CMU SEI. It ports Pharos tooling into Ghidra. Its analyzers are DisasmImprovements (better function partitioning) and FnHash (exact, PIC and mnemonic function hashing). Its GUI tools are GhiHorn (path and reachability analysis backed by Z3), FnXrefs, Fn2Hash/FSE, and the OOAnalyzer JSON Importer, which applies Pharos OOAnalyzer output (recovered C++ classes, vtables and methods) to a Ghidra program. It also has headless/kaijuRun scripts. I checked all of this in the actual repo: I cloned it and found src/main/java/kaiju/tools/{disasm,fnhash,fnhashclassic,fnxrefs,fse,ghihorn,ooanalyzer,statuscheck}, and the README covers each tool.
license: BSD-3-Clause-style "BSD (SEI)" custom license (Copyright 2021 Carnegie Mellon University), with a no-endorsement clause for CMU/SEI names and third-party notices. It is not an exact SPDX match; the closest is BSD-3-Clause.
how_to_use: Use it as an external analysis tool only. Do not depend on it or vendor it. It is a Ghidra extension for studying the user's own legally obtained client binaries (lotroclient.exe / lotroclient64.exe and their DLLs). It would mainly help with the large MSVC C++ class hierarchy that the Turbine engine inherited from AC/DDO. The workflow is to run Pharos OOAnalyzer and import its JSON, which recovers classes and vtables. FnHash can then match functions across client versions or against DDO/AC binaries, and GhiHorn answers reachability questions. Clean-room rule: a "dirty" analyst writes Ghidra-derived findings up as prose specs (file formats, protocol fields, behaviour), and implementers read only those specs. Decompiled code and Ghidra project databases must never enter the repo. The license is permissive, so there is no legal obstacle to using it as a tool. Nothing from it ships in our product.

label: verify:Chorizite/Chorizite.ACProtocol
actual_description: The repo exists and its README says "Parser for AC network protocol". It is a C# (netstandard2.0, NuGet package Chorizite.ACProtocol 1.0.1) parser for the Asheron's Call network protocol. It is driven by Chorizite.ACProtocol/protocol.xml, which has 8562 lines and 489 <type> definitions plus enums and <c2s>/<s2c> message sections. The schema's own header says it is "Heavily based off of zegeger's messages.xml work and ACE enums / code comments". It includes PacketReader/MessageReader classes, can read pcaps through Medo.PcapRW, and has generated C2SMessageHandler and S2CMessageHandler classes. One part of the claim is overstated. The code is not made by Roslyn incremental source generators. It comes from Visual Studio T4 templates (Templates/*.tt with Generator=TextTemplatingFileGenerator: Enums, Types, MessageTypes, FragmentHandlers, GameActionsEvents), and the Chorizite.ACProtocol.SourceGen project is only a helper library for those templates (CSTemplateBase, TextTemplateBase, an XML model reader using System.CodeDom). The generated .cs files are committed to the repo. The rest of the claim checks out: PacketHeaderFlags, BlobFragments and FragmentGroup are all in the schema.
license: MIT
how_to_use: Use it as a reference and copy its design ideas; it is MIT so permissive reuse is fine. The schema covers Asheron's Call, not LOTRO, so it cannot be used to talk to LOTRO directly. LOTRO's protocol is related but different: it is a later Turbine engine, with different opcodes, its own crypto and session handling, and a different fragment layout. What is worth copying is the approach: one declarative XML (or similar) schema for packet headers, header flags and messages, with conditional fields (<if>, <maskmap>, <subfield>), from which readers, writers and handler dispatchers are generated. Use AC's PacketHeaderFlags and blob-fragment reassembly as a starting guess when analysing LOTRO pcaps, then check each field against real LOTRO captures. Do not take AC opcodes or field layouts as LOTRO's. For code generation, consider a cross-platform generator (a Roslyn incremental generator, or a Python/Jinja or Rust build script) instead of T4. T4 needs Visual Studio or extra tooling to run. Keep attribution, because the content comes from zegeger's messages.xml and ACE (AGPL-3.0 for ACE code; this repo only takes enum names and comments from it).

- git ls-remote: HEAD/master at ff7dffd; tag release/1.0.0; one pull ref. The last commit is 2025-10-04 "Bump version". LICENSE is MIT, "Copyright 2024 Chorizite".
- protocol.xml layout: <schema> containing <enums>, <type> definitions, then <c2s> (lines 7855-7954) and <s2c> (lines 7955-8476), then the packet types C2SPacket/S2CPacket.
- PacketHeaderFlags (uint mask): Retransmission 0x1, EncryptedChecksum 0x2, BlobFragments 0x4, ServerSwitch 0x100, LogonServerAddr 0x200, EmptyHeader1 0x400, Referral 0x800, RequestRetransmit 0x1000, RejectRetransmit 0x2000, AckSequence 0x4000, Disconnect 0x8000, LoginRequest 0x10000, WorldLoginRequest 0x20000, ConnectRequest 0x40000, ConnectResponse 0x80000, NetError 0x100000, NetErrorDisconnect 0x200000, CICMDCommand 0x400000, TimeSync 0x1000000, EchoRequest 0x2000000, EchoResponse 0x4000000, Flow 0x8000000.
- C2SPacket header: uint Sequence, PacketHeaderFlags Flags, uint Checksum, ushort RecipientId, ushort TimeSinceLastPacket, ushort Size (excluding the header), ushort Iteration. label: verify:Chorizite/DatReaderWriter
actual_description: C# library (NuGet: Chorizite.DatReaderWriter) for reading and writing Asheron's Call end-of-retail .dat files (client_portal.dat, client_cell_1.dat, client_local_English.dat, client_highres.dat). Supports full B-tree seek/insert/remove/range queries, caching modes and an async API, and targets net8.0, netstandard2.0 and net48. The repo is active: the latest commit is 2026-08-29 ("Bump version"). It covers Asheron's Call only. Grepping the repo found no mention of LOTRO or DDO.
license: MIT
how_to_use: Use it as a reference, and port from it where it helps. Do not depend on it directly. It is MIT (Copyright 2024 ACClientLib), so copying or porting code is legally fine as long as the notice is kept. It is still Asheron's Call-specific: the hard-coded node constants (62 branches / 61 files, 24-byte file entry), the DatFileType enum (Portal/Cell/Local) and all 4,300 lines of dats.xml object schemas are for AC. LOTRO's dat layout is a later fork of the same Turbine design, and its header fields after the magic, file-entry layout, B-tree fan-out and object types must be checked separately (against LotRO-specific tools such as LotroCompanion/lotro-tools and dat-export work). The most useful parts to reuse are: (1) the design of the block allocators and block-chain IO, (2) the schema-first pattern, where an XML definition file plus a Roslyn IIncrementalGenerator emit pack/unpack code; we can use the same idea with our own LOTRO schema, in any language, (3) the synthetic round-trip test pattern (InitNew an empty dat in a temp file, write an object, read it back, compare fields), which needs no copyrighted data, and (4) zlib handling (the compressed payload is a uint32 LE uncompressed size followed by a zlib stream). The claim's phrase "closest lineage reference" is fair for the container layer only. Nothing in it decodes LOTRO content.
key_facts:
Checked by shallow clone (HEAD a40acb4, 2026-08-29). LICENSE.txt is MIT, Copyright 2024 ACClientLib. The GitHub API was rate-limited, so star count and pushed_at were not fetched.

Header (DatReaderWriter/Lib/IO/DatHeader.cs), SIZE=400:
- char[256] Version, then byte[64] Transactions (an empty transaction starts 00 50 4C 00).
- Then Magic, int32 at 0x140, which must equal 0x00005442 ("BT").
- Then BlockSize, FileSize, Type (DatFileType: 1=Portal, 2=Cell, 3=Local), SubSet (the region id for cell dats; for HighRes it is Portal type with nonzero subset), FirstFreeBlock, LastFreeBlock, FreeBlockCount, RootBlock, NewLRU, OldLRU, UseLRU, MasterMapId, EngineVersion, GameVersion, then Guid MajorVersion (16 bytes) and uint32 MinorVersion.
- The default block size for new dats is 1024.

B-tree node (Lib/IO/DatBTree/DatBTreeNode.cs):
- MAX_BRANCHES=62, MAX_FILES=61, SIZE constant 1720.
- Layout: int32[62] branch block offsets, then int32 fileCount at +248, then fileCount x 24-byte entries.
- The end of the branch list is detected when a branch is 0, repeats the previous value, or is 0xCDCDCDCD. A leaf has no branches; otherwise branchCount = fileCount+1.

File entry (DatBTreeFile.cs), 24 bytes:
- uint16 Flags (0x01 = IsCompressed with zlib), uint16 Version (default 2), uint32 Id, int32 Offset (the first block, as a byte offset), uint32 Size, uint32 RawDate, int32 Iteration.

Block chain (StreamBlockAllocator.ReadBlock):
- Each block's first 4 bytes are the next block's byte offset (0 ends the chain). The other BlockSize-4 bytes are payload.

Compression (DatDatabase.cs):
- The stored payload is a uint32 LE uncompressed length followed by a zlib stream (System.IO.Compression.ZLibStream; ZLibDotNet on netstandard/net48).
- On write, the compressed form is kept only if it is smaller than the raw data.

Schema and code generation:
- DatReaderWriter/dats.xml is 4,300 lines, described as "Heavily based off of ACE.DatReader FileTypes". It defines enums such as PixelFormat PFID_* and DBObjHeaderFlags.
- DatReaderWriter.SourceGenerator holds Roslyn IIncrementalGenerator classes (DatsSourceGenerator, DBObjsGenerator, TypesGenerator, EnumsGenerator, DatabaseReadersGenerator, HashTableGenerator) built on Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp 4.8.0.

Tests:
- DatReaderWriter.Tests (MSTest) has per-DBObj tests such as DBObjs/FontTests.CanInsertAndRead. Each one creates a new dat with InitNew(DatFileType.Portal, 0) in a temp file, writes a synthetic object, reads it back and asserts each field. These are the synthetic round-trip tests the claim describes.

Verdict on the claim: every specific item (magic 0x5442 at 0x140, 62/61 B-tree, block chains, zlib, dats.xml with a Roslyn generator, round-trip tests, MIT, C#) is confirmed in source. "Complete" is accurate for AC end-of-retail dats only. Nothing here is LOTRO-specific.

label: verify:Endevir/LOTRO-Enchanced-text-patcher
actual_description: A wxPython GUI tool (Python 2.7, PyInstaller-packaged), part of the LOTRO Russian translation ("Rusification") project. It patches text in client_local_English.dat. The default branch is "Stable", with 24 commits from Jun 23 2017 to Aug 31 2017 (release v1.09). The repo has 2 stars and 5 forks. Endevir made the commits, and some were merged in by PR from Gi1dor/Testing. Files: main.py, Frame.py, MainGUI.py, LoginGUI.py, UpdateGUI.py, SelfPatchGUI.py, FaqDialog.py, ProgressDialog.py, datexport.py (the ctypes wrapper and the text subfile parser/serializer), patchimari.py (the patching workflow), GlobalVars.py, main.spec and Pack.bat. It also checks in Windows binaries: datexport.dll, msvcp71.dll, msvcp90.dll, msvcr71.dll and zlib1T.dll. The claim is accurate. I fetched the GitHub page, the LICENSE and the raw datexport.py/patchimari.py through WebFetch. A local git clone/curl could not be done because the sandbox disk is full (ENOSPC), so the source excerpts came through a summarizing fetcher, not byte-exact reads.
license: MIT (Copyright (c) 2017 Gi1dor). The repo also contains datexport.dll, a proprietary Turbine/SSG DLL taken from the game client and not MIT-licensed, plus redistributed MSVC runtime DLLs and zlib1T.dll.
how_to_use: Use it as reference only, through clean-room spec extraction. Do not depend on it or port it directly. The Python code is MIT, so porting it with attribution would be legal. But it is Python 2, tied to Windows, and does all DAT container I/O through the proprietary datexport.dll, which we must never bundle or call. So the only useful part is the text subfile (0x25) binary layout in datexport.py. Write that up as a format spec and implement it ourselves in our own DAT reader. The datexport API signatures (OpenDatFileEx2/GetSubfileData/PutSubfileData etc.) show what a DAT library needs to do. Treat them as a functional interface reference only, not something to link against. Cross-check the text format against the newer, more complete Russian-project C++ code (Gi1dor/LotroCore / LotRO-Legacy/LotroCore or LOTRO-Translate datlib), which reimplements DAT access without the DLL. Mark that as needing separate verification.
key_facts:
From the source of datexport.py:
- Text files are identified by is_text_file(file_id): (file_id >> 24) == 0x25.

Subfile header:
- u32 file_id (LE)
- 4 bytes unknown_1
- 1 byte unknown_2
- num_fragments as a 1–2 byte VLE

VLE rule: read a byte b. If b & 0x80, then value = ((b ^ 0x80) << 8) | next_byte. The writer emits (n>>8)^0x80 then n&0xFF when n >= 0x80, otherwise a single byte.

Fragment layout:
- u64 fragment_id
- u32 num_pieces
- each piece: VLE char count, then UTF-16LE string
- u32 num_arg_refs, then num_arg_refs x u32
- u8 num_arg_string_arrays
- each array: u32 element count, then elements as VLE size + UTF-16LE string

Serializer: SubFile.get_data(args_order, args_id, ...) writes the same layout back through a utf-16le codec writer.

datexport.dll API through ctypes (cdll.LoadLibrary('datexport')):
- OpenDatFileEx2(handle, path, flags uint, *int x4, *ulong, byte[], byte[])
- GetNumSubfiles(h)
- GetSubfileSizes(h, *int fileids, *int sizes, *int iterations, offset, count)
- GetSubfileVersion(h, file_id)
- GetSubfileData(h, file_id, buf, 0, *version)
- PutSubfileData(h, file_id, buf, 0, len, version, iteration, c_byte(0))
- PurgeSubfileData(h, file_id)
- Flush(h)
- CloseDatFile(h)

patchimari.py replaces fragment pieces split on the marker u'<--DO_NOT_TOUCH!-->'.
language: Python 2.7 (wxPython GUI, ctypes wrapper over a native Windows DLL)

label: verify:OneLauncher (JuneStepp)
actual_description: OneLauncher is a cross-platform (Linux/macOS via WINE, Windows) launcher and addon manager for LOTRO and DDO, written in Python with a PySide6 UI. It is not a client reimplementation: it does not reimplement the game client. It logs in through GLS, picks a world, handles the login queue, patches through the official patchclient.dll, then starts the official client binary with the right arguments. The claim's "kind: client-reimpl" is wrong; it should be launcher / launch-protocol reference. Everything else in the "provides" list checked out against the cloned source, with one correction: the patch runner file is src/run_patch_client/run_patch_client.c, not run_ptch_client.c. It is actively maintained: HEAD e921eb5 dated 2026-08-03 ("fix(addon_manager): https context"), with branches HEAD, fixes and macos-11.
license: GPL-3.0-or-later
how_to_use:
Use it as a reference and possibly as a dependency, but not for the core engine. The license is GPL-3.0-or-later, confirmed in LICENSE.md and in pyproject.toml (license = "GPL-3.0-or-later"). Copying its code means the reimplementation must also be under GPL-3.0+ terms. Two options:
(a) License the project GPL-3.0-or-later, like OpenMW. Then porting is fine, keeping attribution.
(b) Choose a permissive license. Then extract only facts from it: endpoint names, config keys, the argument template tokens, the XSD element lists and the HRESULT meanings. Write our own code from that spec.

Since it is a separate program, a simple way is to keep launching and patching out of the engine. Either let users run OneLauncher to start our client, or write our own small launcher from the facts below. Our client mostly needs to accept the same command-line arguments the official client takes (--glsticketdirect, -h host, --chatserver, --language, --authserverurl and so on) so that the OneLauncher/official launcher flow can drive it.

The files themselves do not contain copyrighted Turbine/SSG assets. The XSDs are the project's own schemas describing server responses. The client option list in the start_game.py docstring is a capture of the official client's help output, which is factual information about its interface.

how_to_use:

The tool's Apache-2.0 license is not a problem; using it never puts its code into our project.

how_to_use:
REFERENCE-ONLY / AVOID redistribution.

  - bitsets: (i,j,k)
  - enums: e<enumId>:<value>
  - numbers: 123, 123f, 123L

The per-character PropertiesSets are runtime state, not dat content, so they presumably come from the client process ("synchronized with the local LOTRO client on Windows"). The actual memory and DAT reading is in com.dam.delta4j:delta-lotro-dat-utils (11.12 in the extractor's pom), and I found no public source repo for that library on GitHub; the dmorcellet account has no dat-utils repo. Treat dat-utils as unpublished: only binary jars ship via SourceForge.
2. The real "lotro-data-extractor" for dat files is lotro-tools (delta.games.lotro.tools.extraction.MainDatLoader). It builds a DataFacade with DataFacadeBuilder.buildFacadeForTools() and runs per-domain loaders such as MainStatsLoader; packages include achievables, agents, combat, effects, geo, items, loot, skills, sounds, ui and more.

label: verify:LotroCompanion/lotro-companion-distrib
actual_description:
This is the binary distribution and release-packaging repo for LOTRO Companion, Damien Morcellet's Java/Swing character-tracking tool. It is not a source repo. I checked it with git ls-remote and a shallow clone.
- **master branch:** the HEAD is commit 527341b, dated 2024-03-30, "Added scripts to update a distrib". The newest release tag is 21.1.0.38.1, released 08/12/2023 per HISTORY.txt.
- **Other branches:** lld_soa and lld_soa-ru were last touched on 2023-01-28.
- **Libraries in lotro-companion/lib/ (compiled jars only, no .java files):** delta-lotro-companion-21.1, delta-lotro-core-21.1, delta-lotro-dat-utils-11.0 (built 2023-11-09), delta-lotro-data-extractor-5.15, delta-lotro-maps-4.0, delta-lotro-memory-5.19, delta-common-1.11, delta-common-ui-1.25, delta-common-l10n-1.0 and delta-json-1.1.1.
- **Third-party jars:** JNA 5.7.0, logback, slf4j, JFreeChart and JCommon.
- **Other contents:** a kickstarter/updater (delta-kickstarter, delta-updates-manager), an Ant build.xml, go.bat, releng scripts (update_data.sh, updateEoA.sh, maven.txt) and remote-site/latest.txt.
- **Lore data:** data/lore/*.xml holds game-derived data (items, deeds, effects, NPCs, enums, labels in de/fr), copied from the lotro-data, lotro-items-db and lotro-maps-db repos.
- **Icon archives:** the icon zips (itemIcons.zip, skillIcons.zip and so on) are 0-byte placeholders in git.

The claimed versions are correct except for delta-lotro-core: the claim gives no version, and the actual file is 21.1.
license: Apache-2.0
how_to_use:
Use it as reference only. Do not depend on it and do not port from it.

1. **The license does not "settle the legal status".** The Apache-2.0 LICENSE and NOTICE cover only Morcellet's own code: the NOTICE says the delta-*.jar files were written by him. They do not cover the game-derived lore XML in the repo, the icons, or anything about SSG's client. They give no legal cover for a client reimplementation. The claim overstates this.
2. **The two most relevant pieces are binary-only here.** There is no public source for dat-utils or the memory reader.
   - git ls-remote for LotroCompanion/lotro-dat-utils, LotroCompanion/lotro-memory and the dmorcellet/ equivalents all asked for credentials. That usually means the repo is private or does not exist.
   - Getting anything out of them would mean decompiling Apache-2.0 bytecode. That is legally allowed with attribution, but it is a poor source of facts for clean-room work.
   - If we do look, read class and package structure to see the scope only: archive, B-tree/directory, property definitions, wstate loaders, string renderers, the script and geo sub-packages.
3. **Better sources exist.** LotroCompanion/lotro-core, lotro-data-extractor, lotro-maps and lotro-companion do have public source; their ls-remote HEADs answered. Use those instead.
4. **delta-lotro-memory has no value for a client reimplementation.** It reads a running Windows LOTRO process through JNA and needs admin rights. That is a third-party tool with possible ToS problems, so avoid relying on it.
5. **Do not copy the lore XML into our repo.** It is SSG-derived data. Our client should read the user's own .dat files instead.

Main uses for us:
- the lore XML schemas and enum names, as a cross-check on how .dat properties are interpreted;
- the version and update history (HISTORY.txt), to match dat-format changes to game updates.

The jar has no license file of its own and its embedded pom.xml declares no <licenses>.)
how_to_use: Use it as a reference and for format and spec extraction, plus as an oracle for testing. Do not port it as the core library. Because the distribution NOTICE puts the delta-*.jar files under Apache-2.0, studying a CFR or javap decompile and even porting from it is probably permissible with attribution. That basis is weak, though: the source is not published, the jar has no license of its own, and the pom has no license. Safer path: (1) prefer the open-source LotroCompanion repos (lotro-core, lotro-data-extractor, lotro-tools, lotro-maps) for any code we reuse; (2) for the DAT layer, write clean-room specs from javap and decompiled behaviour (record layouts, enum lists, constants) and implement them in our own language; (3) run the jar from a test harness on users' own .dat files to produce golden outputs for cross-checking our parser; (4) ask the author (dmorcellet) whether dat-utils is formally Apache-2.0 or whether the source can be published before copying non-trivial code. The resource files classes.xml, functions.xml, StringHashMap.txt and KnownVariables.txt are community-derived name and hash tables. They are valuable, but check their provenance before redistributing them; they are mostly name lists derived from the game's own hashes.
key_facts:
Package layout: delta.games.lotro.dat.{archive, data, data.strings, loaders, loaders.wstate, loaders.ui, loaders.script, patchs, utils, utils.hash, wlib}.
- DATArchive(File) API: open/close, getRootEntry(), ensureLoaded(DirectoryEntry), loadEntry(long did) -> byte[], loadDetailedEntry(did), getEntry(did). Related classes: DirectoryEntry, FileEntry, DetailedFileEntry, DATArchiveIndexBuilder.
- DATFilesDirectory.getArchiveKeys(long did) maps a DID to archive keys; the string constants are "1".."5" and "14".
- PropertyType has 22 constants: STRING, STRING_TOKEN, WAVE_FORM, TIMESTAMP, TRI_STATE, VECTOR, INSTANCE_ID, ENUM_MAPPER, FLOAT, PROPERTY_ID, STRUCT, ARRAY, STRING_INFO, BITFIELD_64, INT, COLOR, POSITION, BIT_FIELD32, LONG64, DATA_FILE, BOOLEAN, BIT_FIELD.
- The constant 0x34000000 (property definitions DID) appears in the jar, along with 0x100011F9 and 0x1000140D. No 0x56000000 literal was found.
- WLibLoader checks a fourcc/magic of 0xFEDC1234 ("Unexpected value for fourcc") and loads classes.xml.
- BufferUtils is little-endian by default with MSB variants. Its readers: readTSize, readVle, readUInt8/16/24/32, readInt16/32, readLong64, readFloat, readDouble, readBoolean, readAsciiString, readPascalString, readPrefixedUtf16String, readPrefixedArrayUInt32/UInt16.
- StringInfo has two subtypes: LiteralStringInfo and TableEntryStringInfo (a table DID plus token), rendered through renderer/TagsManager.
- KnownVariables.txt is used by HashUtils / KnownVariablesManager to reverse string hashes.
- Dependencies: delta-common 1.11 and delta-json 1.1.1.

actual_description: The GitHub description reads "Core classes for Lotro-related applications (such as lotro-companion)". It is a Java/Maven library (artifactId delta-lotro-core, version 24.10, groupId parent com.dam.delta4j, author "DAM") with about 1,945 .java files. It holds the domain model and the XML I/O used by LOTRO Companion: accounts, characters (classes, races, stats, gear, traits, virtues, skills, storage, XP), kinships, houses, and a big "lore" package (items, quests, deeds, crafting, reputation, maps, geo, emotes, titles, relics, instances, travels, world events and more). The repo is active: HEAD 6cac595 "Version 24.10" was committed 2026-10-03. The claim is accurate about what the library does, but its license claim is not backed by anything in the repo.
license: none/unknown. The shallow clone has no LICENSE file and no README. pom.xml has no <licenses> element. No source file has a license header. The GitHub page HTML shows no license either (the API was rate-limited, so I couldn't confirm through the API). The sibling repo lotro-companion also has no LICENSE (raw LICENSE returns 404) and its README says nothing about licensing. The claimed "Apache-2.0" is unverified and appears to be wrong. Legally this means all rights are reserved by default.
how_to_use: Use it as reference-only, and do not depend on or port it. There is no license, so copying or linking its code into our project is not allowed. It also depends on the author's own delta4j libraries (delta-common, delta-common-l10n, delta-lotro-values), which are not on Maven Central as far as I can tell. And it is a tool or companion model built on XML files that lotro-tools pre-extracts from the DATs. It does not model the client runtime or parse DATs or the network protocol. Its value to us is as a factual map of game-logic concepts and their names: enum sets like ItemClass, EquipmentCategory, Genus and AgentClass, the item quality, binding and sturdiness taxonomies, the position model (region plus lon/lat), and the quest, deed and reward structures. We can check our own clean-room parsers of client_gamelogic.dat against that taxonomy. Facts like enum value lists are game data and not code expression, but we should take them from our own DAT parsing rather than copying. If we want to reuse it, ask the author (DAM, via the LotroCompanion Discord or GitHub) for an explicit license. The DAT-reading work actually lives in LotroCompanion/lotro-tools (exists, HEAD 1d1248c) and should be verified separately. LotroCompanion/lotro-dat-utils and lotro-maps-core did not resolve publicly; they returned an auth prompt, which means private or nonexistent.

Items are kept in the separate repo LotroCompanion/lotro-items-db, which this check did not open. (2) enums/ holds 101 XML files, not 71. key_facts:

label: verify:LotroCompanion/lotro-data-extractor
actual_description: The repo exists and is active. The default branch is master, HEAD is d9a85422 ("Version 5.29", committed 2026-10-03), and there are about 193 commits and tags from 1.0 to 5.29. The GitHub page shows "No description, website, or topics provided", 2 stars and 0 forks. It is a small Java/Maven library (artifact com.dam.delta4j:delta-lotro-data-extractor; 59 main files, 1 test file, about 5.9k lines) by "DAM", the LotRO Companion author. It does NOT read client memory itself. It takes already-decoded objects, delta.games.lotro.dat.data.PropertiesSet and delta.games.lotro.dat.wlib.ClassInstance (WLib class instances), and maps them into the LotRO Companion character model. Those objects come from separate libraries: the memory reader delta-lotro-memory and the DAT reader delta-lotro-dat-utils 11.12, which are lotro-companion's pom dependencies. `git ls-remote` asks for credentials on github.com/LotroCompanion/lotro-memory and on github.com/LotroCompanion/lotro-dat-utils, so those repos are private or do not exist at those names. The word "WState" appears nowhere in the source. The extractor packages cover achievables (quests and deeds), allegiances, character data and stats, cosmetics (outfits), effects, emotes, hobbies, housing, items, bags, equipment and vaults, legendary items and relics, PvP, reward tracks, skirmishes, social (friends and kinship), storage and wardrobe, titles, traits (trait trees, racial, mounted, big battles, virtues, stat tomes) and travels (the travel registry). The claim's list of what it covers is broadly right. Its mechanism is overstated: the code reads properties and WLib objects that something else supplies. It does not scrape memory.
license: none/unknown
key_facts:
- The claimed "Apache-2.0" license is FALSE. The clone has no LICENSE, COPYING or README file, pom.xml has no <licenses> element, no source file has a license header, and the GitHub sidebar shows no license. The sibling clones lotro-companion, lotro-core and lotro-tools have no LICENSE file either. Default copyright (all rights reserved) applies.
- Input types: PropertiesSet.getProperty(String name) returns values keyed by property name from the DAT property dictionary (in client_gamelogic). These are typed Java values: Integer for DIDs, enums and timestamps; Long for XP and reputation; String; and nested PropertiesSet or arrays.
- About 97 distinct named properties are used. Examples: XP_EarnedXP (Long), Time_TotalInGameTime, Title_ActiveTitleDID, Craft_Vocation, Area_CurrentArea, Dungeon_CurrentDungeon, Currency_Amount (in coppers), Time_LastLogoutTimeStamp (Unix seconds), Trait_No_Purchase_Required, Advancement_Level, Agent_Class, Allegiance_*, Bank_Repository_*, BoS_* (wardrobe), Combat_BaseDPS/Damage/DamageType/DamageVariance, Container_Slot, Craft_ItemInscription. Faction reputation uses per-faction tier and reputation property names stored in lotro-core's Faction model.
- ClassInstance.getAttributeValue(String) uses numeric attribute IDs written as strings (hashed or numeric WLib attribute names). Examples:
  - travel registry: "194458403" holds Map<Integer,ClassInstance> of TravelRecord keyed by the TravelLink enum; on a TravelRecord, "111647278" is the DatPosition and "47172757" is the name.
  - quest record: "240034292" is the completion count and "212351221" is a timestamp in seconds.
  - legendary data: entries of class id 2337.
- DatPosition has region, blockX, blockY, cell and a local position (x, y). PositionDecoder.decodePosition(blockX, blockY, x, y) turns it into lon/lat. LandblocksManager.getLandblock(region, bx, by).getParentData(cell, pos) gives the zone ID. This confirms the AC-style landblock/cell world addressing.
- Game timestamps are 32-bit Unix seconds (TimeUtils multiplies by 1000).

actual_description: Both repos exist and are public. lotro-jukebox is a Java Swing desktop app ("A jukebox for LOTRO lovers") for finding and playing LOTRO sound files. Its last commit is 35fdf75 on 2024-08-14, and params.txt says "1.0 Update 41, 15/08/2024". lotro-jukebox-core is the model and XML I/O layer: SoundDescription, SoundFormat, SoundType, SoundContext and the XML parsers and writers. The code that reads sounds out of the .dat files (delta.games.lotro.dat.data.DataFacade, SoundInfoLoader.decodeSoundInfo and decodeSound) comes from the Maven dependency com.dam.delta4j:delta-lotro-dat-utils:11.3. That library is not public: git ls-remote on github.com/LotroCompanion/lotro-dat-utils asks for credentials, so it is private or missing. It is also not in the org's public repo search, and the org has no public packages. The jukebox only writes the decoded bytes to a temp file and plays them with delta-sound-player. The catalogue covers 4118 sounds plus context mappings, not "every sound in client_sound.dat". The claim's "verified-by-fetch" confidence holds for existence only. It does not hold for the license or for "provides".
license: none/unknown. Neither repo has a LICENSE file, neither pom.xml has a <licenses> element, and the GitHub page shows no detected license. The claimed Apache-2.0 is not supported. Without a license, the default is all rights reserved.
how_to_use: Reference only; do not depend on it and do not port it. There is no license, so the code cannot legally be copied or redistributed. Also, the part that matters for a client reimplementation (the DAT reader and SoundInfo/sound decoder) is in the private delta-lotro-dat-utils library, which is not in these repos. Useful facts to take from it: the two-step lookup (SoundInfo record, then raw sound record, then OGG/WAV bytes), the DID range of sound records, and the catalogue of sound IDs and names with area, dungeon, instrument and music-item context mappings, used as test fixtures and validation targets. Treat sounds.xml and the context files as factual ID data cross-checked against your own DAT parser. Do not ship them, because they contain names extracted from SSG data. Get the actual sound container format from openly licensed DAT tools or from clean-room analysis of the user's own files. If reuse is ever wanted, ask the author (DAM / LotroCompanion) for a license.
key_facts: Pipeline, from lotro-jukebox SoundLoader.java: data=facade.loadData(soundInfoID); SoundInfo si=SoundInfoLoader.decodeSoundInfo(stream); rawRec=facade.loadData(si.getSoundID()); bytes=SoundInfoLoader.decodeSound(stream). The result is a playable OGG Vorbis or WAV file stream. So a sound is a two-level indirection: a SoundInfo DID points to a raw-sound DID, and the raw-sound record wraps the original OGG/WAV file bytes (the exact wrapper header is in the private decoder, not here). In data/sounds/sounds.xml, sound/SoundInfo IDs start at 704643072 = 0x2A000000, so DID class 0x2A is sound. Each entry has id, name (e.g. amb_rain_heavy01), date (unix timestamp), format, size (bytes), duration (ms), sampleRate (e.g. 44100.0) and type (AMBIENT/SFX/... comma list). The file has 4118 entries: 4084 OGG_VORBIS and 34 WAV. The WAV entries appear to be older assets (2007 timestamps). The core SoundFormat enum is {OGG_VORBIS, WAV}. areas.xml maps area DIDs (0x70xxxxxx, e.g. 1879051236 "Gorothlad", with an icon DID 0x41xxxxxx) to sound IDs; it has 618 areas. Other context files are dungeons.xml, instruments.xml and musicItems.xml. Dependencies are com.dam.delta4j delta-lotro-dat-utils 11.3, delta-common 1.13, delta-common-ui 1.28, delta-sound-player 1.0-SNAPSHOT, slf4j and logback. Clones are at ~/.cache/tessera/clones/lotro-jukebox and .../lotro-jukebox-core.

how_to_use: reference-only. There is no license, so by default all rights are reserved. Do not copy or port its code and do not depend on it. Read it to understand the map coordinate model (lon/lat geo units and the ScaleToMap georeference math), how map links and markers are structured, and how radar tiles are keyed by region and landblock. Then write our own clean implementation from a spec. It does not parse .dat files, so it is not a source for file formats. To get the UI_Map_* property semantics, look at the LotroCompanion extraction tooling (lotro-tools / dat utils), which is also unlicensed. It is useful mainly for the in-game map and minimap UI part of the client reimplementation. If we want to reuse code, we can ask the author for a license.
key_facts:
- GeoPoint holds two floats, longitude and latitude, in LOTRO's in-game coordinate system.
- GeoReference(start GeoPoint, geo2pixel float) has a comment saying geo2pixel = "ScaleToMap" and pixel2geo = 1/geo2pixel = "ScaleToIg". The formulas are:
  - pixel.x = round((lon - start.lon) * geo2pixel)
  - pixel.y = round((start.lat - lat) * geo2pixel), so y is flipped and north is up.
  - The inverse is lon = start.lon + px * pixel2geo and lat = start.lat - py * pixel2geo.
- Georeferenced basemap XML has the shape <maps><map id name imageId><geo factor><point .../></geo>, with <min>/<max> tags for bounding boxes.
- Marker fields: id, GeoPoint position, label, did (the dat ID of the linked game object), categoryCode, parentZoneId.
- MapLink fields: parentId (a parchment map ID, area ID or dungeon ID), contentLayerId, MapLinkType (includes TO_PARCHMENT_MAP), hotPoint GeoPoint, targetPoint GeoPoint, targetMapKey, text.
- A markers index binary file is just a series of big-endian int32 marker IDs, with count = file length / 4 (MarkersIndexBinaryParser).
- The radar layer pulls images from a RadarImageProvider via getImage(region, blockX, blockY), so radar/minimap tiles are per landblock in each region. The cache key is "region-blockX-blockY".
- Repo layout: src/main/java/delta/games/lotro/maps/{data,ui,utils}, plus a few tests. Local clone: ~/.cache/tessera/clones/lotro-maps.

label: verify:LotroCompanion/lotro-maps-db
actual_description:
Confirmed: a data repository from the LotroCompanion project (maintainer Damien Morcellet). It holds map and marker data taken from the LOTRO client .dat files, for use by the LotroCompanion map tools. It is actively maintained: the latest commit is 94c6f56 on 2026-10-02 ("Update of Russian labels (49.6) and Spanish labels (v0.9.1-beta)"). Tags follow game update versions (6.0 through 14.0, 10.1.24.1, 12.5.26.0.2, and so on). The tree has 5,423 files:
- maps/: 1,530 basemap PNGs plus maps.xml
- markers/: 445 marker XML files
- indexes/: 3,396 .bin files under indexes/did and indexes/layers
- categories/: 39 files, category icon PNGs plus categories.xml
- labels/: basemaps.xml and markers.xml for each of de, en, es, fr and ru
- links.xml
The claimed size of about 1.2 GB could not be checked. The GitHub API was rate-limited, and a full fetch was impossible because the local disk (/) is 100% full with only about 6 MB free. The many PNGs make a large size plausible.
license: none/unknown
how_to_use:
Use it only as a reference. Do not depend on it, vendor it, or redistribute it.
- **Licence:** there is no LICENSE file (GitHub /blob/master/LICENSE returns 404), so the default is all rights reserved.
- **Assets:** the PNG basemaps and category icons are copyrighted Turbine/SSG art taken from the client .dat files. Shipping them would break the clean-room, users-supply-their-own-data rule.
- **What we can use:**
  1. The XML schemas show which map fields matter: DIDs, geo factor, bounds, cross-map links and marker categories.
  2. The data can serve as ground truth to test our own .dat map extractor against. When a user has the real client, our parser should produce matching map IDs, image DIDs, geo factors, bounds and marker positions.
- **Better reference for the extraction code:** the LotroCompanion source repos (e.g. lotro-tools, lotro-maps, lotro-dat-utils; Java). Check each one's licence separately.
key_facts:
All sample files below were read directly from raw.githubusercontent.com on the master branch.
- **maps/maps.xml**:
  - Format: `<map id="268437554" name="Middle-earth" imageId="1090552121"><geo factor="1.0"><point longitude=".." latitude=".."/></geo><min longitude latitude/><max longitude latitude/></map>`.
  - Map IDs are DIDs in the 0x1000xxxx range (e.g. 268437557 Eriador, 268437576 Ered Luin with factor 43.4375).
  - imageId is a DID in the 0x41xxxxxx range, which is an image/texture DID.
  - Top-level maps use 1024x768 pixel space (min 0,-768 to max 1024,0). Region maps use LOTRO longitude/latitude coordinates, with geo factor = pixels per degree.
- **links.xml**: `<link parentId=".." contentLayerId="0" target=".." label="To: Rohan" from="601.0/-313.0"/>`. These are the clickable map-to-map navigation hotspots.
- **markers/markers-R-X-Y.xml** (e.g. markers-5-9-7.xml): `<marker id="1500516352" label=".." category="73" did="1879518956" parentZoneId="1879500817" longitude="-31.32" latitude="-33.78"/>`.
  - did is the entity DID (0x7000xxxx range) and parentZoneId is the zone DID.
  - The filename suffix probably encodes region and block coordinates. This is inferred, not confirmed.
- **categories/categories.xml**: `<category code="2" name="Quest" icon="2"/>`. Examples: 21 Tunnel Entrance, 22 Dock-master, 23 Far-ranging Stable-master, 24 Eagle, 27 Task, 29 Item-master, 30 Homestead, 31 Town Crier, plus 71 and 73. Each category has its own icon PNG.
- **indexes/did/<DID>.bin and indexes/layers/*.bin**: binary indexes made of packed 32-bit values (the first bytes are 0x1579101b, 0x1579101c, ...). They look like marker-ID lists keyed by content DID or layer. The exact meaning was not verified.
- **labels/{de,en,es,fr,ru}/{basemaps,markers}.xml**: localised label overrides.
- **Takeaway for our project:** the in-game map system can be fully described by map DIDs, image DIDs, a geo-factor/origin projection, link hotspots and categorised markers tied to zone DIDs.
language: XML + PNG images + binary index files (data only, no code)

A separate implementer then writes the C++/Rust/etc. code from that spec. Pair it with lotro-dat-utils, the dependency that holds the real low-level DAT, BufferUtils and PropertiesSet decoding; verify that repo separately. This repo explains what the game data means: landblocks, maps, quests, items, sounds and UI layouts. That is exactly what a client reimplementation needs beyond raw archive reading. Verified by shallow clone (HEAD 1d1248c, 2026-10-02). Every class named in the claim exists at these paths under src/main/java/delta/games/lotro/tools/:
- extraction/geo/landblocks/{LandblockInfoLoader, BlockMapLoader, PropertyDescriptorsManager, GeneratorLoader, LandblockLoader}
- extraction/geo/maps/{MapsSystemLoader, GeoreferencedBasemapsLoader, RegionLoader}
- extraction/geo/dungeons/DungeonLoader
- extraction/geo/areas/GeoAreasLoader
- extraction/geo/markers/{MapNotesLoader, QuestMapNotesLoader}
- extraction/common/PlacesLoader
- extraction/sounds/{SoundAnalyzer, GeoMusicLoader, ScriptsInspectorForSounds, MainSoundsDataLoader}
- extraction/ui/{SlotIconsLoader, BagIconsLoader, FieldIconsLoader}
- reports/{DATInspectionTool, MainHeightmapBuilder, ClassesTreeGenerator}
- extraction/utils/WeenieContentDirectory

voicesExtractor is a separate subproject at tools/voicesExtractor (MainVoicesExtractor, ScriptsInspectorForVoices, npc/NpcVoice(s)) and ships a prebuilt jar. Other subprojects include tools/datDisplay.

Concrete format facts from the source:
- **Root directory DID.** 0x28000000 is the root DataIdMap ("DID mapper"), decoded with DataIdMapLoader.decodeDataIdMap. It maps labels to sub-directory DIDs. Labels used here are "WEENIECONTENT", "REGION", "EMAPPER" (enum mappers) and "STRINGTABLE".
- **WeenieContent lookup.** Fetch the WEENIECONTENT label from the root map, then decode that sub-DataIdMap. Skip labels that start with "\0\0". The named content's weenie ID plus DATConstants.DBPROPERTIES_OFFSET gives the DID of its properties set.
- **Landblock DIDs.**
  - LandBlockInfo DID = 0x80200000 + region*0x10000 + blockX*0x100 + blockY.
  - BlockMap (terrain) DID = 0x80100000 + region*0x10000 + blockX*0x100 + blockY.
- **LandBlockInfo layout.**
  - Header: uint32 DID, uint32 flags (HAS_CELLS=1, HAS_LINKS=2, HAS_INDICES=4), uint32 sizeHint.
  - Then TSize-counted arrays, each present only when its flag is set.
  - Then static entities (uint32 count), links (uint32 count), weenies (TSize count), plus readAssert(0) separators and an optional trailing uint32.
  - Cross-link record: uint32 fromIndex, uint32 fromLbiDID, uint32 toLbiDID, uint32 type, uint32 toIndex, uint32 mask.
  - Housing/phasing type codes: 0x1000000B House_Permission, 0x0C House_Decoration, 0x0D House_Landmark, 0x0F ForSaleSign, 0x10-0x12 House_Storage1-3, 0x13 House_PropertyDriver, 0x19 Phasing.
- **Region to property-descriptor DIDs** (PropertyDescriptorsManager): region 1 = 0x18000000; regions 2 and 14 = 0x18000014; region 3 = 0x18000015; regions 4 and 5 = 0x1800001A.
- **UI layout DIDs** (UILayoutLoader): 0x22000041 is the maps system, 0x2200084B holds the slot icons, 0x22000889 is mounted combat. Media desc 0x4112B675 is inv-slot_mounted.
- **Well-known property sets.**
  - 0x7900025B TraitControl (e.g. Trait_Control_LevelToTotalClassTraitPointsProgression).
  - 0x7900020E and 0x7900020F are used by the class and race/deed loaders.
  - 0x79000230 InventoryControl (InventoryControl_SmartSortInfo_Array, InventoryControl_DistributionToLevelOffsetList).
  - 0x78000011 holds the bag icons.
  - Others referenced: 0x78000001, 0x7000EAA6, 0x79000255, 0x79000229, 0x7900021E, 0x79000210 and 0x79024867.
- **Enum mapper.** 0x2300036E is the enum-mapper DID class (0x23xxxxxx).
- **Brute-force scans.** Dungeons and field icons are found by scanning DIDs 0x70000000-0x77FFFFFF (the 0x70/0x79 classes are property/weenie data).
- **Sound DIDs.** MainSoundsDataLoader seeds from 0x07000009, 0x0700042E, 0x070017F8, 0x0700042F (notes), 0x0700000D, 0x0700001C, 0x07000008 and 0x07000000.
- **Byte-level primitives** (readUInt32, readUInt32AsLong, readTSize, readAssert) live in BufferUtils/LoaderUtils in the delta-lotro-dat-utils dependency, which is not in this repo.

Corrections to the claim:
1. "No LICENSE file in repo" is accurate, and the pom also lacks a licenses section.
2. "LotroCompanion distribution declares Apache-2.0 for all delta-* code" is overstated. SourceForge declares "Apache License V2.0" for the LOTRO Companion project. No LICENSE file exists in lotro-companion, lotro-core, lotro-dat-utils or lotro-tools (raw-URL probes on master all returned 404), and nothing states that the declaration covers every delta-* repo.
3. voicesExtractor is a separate tools/ subproject, not under extraction/sounds.

Verification was cut short when the local disk filled up (ENOSPC), so BlockMap and heightmap internals were not read.

- geo/landblocks contains BlockMapLoader, GeneratorLoader, LandblockInfoLoader, LandblockLoader, LbiInspector, LbiLink, Weenie, PropertyDescriptorsManager and MainLandblocksBuilder.

  1. uint32 DID echo
  2. uint32 flags (HAS_CELLS=1, HAS_LINKS=2, HAS_INDICES=4)
  3. uint32 size hint
  4. if HAS_LINKS: TSize count + cross-links
  5. if HAS_INDICES: TSize count + indices
  6. if HAS_CELLS: TSize count + cells
  7. uint32 count + EntityDescriptors (EntityDescLoader), for static entities
  8. uint32 count + LbiLinks
  9. a property set (DBPropertiesLoader)
  10. TSize count + Weenies
  11. an optional trailing uint32
- Parsing helpers come from dat-utils: DBPropertiesLoader, EntityDescLoader, GeoLoader and BufferUtils. TSize is dat-utils' variable-length count.

Use it as reference only, through clean-room spec extraction. Do not depend on it and do not port it.

- Documenting how gamelogic DIDs and property names map to game concepts (items, quests/achievables, skills, effects, NPCs, mobs, loot, travel, housing).
- The landblock and landblock-info DID scheme (0x80200000 + region<<16 + x<<8 + y) and the layout of landblock-info records.

label: verify:PyLotRO (Lynx3d fork; original by AJackson)
actual_description: The claim checks out. PyLotRO is a PyQt4 Linux/macOS launcher (run through Wine or CrossOver) for LOTRO and DDO. It was written by Alan Jackson ("AJackson"), built on his earlier LotROLinux and on SNy's CLI launcher. Lynx3d's copy imports the upstream history: there are 37 commits, the first dated 2009-04-08 by Alan Jackson ("0.2.0 release"), and Lynx3d's commits from 2013 add Python 3 support, certificate checks, TLS workarounds and a progress monitor. The last commit is 143b38e on 2013-11-21 ("Implement a basic progress monitor"). It has a master branch and open PRs #2-4. It is a launcher only. It does not reimplement the client, and it contains no .dat parsing, rendering or game-protocol code. The "client-reimpl" kind in the claim is wrong: it should be "launcher". The GitHub API was rate-limited, so I could not check whether GitHub marks it as a formal fork.
license: GPL-3.0-or-later
how_to_use: Use it as reference only. Pull out the protocol shapes (SOAP envelopes, XML element names, the argument-template placeholders) and write them up as a spec. Do not copy the code unless the project itself is GPL-3.0-compatible. The code is outdated (2013, Python 2/3 with PyQt4), and SSG has changed the auth endpoints since then. Treat it as a historical record of the GLS login flow. Check every detail against a maintained launcher before relying on it. The best candidate is OneLauncher (github.com/JuliusNmn/OneLauncher or its successor), which descends from PyLotRO and is GPL-3.0. It is relevant to the launcher/login front-end only, not the engine.
key_facts:
Checked against a clone at commit 143b38e.

PyLotROLauncher/PyLotROUtils.py, GetDatacenters:
- POSTs a SOAP 1.1 envelope with Content-type `text/xml; charset="UTF-8"` and SOAPAction `http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS/GetDatacenters`.
- Body is `<GetDatacenters xmlns="http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS"><game>%s</game></GetDatacenters>`.
- The response is parsed for `AuthServer`, `PatchServer` and `LauncherConfigurationServer`, plus a list of `World` elements.

World status XML:
