label: verify:Middle-earth-Revenge/DATUnpacker (LOTRO/DDO DAT unpac
actual_description:
The repo is real. I checked it with git ls-remote and a full clone (HEAD dc5fabe), and its GitHub page loads. GitHub describes it as "Mirror: Tool for extracting files from Turbine game archives". It is a public archive, read-only since 2021-02-25, created 2021-02-23 under the Middle-earth-Revenge org, with 1 star and 1 fork. It is a mirror of "DAT_UNPACKER" by "Dancing On A Rock Hacker" (2011-2012), originally hosted at https://lotrounpacker.ucoz.com; the Wayback Machine has a 2025-09 snapshot of that site. It is a small C# (.NET 4.0) Windows console app of about 1,388 lines across 5 .cs files that dumps subfiles from LOTRO/DDO .dat archives. The commit history has two commits: "initial commit" (2020-10-03, Andrew Shur) and "Add /FORMATS notes" (2020-10-09, ENDrain). So the FORMATS notes are from 2020, not 2011.

Where the claim is wrong or overstated:
(1) The tool does NOT parse the .dat container format itself. Every read goes through P/Invoke into Turbine's own proprietary DatExport.dll, which ships with the game client, plus a zlib build called "zlib1T". It contains no B-tree, block or header parsing at all.
(2) The FORMATS notes are four short, guessed pseudo-struct text files with many "unknown" fields. They do not document the formats thoroughly.
(3) The type-range labels 0x19/0x25/0x28/0x40 are correct.
(4) "C#" and "GPL-3.0" are correct. GitHub detects the license as GPL-3.0 from LICENSE, which is the full GPLv3 text. COPYING.txt and the file headers say "GPL v3 or (at your option) any later version", so the precise SPDX identifier is GPL-3.0-or-later.
license: GPL-3.0-or-later
how_to_use:
Use as a reference only, for clean-room facts. Do not depend on it and do not port it.

Why:
(a) The code is GPL-3.0-or-later. Copying it would force our project to use a GPL-compatible license.
(b) It is Windows-only and calls Turbine's proprietary DatExport.dll. A clean-room reimplementation must not depend on that DLL or redistribute it, so the code has no use as a library for us.
(c) The value is in the facts, which are not copyrightable and can be put into our own spec:
- the DatExport.dll API surface, which tells us the container's logical model (subfile DID, size, iteration, version, compression flag; master map; block size; dat/game-data version numbers; datIdStamp; firstIterGuid)
- the compression wrapper (a 4-byte length prefix, then a zlib stream)
- how DID prefixes map to categories, and where the payload header starts in each
- the rough layouts in the 0x19/0x25/0x28/0x40 notes

Check each fact against newer, actively maintained parsers before relying on it; this tool is 2011-era, and later DAT format changes are not reflected. For example, check the native DAT readers in LotroCompanion/lotro-tools, or other Middle-earth-Revenge repos such as LocalDataExtractor, which the org page lists.

Do not use it for parsing the DAT container itself. That has to come from another source or our own clean-room analysis of user-supplied files.
key_facts:
Taken from the source itself (LOTRO_UNPACKER/DatExport.cs, DatFile.cs, Subfile.cs, Program.cs, FORMATS/*.txt):

1. Container access is entirely through Turbine's DatExport.dll. Exported functions it uses:
- OpenDatFileEx2(handle, fileName, flags, out didMasterMap, out blockSize, out vnumDatFile, out vnumGameData, out ulong datFileID, char* datIdStamp[0x40], char* firstIterGuid[0x40])
- GetNumSubfiles
- GetSubfileSizes(handle, out did, out size, out iteration, index, count)
- GetSubfileVersion(handle, did)
- GetSubfileCompressionFlag(handle, did), which returns a byte; 1 means compressed
- GetSubfileData(handle, did, buf, writeOffset, out version)
- CloseDatFile
Open flags (Dcof*): UseLRU=1, Expandable=2, ReadOnly=4, Create=8, CreateIfNeeded=0x10, OptionalFile=0x20, FreeThreaded=0x40, LoadIterations=0x80, Journalled=0x100, SkipIndexCheck=0x200. The tool opens with 130 (0x82 = Expandable|LoadIterations), adding 4 for read-only. A handle table of 0x40 slots is allocated.

2. Compressed subfiles: the first 4 bytes are the decompressed length (uint32, little-endian), and the rest is a zlib stream passed to zlib uncompress().

3. Payload type is chosen by the first 3 hex digits of the 8-hex-digit DID:
- 0x0A0xxxxx (sound): 8-byte header, then a RIFF (.wav) or OggS (.ogg) payload.
- 0x040xxxxx: if bytes 8..11 are 57 E0 E0 57 ("WaaW"), it is a Havok .hkx payload starting at offset 8.
- 0x050xxxxx: the same WaaW magic at offset 17; the payload starts at 17.
- 0x410xxxxx / 0x411xxxxx (textures/images):
  - JPEG if FF D8 FF appears at offset 24 (24-byte header).
  - "DXT1"/"DXT3"/"DXT5" FourCC at offset 16: width/height uint32s at offsets 8 and 12. DXT1 data starts at 16, DXT3/5 at 24. The tool builds its own 128-byte DDS header.
  - Otherwise uncompressed: 24-byte header, written out as a 24bpp DDS (RGBBitCount 0x18) with masks FF0000/00FF00/0000FF.
- Everything else is written as .bin.

4. FORMATS notes (community guesses):
- 0x19xxxxxx: masterFileID, record count. Each record: index, a len-prefixed group_name, recordID, link to 0x40xxxxxx, type1, type2, link to 0x42xxxxxx, type3, type4, 15 unknown bytes, link to 0x78xxxxxx, then more unknowns, ending with 0xFFFFFFFF.
- 0x25xxxxxx (string tables): masterFileID, dword 1, type byte, then a count (byte, or a 2-byte count if the high bit 0x80 is set). Each entry: qword hash, then nested counts of UTF-16 strings with the same variable-length length prefix, plus dword arrays.
- 0x28xxxxxx: masterFileID, then repeated (type, varcount, [index, fileID] pairs) and (type, varcount, [index, len-prefixed ASCII description]).
- 0x40xxxxxx: masterFileID, type byte, count (forced to 6 when type==4), word + byte unknowns, count dwords linking to 0x41xxxxxx (textures), then 0x00, 0x0F.

5. Output layout: data\<name>\<c1>XXXXXXX\<c1c2>XXXXXX\<c1c2c3>XXXXX\<DID>.<ext>. An incremental dictionary.bin stores (int32 DID, int32 version) pairs so unchanged subfiles are skipped.

6. CLI: DAT_UNPACKER.exe <file> <flags> <hex_did>. Flags: wav=1, ogg=2, jpg=4, dds=8, hks=16, raw/bin=256, single file=512, list only=1024. Default is 271.
language: C# (.NET Framework 4.0, Windows-only; P/Invoke to native DatExport.dll and zlib1T)
last_activity: Last commit 2020-10-09 (dc5fabe "Add /FORMATS notes" by ENDrain); repo created 2021-02-23 and archived 2021-02-25; original tool dates from 2011-2012

key_facts:
DatExport.cs: P/Invoke signatures for Turbine's datexport.dll:
- int OpenDatFileEx2(int handle, string fileName, uint flags, out int didMasterMap, out int blockSize, out int vnumDatFile, out int vnumGameData, out ulong datFileID, StringBuilder datIdStamp, StringBuilder firstIterGuid)
- void CloseDatFile(int handle)
- int GetNumSubfiles(int handle)
- void GetSubfileSizes(int handle, out int did, out int size, out int iteration, int offset, int count)
- int GetSubfileVersion(int handle, int did)
- byte GetSubfileCompressionFlag(int handle, int id)
- int GetSubfileData(int handle, int did, IntPtr buffer, int writeOffset, out int version)
- zlib1T.dll: int uncompress(byte[] dest, ref int destLen, byte[] src, int srcLen), the standard zlib uncompress

Dcof open flags: UseLRU=0x1, Expandable=0x2, ReadOnly=0x4, Create=0x8, CreateIfNeeded=0x10, OptionalFile=0x20, FreeThreaded=0x40, LoadIterations=0x80, Journalled=0x100, SkipIndexCheck=0x200.

DatFile.cs: opens with flags = 130 (0x82 = Expandable|LoadIterations), ORed with 4 (ReadOnly) for read-only access. Handles come from a static pool of 64. Subfiles go into a dictionary keyed by DataID.

Subfile.cs GetExtension(): sniffs the type from the DID-prefix category plus magic bytes:
- category "0A0": RIFF at offset 8 gives .wav, OggS at offset 8 gives .ogg. So sound subfiles carry an 8-byte header before the payload.
- "040": "WaaW" (57 E0 E0 57) Havok signature at offset 8; "050": same signature at offset 17.
- "410"/"411": FF D8 FF at offset 24 gives .jpg (24-byte texture header).
- Other textures: the tool builds a 128-byte "DDS " header for DXT1, DXT3, DXT5 or uncompressed data, with width and height taken from buffer offsets 8-15.
- Anything unrecognised gets .bin.

FORMATS notes (pseudo-structs):
- 0x19XXXXXX: masterFileID dword, record count dword, then records of index dword, name length byte, name string, record ID, dword links to 40/42/78XXXXXX, type1-4 dwords, terminated by 0xFFFFFFFF.
- 0x25XXXXXX (string table / localized text): masterFileID dword, version 0x01 dword, type byte, then a variable-length count (byte, or word if the first byte & 0x80). Each entry is a qword hash followed by count1/count2 loops of length-prefixed UTF-16 strings (char[len*2]) and count3/count4 loops of dwords.
- 0x28XXXXXX: masterFileID, then repeated {type1 byte, varcount, (index dword, fileID dword)*} and {type2 byte, varcount, (index dword, len byte, char[len] description)*}.
- 0x40XXXXXX: masterFileID dword, type byte, record count byte (6 when type == 4), unknown word and byte, a loop of dword links to 41XXXXXX, and two terminator dwords (0x00 and 0x0F).
- Variable-length count rule: if the first byte has 0x80 set, the count is a word.

actual_description: This is a real GitHub fork of NeuralFoundry/lotro-freecam-toolkit. It is a Frida-based JavaScript injection script that gives the live LOTRO 64-bit client a free-flying "freecam". It reuses the client's own FlightCameraController, the camera used for cinematics, and has a "cinematic" build that hooks and patches engine globals to raise terrain and grass draw distance and adds a GDI overlay. The mirror is an older snapshot. It has 5 commits, all by NeuralFoundry and all dated Jul 18, 2026: "Initial commit", "Add files via upload" and several "Update README.md". It holds only README.md, lotro_freecam_minimal.js (about 300 lines) and lotro_freecam_cinematic.js (about 5,000 lines, 228 KB). Upstream has since grown to about 18 commits plus .bat/.ps1 launchers. It supports builds 4808/4900/4901/4902/4905 (latest 4905.0070.9961.4022, checked against an EXE dated 2026-09-05). The mirror README targets only build 4808.0070.7360.4034. So the claim ("mirror of the freecam, older revision", JavaScript) is accurate. Caveat: git ls-remote/clone could not be run because the local disk was full (ENOSPC), and the GitHub API returned 403. Verification is from the github.com HTML pages and the raw README.
license: none/unknown — there is no SPDX license. The README has a custom permissive statement: "Do what you want with it. Credit is appreciated but not required, and there is no warranty of any kind. Provided as-is for personal use." It reads like a public-domain grant but is legally vague. key_facts:
The facts come from the mirror README, which targets lotroclient64.exe build 4808.0070.7360.4034 (module size 0x22b4000). The script checks the module size and refuses to run on any other build.
- Camera: the client has a FlightCameraController that cinematics use. Ctrl+F8 pushes it onto a camera stack, which returns a token. Movement uses three per-frame axis functions (forward, strafe, vertical) scaled by frame time. The avatar stays still, so nothing is sent to the server. This confirms a stack-based camera-controller design.
- World streaming: the world is split into landblocks of 160 world units, each split into 16 sectors. The high-detail ring defaults to 224 sectors (14 landblocks) and the medium band to 384 sectors (24 landblocks). Distant terrain uses 2D imposters at the lowest LOD. Grass streams 16 landblocks in each direction (a 33x33 grid, 1,089 landblocks). The streaming pipeline has land sources (3x3 source groups), landscape-provider surfaces/requests, and radius-based residency/eviction.
- Settings globals: build-specific addresses for texture filtering and anisotropy, draw distance, imposters, frill (grass) quality, shadows, lighting, normal maps, and the StaticPVS and AllowLODs flags. A residency limit sits at 0x995a16.
- Hooks: main game tick 0x971df0 (0x974b20 / 0x974ee0 in other builds), mip bias 0x860ff0, provider completion 0x4fe890, camera input 0x973b00, frill centre update 0x956470.
- Overlay: a separate layered Win32 GDI window, with no D3D hooking.

Reference-only, and only at the level of architecture facts. Do not depend on it and do not port it. It is a runtime memory-injection tool for the proprietary client. It hardcodes addresses taken from the copyrighted binary, and its own README says Frida injection violates the LOTRO ToS. Copying its offsets or hooking approach does nothing for a clean-room reimplementation and could taint it legally. Do not have clean-room implementers read the JS source.

The README's high-level facts are a useful independent cross-check for our own design, recorded as "observed behaviour" notes. Those facts are: 160-unit landblocks with 16 sectors, the default streaming radii, the 33x33 grass grid, imposter LOD for distant terrain, and a stack of camera controllers that includes a flight or cinematic camera. They should be confirmed against .dat-format work such as LotroCompanion/lotro-tools/dat parsing.

If we cite it at all, prefer the upstream NeuralFoundry/lotro-freecam-toolkit, which is more current. This mirror is an older 5-commit snapshot and adds nothing over upstream. label: verify:Middle-earth-Revenge mirror of lotro-server
actual_description: The repo is real. I confirmed it with git ls-remote (HEAD 5ce7a7a, branch master) and a full clone. It is a small, abandoned C# research server from the "Middle-earth Revenge" community, which calls itself "LOTRO-Tools", and it only gets as far as the login screen. It has 59 commits: 51 by bwgypyth, 8 by Ananta Das. Work started 2013-03-02, GitLab-style merge requests run through 2015, and the last commit is 2020-03-02, which ported it to .NET Core and replaced the checksum code with a stub. The repo contains 98 .cs files in these projects: Server (a UDP listener with session, setup and packet handlers), Protocol (packet classes named after their hex opcodes, e.g. Header/_06_43, Data/_00_01_D6_80, plus session-setup classes Synchronize/SYNACK/Acknowledgment/OldClientVersion), liblotro (big-endian reader/writer, Encrypt/Decrypt, a stubbed Checksum, and RSA in HelperMethods), Account, Client, Settings, PacketBrowser (a WPF tool for viewing packets), packet capture with automatic decryption (SharpPcap/WinPcap), and LOTROendecrypt tools. It also includes a 2013 PDF called "LOTRO-Investigation v0.2 (Riders)" by tAmMo, which analyses the packets. The 2013 changelog says the server got the client to the character-creation screen and could sometimes create a pseudo-character. The claim calls this a "mirror (preservation)". I could not confirm that: the GitLab origin URLs I tried either require login or do not exist. The 2015 commits named "Merge branch 'master' into 'master'" do suggest it was once hosted on GitLab.
license: none/unknown
how_to_use:
Use it as reference only, and only at the level of protocol facts. Do not copy or port any code or data from it. The reasons:
(1) It has no license. There is no LICENSE file, and the AssemblyInfo files say "Copyright © 2013-2020 bwgypyth", so legally all rights are reserved.
(2) It contains material taken directly from the game client. Helper/data/table_jump_client_raw and table_lookup_client_raw are about 256 KB each, and Decrypt.cs says they were dumped from the running client's memory. The README says the client was patched to inject a generated RSA public key, and HelperMethods.cs comments refer to a "private key extracted from the client".
(3) Some code looks decompiled. Decrypt.cs has a method called method_0, the naming style of a .NET deobfuscator, which suggests it came from a disassembled Helper.dll. A prebuilt Helper.dll is also committed.
(4) It is a server, not a client, it is stuck at the 2013 Riders-of-Rohan protocol, and its checksum code is now a stub.
For a clean-room project, a separate person should read the PDF and the packet layouts and write a plain-language protocol spec for the client's networking layer. Nobody should look at or reuse the lookup tables, the key handling or the Helper.dll logic. The packet-capture and PacketBrowser tools are a reasonable model for building our own tool to inspect captured packets.
key_facts:
- Transport is UDP. The listen port is set in config (Settings/Config.cs has ServerPort and WorldServerPort; no default port was checked).
- The packet header is big-endian, 0x14 bytes by default (Protocol/Generic/PayloadHeader.cs), in this order: u16 SessionID, u16 DataLength, 4-byte Action/flags, u32 SequenceNumber, u32 Checksum, u32 ACKNR. The constant 0xBADD70DD is used as a default value.
- The session handshake goes Synchronize (client) -> SYNACK -> Acknowledgment. The server compares the client's version string with RequiredClientVersion and sends OldClientVersion if they differ. Other server messages: ConfirmSequence, TerminateServer, WrongGLSTicket, DoubleLoginNOK. Data objects include NoGLSTicketDirect, AccountName/EncAccountName, ServerName, CharaData, BadCharaName and ClientIP. GLS is the login-ticket service.
- Encryption: per the 2013 PDF, the first two client packets and the first server packet are unencrypted, and encryption starts at the second server packet. Decrypt.cs processes the payload in 4-byte blocks, with the first block starting at offset 4, using separate jump and lookup tables for client and server.
- Key exchange: the session key is RSA-encrypted with the server's public key and decrypted by the server with RSACryptoServiceProvider.ImportCspBlob/Decrypt (HelperMethods.cs line ~265). The real key was replaced by a patched-in key.
- Packet checksums are made from a header part and a data part, using a checksum table that is updated as packets go by (only the function signatures remain in liblotro/Checksum.cs).
- Changelog todos mention retransmitting missed packets and handling pings. Without them the client disconnects or crashes, so reliable sequencing with ACKs is required.
- Files: ~/.cache/tessera/clones/mer-lotro-server (see README.md, CHANGELOG.txt, LOTRO-Investigation.pdf, liblotro/, Protocol/).
language: C# (.NET Core after the 2020 port; earlier .NET Framework/WPF)
last_activity: 2020-03-02 (last commit 5ce7a7a, "Rename README.txt to README.md"); substantive work 2013–2015

key_facts:
DAT container (datfile.py):
- Header magic: u32 at 0x101 == 0x4C50 ("PL"); u32 at 0x140 == 0x5442 ("BT").
- Header fields: block_size @0x144, file size @0x148, version @0x14C, root directory offset @0x160.

Directory B-tree node:
- 8 zero bytes, then up to 62 (blockSize:u32, dirOffset:u32) subdir pairs. A zero size ends the list.
- Entry count is a u32 at node+8*63 (0x1F8). Subdirs are truncated to count+1.
- Then count entries of 0x20 bytes each: unk1 (low u16 = flags, bit0 = compressed; high u16 = policy), file_id (DID), file offset, size1, timestamp, version, size2 (block size), unk2.
- Lookup is a standard B-tree descent by DID.

File content:
- At the file offset: [numExtraBlocks:u32][legacy:u32, must be 0]. The first chunk is blockSize-8-numExtra*8 bytes, followed by a table of numExtra (size:u32, offset:u32) pairs pointing to further blocks.
- If flags&1, the content is zlib(raw[4:]), where raw[0:4] is the uncompressed size.
- Content starts with its own DID as a u32 LE.
- An alternative asset record layout [next:4][pad:4][usize:4][zlib body] is used for mesh and other assets.
- DatChain handles client_mesh.dat plus client_mesh_aux_N.datx.

PropertiesSet (propset.py):
- The property dictionary is the master-property DID 0x34000000 in client_gamelogic.dat.
- Resource = u32 DID; TSize count; then property entries of pid:u32 (plus a duplicate pid when doublePid), each followed by a value typed by the dictionary.
- Type codes: STRING=1 (VLE len + ISO-8859-1), STRING_TOKEN=2, WAVE_FORM=3, TIMESTAMP=4 (f64), TRI_STATE=5, VECTOR=6 (3*f32), INSTANCE_ID=7 (u64), ENUM_MAPPER=8, FLOAT=9, PROPERTY_ID=10, STRUCT=11 (u8 skip + u8 nbFields, then doublePid props), ARRAY=12 (u32 n, then single-pid props), STRING_INFO=13, BITFIELD_64=14, INT=15, COLOR=16 (4*u8 on disk; 4*f32 RGBA in memory), POSITION=17, BIT_FIELD32=18, LONG64=19, DATA_FILE=20 (DID), BOOLEAN=21, BIT_FIELD=22 (VLE bitcount + bytes).
- VLE: if b==0xE0, read u32; if b<0x80, the value is b; otherwise read b2. If (b&0x40)==0 the value is b2|(b&0x7F)<<8; otherwise read c=u16 and the value is (b&0x3F)<<24|b2<<16|c.
- TSize = skip 1 byte, then VLE.

WLib (wlib.py, DID 0x56000000 in client_gamelogic.dat):
- Header: u32 DID, u32 stopCode, u32 version (30, 36 or 38). Version 38 has one extra u32; version 36 skips 16 bytes.
- Body is a run of chunks: fourcc 0xB8C577F4, typecode, size, payload.
- Typecode 16 = CLASS_DEFS: per class, isDefined u8, class_index u16, pair_count u16, raw_size u32, the pairs, then VLE-counted refs, offsets and offset indices.
- Typecode 512 = CLASS_VARS: TSize num_classes; per class, class_index u32, TSize nvars, then (name_hash u32, slot u16, typeCode u8) per var.
- Typecode 1024 = PARENTS_MAP: u32 len, then parent indices.
- WSL type codes: 1=REFERENCE, 2=INT, 3=FLOAT, 130=LONG, 131=SIGNED_DOUBLE, 195=DOUBLE.
- Instance buffers hold only the class's own attributes, in slot order, not flattened with inherited ones.
- Class names come from resources/classes.xml (e.g. class 1654 = PlayerAvatar). Attribute names come from resources/StringHashMap.txt (hash to name, JSON). Both were copied verbatim from LOTRO Companion's delta-lotro-dat-utils-11.11.jar (Apache-2.0, Damien Morcellet).

Native package IDs (in memory):
- 166 PropertiesSet, 52 DBProperties, 39 single property, 225 UTF-16 string, 199 StringInfo, 160 Position, 57 dynamic bitset.
- Arrays: 17 (int32), 176 (DataRef int32), 104 (u64).

Appearance properties:
- AC_Color_* (COLOR), AC_Texture_*, AC_BoneScale_Test, AC_Avatar_Height, AC_Mesh_Head.
- AC_BoneSlider_Value_Array: a hex-string with one byte per slider, where 0x80 is neutral.
- Appearance_InstanceList: an array of Appearance_KeyInfo structs.

Provenance and accuracy:
- propset.py's docstring says it was "Ported byte-for-byte from dmorcellet's closed delta-lotro-dat-utils-11.11.jar (decompiled with CFR)". This contradicts resources.md and NOTICE, which say "no decompiled code was copied".
- The memory-model and native-package content describes the live process (lotroclient64.exe), not the on-disk formats.
- Upstream public LotroCompanion repos exist (github.com/LotroCompanion/lotro-companion, lotro-tools). dmorcellet/lotro-dat-utils is not public under that name.
how_to_use:
Use as reference only, and treat it as a secondary source. Do not depend on it or port it wholesale.

The on-disk format facts are useful to cross-check our own clean-room DAT, PropertiesSet and WLib readers: the DAT B-tree and block layout, the VLE/TSize encoding, the PropertiesSet type table, and the WLib chunk format at 0x56000000. Re-derive and verify each of them against real .dat files and the primary upstream source (the LOTRO Companion / dmorcellet projects, which are Apache-2.0).

Cautions:
- By its own admission the code is a near-literal port of CFR-decompiled Companion jars. That is license-compatible, since Apache-2.0 permits derivatives with attribution, but it is not independent work, and it adds no authority beyond Companion itself. Cite Companion as the origin.
- The repo is tiny, two days old and entirely AI-authored. Each fact needs empirical verification.
- The memory-scraping half (memory-model.md, native-packages.md, discovery/, lotro_mem*.py) reads a running proprietary client's process memory. It is off-mission for a reimplementation and potentially a ToS concern. Use it at most as hints about the runtime object model; do not incorporate it.
- The bundled classes.xml and StringHashMap.txt are Apache-2.0 Companion resources. They can be redistributed with attribution and the NOTICE, but it is preferable to have users extract them from their own install, or to regenerate them ourselves.

label: verify:lotro_extractor (Mirarkitty)
actual_description: A Python tool, Linux and Wine only, that reads a running LOTRO client's memory (/proc/<pid>/mem, the Linux equivalent of ReadProcessMemory, through a privileged helper lotro_memread.py set up by install_helper.sh). It pulls out character quests, deeds, outfits, money, reputation and appearance, and can optionally write LOTRO Companion status and character files. It also includes a small dat reader (datfile.py), a WLib parser (wlib.py), PropertiesSet and WSL decoders, and 12 Markdown docs: memory-model, wlib, native-packages, appearance, discovery, pipeline and others. The claim is accurate: the memory model, WLib DID 0x56000000, property registry DID 0x34000000, VLE/TSize and appearance parameters are all documented there. Caveats: the repo is very young, with 6 commits made on 1–2 Aug 2026. GitHub lists Claude (an AI) as the author of every commit. It is a one-person, AI-assisted project with no track record. Its dat and resource knowledge comes from Damien Morcellet's LOTRO Companion / delta-lotro-dat-utils: datfile.py refers to "dmorcellet's DATArchive.loadEntry", and resources/classes.xml and StringHashMap.txt are copied unchanged from delta-lotro-dat-utils-11.11.jar, under Apache-2.0 with NOTICE attribution. Verified by WebFetch of the repo page, the docs/ tree, the raw docs, LICENSE and the commit history. Bash was unavailable (ENOSPC on the host), so I did not clone the repo or run its code.
license: Apache-2.0
last_activity: 2026-08-02 (6 commits total, 2026-08-01..02; author shown as Claude)
key_facts:
DAT container (datfile.py): 2048-byte header. Magic 0x4C50 at 0x101, BT magic 0x5442 at 0x140, blockSize at 0x144, fileSize at 0x148, version at 0x14C, root directory offset at 0x160. A directory node has an 8-byte zero prefix, then 62 (blockSize u32, dirOffset u32) subdirectory pairs, then the entry count u32 at 0x1F8, then file entries of 8 u32 each: [unk1 flags/policy][file_id][offset][size1][timestamp][version][size2][unk2]. Compression flag is (unk1&0xFFFF)&1. File data is a block chain: header [numExtraBlocks u32][legacy u32]; first chunk = blockSize-8-numExtraBlocks*8; extra blocks are (size, offset) pairs. Compressed files are zlib with a 4-byte uncompressed-size prefix (zlib magic 0x78 01/9C/DA).
WLib (client_gamelogic.dat DID 0x56000000): header u32 selfDID, u32 stopCode, u32 version (30, 36 or 38; v38 has +1 u32, v36 has +16 bytes). Chunks repeat: u32 fourcc 0xB8C577F4, u32 typecode, u32 size, payload. A fourcc equal to stopCode skips 1 byte. Chunk typecodes: 16=CLASS_DEFS, 512=CLASS_VARS, 1024=PARENTS_MAP. CLASS_DEFS entry: u8 isDefined, u16 classIndex, u16 pairCount, u32 rawSize, pairs of (u32 default, u32 typeCode), then vle-counted u16 refs, u32 offsets, i16 offidx. CLASS_VARS: tsize numClasses; per class u32 classIndex, tsize numVars; per var u32 nameHash, u16 slot, u8 typeCode. PARENTS_MAP: u32 len, then u32 parentIndex per class. Value types: 1 REFERENCE, 2 INTEGER, 3 FLOAT, 130 LONG, 131 SIGNED_DOUBLE, 195 DOUBLE.
VLE: 0xE0 escapes to an explicit u32; high bit clear = 1 byte; bit 6 clear = 2 bytes; otherwise the 3.5-byte form. tsize = skip 1 byte, then vle.
Property registry DID 0x34000000 (27268 entries). In-memory property type codes: 1 STRING, 4 TIMESTAMP(f64), 6 VECTOR(3f32), 7 INSTANCE_ID(u64), 8 ENUM_MAPPER, 9 FLOAT, 10 PROPERTY_ID, 11 STRUCT, 12 ARRAY, 13 STRING_INFO, 14 BITFIELD_64, 15 INT, 16 COLOR(4f32 RGBA), 18 BIT_FIELD32, 19 LONG64, 20 DATA_FILE, 21 BOOLEAN.
Native package IDs: 166 PropertiesSet, 52 DBProperties, 39 single property, 225 UTF-16 string, 199 StringInfo, 17/176/104 arrays, 25/182/111 lists, 11/35/23/117/97/18/105/138/134 hashes, 13/37 multi-hashes.
WSL slot encoding: 4-byte value (or 12 bytes for LONG/DOUBLE, split low/typecode/high) plus a trailing 4-byte typecode.
Client memory layout (build 4901.0070.8449.4010, x64, base 0x140000000; only useful for that build): entities hash with 24-byte buckets; world entity +192 is the property provider; provider +56 is the hash; property entries are 32 bytes. References table has 32-byte entries (bitfield, factoryInfo, wslPackage, nativePackage); 0x10000000 is the native flag; values >= 0x70000000 are literal DIDs.
Appearance properties: AC_Color_Skin/Hair/Eyes/Lips/WarPaint (COLOR); AC_Texture_* indexes; AC_Avatar_Height; AC_BoneScale_Test; AC_Mesh_Head (q = style/100). AC_BoneSlider_Value_Array is a hex-string with one byte per slider, 0x80 = centre. Appearance_InstanceList slots: head 0x10000009, hair 0x10000032, beard 0x10000018.
how_to_use: Use it as a reference only; do not depend on it. Its value to a reimplementation is the format documentation for the WLib class-metadata container (0x56000000), the VLE/TSize encoding, the property type codes and registry (0x34000000), the WSL slot and native package encodings, and the appearance property semantics (needed to rebuild characters in a client). Read these as specs, cross-check them against real dat files, and write our own implementation. The Apache-2.0 license would allow porting the small datfile.py and wlib.py parsers with NOTICE attribution. But the code is AI-generated, 2 months old and unproven, and the real source of this knowledge is Damien Morcellet's LOTRO Companion / delta-lotro-dat-utils (dmorcellet on GitHub), so treat that as the primary reference and this repo as a second, independent write-up. Do NOT bundle resources/classes.xml or StringHashMap.txt; extract them at runtime from the user's own Companion install or regenerate them from the dat files. Do not use the live-process memory-reading approach (privileged /proc/<pid>/mem reads, signature scanning, build-specific offsets) in the project. A reimplemented client never runs the original binary. Reading the live client's memory likely breaks SSG's ToS/EULA, and the struct offsets are runtime artifacts of the copyrighted binary that a clean-room design should not copy. Use them at most to understand data semantics, never as an implementation template.

label: verify:Mirarkitty/lotro_mesh_viewer
actual_description:
The repo exists. I confirmed it with git ls-remote (HEAD a896ebb6, branch main) and a full clone with 21 commits, dated 2026-08-01 to 2026-08-02. The author field on every commit is "claude", so the code and docs were largely written with an AI assistant. The last commit is "Sync weapons follow-ups: hip stowing, worn class items, held search+dye".

It is a Python toolkit that reads the LOTRO client_*.dat archives directly, plus a local three.js/Flask viewer and an outfit composer. The files include datfile.py, mesh_decode.py, tex_extract.py, shaders.py, propset.py, selector.py, wearable2.py, compose.py, weapon_resolve.py, charparts.py, havok_anim.py, export_skinned.py, items_catalog.py, explore.py, app.py, outfit_app.py, index.html, anim.html and outfit.html. There are about 3,000 lines of byte-level docs in docs/: dat-format, mesh-format, textures, shaders, properties, wardrobe, weapons, dyes, hair-face, animation and limitations, plus per-script docs. Some stray .orig backup files are committed. No game assets are included apart from a few documentation screenshots.

Every topic in the claim is covered in the docs and code. One claim is false: it says it is "the first published LOTRO mesh decoder". gitlab.com/kilves/lotro-mesh-converter is a Rust tool (MIT, 2023-03-04) that already converted unpacked 0x06 meshes to GLB, without bones. The repo's README only compares itself to jtauber/lotro, which has no mesh parser.
license: GPL-3.0-only for the repository as a whole. Every file except havok_anim.py is also available under MIT (LICENSE.MIT, "Copyright (c) 2026 the lotro_mesh_viewer authors"). havok_anim.py is GPL-3.0-only because it ports PredatorCZ/HavokLib's spline decompressor. The claim's license statement is accurate.
how_to_use:
Use the docs as a spec and port the MIT parts. Do not take it on as a runtime dependency: it is Python research code, and the mesh decoding relies on guessing the layout rather than reading defined fields.

1. The docs in docs/*.md are written to let someone re-implement the formats without the code. Use them to write a clean-room format spec for the C++/Rust engine: the DAT container, GfxObj, the surface/material/texture chain, wardrobe records, PropertiesSets, held items, dyes and the skin-stride table.

2. Every file except havok_anim.py is MIT, so porting logic from them is legally fine. Keep the copyright notice and track where each piece came from.

3. Do not copy or port havok_anim.py. It is GPLv3 because it comes from HavokLib, and porting it would make our engine GPL. Either accept GPL for that module only, or write a fresh decoder from public hkaSplineCompressedAnimation descriptions. The tagfile layout can come from exyorha/hkxparse; check that repo's license first.

4. Treat the findings as provisional. The authors' own limitations.md lists several "solved" claims that turned out wrong. The stride and index-region detection is guesswork rather than a decoded field. Several parts are self-rated: animation is "mostly working", and weapon attach transforms are hand-tuned rather than read from client data. All of it was produced with AI assistance by one pseudonymous author. Check every fact against real .dat files with our own tests.

5. For better coverage, cross-check against kilves/lotro-mesh-converter (MIT, Rust) and jtauber/lotro.
key_facts:
All of the following was read from the repo's docs and source.

**DAT container header**
- 0x101 = "PL" magic; 0x140 = "BT" magic
- 0x144 = block_size (0x4400)
- 0x148 = file size
- 0x14C = version
- 0x160 = root directory offset

**B-tree directory**
- Each node is: 8 zero bytes, then up to 62 (size, offset) subdir pointers.
- At node + 8*63 comes a u32 entry count.
- Each entry is 0x20 bytes: unk1 (flags u16 | policy u16), file_id, file_offset, size1, timestamp, version, size2, unk2.
- flags & 1 means the entry is zlib-compressed.
- Lookup is a standard B-tree search.

**Reading records**
- Mesh and texture records are stored contiguously. Their framing is [next-ptr 0][pad 0][u32 uncompressed_size][zlib stream from offset 12].
- The general reader (read_content, after dmorcellet's DATArchive.loadEntry) starts with a [numExtraBlocks][legacy] header. The first chunk is min(block_size - 8 - n*8, size1) bytes, followed by a table of (size, offset) extra runs.
- For compressed entries, raw[0:4] is the uncompressed size, then the zlib data. Content starts with the record's own DID.
- Some content lives only in the .datx auxiliary archives (e.g. client_mesh_aux_1.datx), so lookups must check both.

**DID type map (high byte = type)**
- 0x06: GfxObj meshes, about 39.8k, in client_mesh.dat
- 0x05: Havok animation clips, about 25.4k, in client_anim.dat
- In client_general.dat:
  - 0x01: Setup records (about 1k)
  - 0x20: worn-appearance records (about 4.2k)
  - 0x2B: compiled HLSL shader instances (about 400)
  - 0x30: materials (about 24k)
  - 0x31: surfaces (about 13.7k)
  - 0x40: texture mip-chains (about 80k)
  - 0x1F: held-item templates (about 29k)
  - 0x04: Havok hkaSkeleton records (about 28.5k)
- 0x41: DXT textures, in client_surface.dat and client_highres.dat
- In client_gamelogic.dat:
  - 0x70: items; each has a PropertiesSet at 0x79 = 0x70 + 0x09000000
  - 0x34000000: the property dictionary
  - 0x47: chargen records and PhysObj entities
  - 0x0C: other game entities

**GfxObj mesh (0x06)**
- Header: Id, Flags (0x1 = static, 0x1000____ = skinned), [S][S x 0x31 surface DIDs], [T][T x 0x30 material DIDs].
- Each submesh: u32 vertexCount, then vertices at a fixed stride, then a float bbox[6], then [boneDataCount][u32 bone data].
- After all submeshes comes a separate index region: per submesh, u32 indexCount followed by u16 submesh-local indices.
- Each vertex starts with pos f32[3] and normal f32[3]. UV is always at offset 24.
- Strides range from 44 to 264. Different submeshes in one mesh can use different strides. There is no stride field, so it is detected by scanning for unit-length normals.
- Data is not aligned to 4 bytes. Meshes are Z-up.
- Skin tail layout by stride (influences / index offset / weight offset). Bone indices are u8, weights are f32.

| Stride | Influences | Index offset | Weight offset |
|---|---|---|---|
| 61 | 1 | 56 | 57 |
| 65 | 1 | 60 | 61 |
| 66 | 2 | 56 | 58 |
| 70 | 2 | 60 | 62 |
| 71 | 3 | 56 | 59 |
| 73 | 1 | 68 | 69 |
| 74 | 2 | 64 | 66 |
| 75 | 3 | 60 | 63 |
| 76 | 4 | 56 | 60 |
| 79 | 3 | 64 | 67 |
| 80 | 4 | 60 | 64 |
| 84 | 4 | 64 | 68 |

**Surfaces and materials**
- A 0x31 surface is 22 bytes: [self][0x2B shader][slot key 0x10000050][u32 1][0x30 material][u16 1].
- A 0x30 material has slots of the form {slotId, slotId2, type=4, 0x40 DID, ...}. The first 0x40 slot is the diffuse texture.
- A 0x40 record is an ordered list of 0x41 DIDs, one per resolution.
- 0x41 textures: find the "DXTn" fourcc. Width and height are the 8 bytes just before it, and block data starts at fourcc + 8. Validate by exact size.

**Item appearance**
- Garments: item, then its PropertiesSet, then Item_WornAppearanceMapList keyed by (species, sex), giving an AppearanceKey and a 0x20 DID. The 0x20 entry whose key matches gives the mesh 0x06 and material 0x30.
- Held items: the PhysObj property gives a 0x47 record [classTag][self][7][template].
  - The template can be another 0x47; the code follows up to 8 hops.
  - The template is a 0x1F record whose last u32 is a 0x04 DID.
  - That 0x04 record ends with a trailer [u8 count][count x u32 0x06 mesh DIDs].

**Dyes**
- Each dye is a single scalar floatCode (about 0.01 to 0.80; 99.0 means "Unique"). The values come from LotroCompanion lotro-data lore/colors.xml.
- Render rule: final = alpha < 128 ? tex.rgb * dyeRGB : tex.rgb.

**Havok animation and skeletons**
- 0x04 skeletons and 0x05 clips are Havok binary tagfiles, not packfiles. Magic is 0xCAB00D1E 0xD011FACE, tagfile version 3.
- 0x05 records have a 13-byte prefix: f32 duration, u32 track count (doc) or constant 0x2C (code docstring), u8 0, u32 tagfile size + 1.
- Clips use hkaSplineCompressedAnimation. Tracks map to bones by position.

**Credits the repo gives**
- ACE GfxObj parsers, jtauber/lotro, LotroCompanion / dmorcellet lotro-dat-utils, HavokLib, hkxparse.
language: Python (numpy, Pillow, optional Flask), with HTML/JS three.js viewers

label: verify:Endevir/DatExplorer (Mogwai.DDO.Explorer)
actual_description: The repo exists. Endevir/DatExplorer is a GitHub fork of Mogwai-TheFurry/DatExplorer, which is the upstream and the URL to cite. Both have the same HEAD, 748ecee1 ("move to AGPL", 2018-01-23), with about 12 commits upstream. It is a small, unfinished Windows Forms C# explorer for DDO .dat files, solution Mogwai.DDO.Explorer.sln. It has three projects: a core library, a WinForms UI and tests. It walks the directory tree, lists files with id, offset, size, timestamp and flags, decompresses zlib entries with Ionic.Zlib, and previews DXT textures, OGG and WAV audio. Nothing in the code mentions LOTRO; it was written for DDO. Endevir is a LOTRO modder (Elanor / text-patcher), which suggests the fork was for LOTRO use, but the repo does not say this. The repo has no description or README, only a _config.yml.
license: AGPL-3.0-only (the LICENSE file is the GNU AGPL v3 text; the last commit is "move to AGPL")
last_activity: 2018-01-23 (last commit 748ecee1d68e6d81ab77ec32f7b26bee2d92a9e2, the same in the fork and upstream). Inactive for more than 8 years.
key_facts:
Checked by shallow-cloning both the fork and the upstream and reading Mogwai.DDO.Explorer/*.cs and UI/Form1.cs.

**Header (DatDatabase.cs)**
- The reader seeks to 0x140 and reads 15 uint32 LE values in this order:
  - magic @0x140
  - blockSize @0x144
  - fileSize @0x148
  - fileVersion @0x14C
  - unknown @0x150
  - firstFreeBlock @0x154 (the code itself marks this as a guess)
  - lastFreeBlock @0x158
  - freeBlockCount @0x15C
  - rootOffset @0x160
  - 4 unknown zero dwords @0x164–0x170
  - datpackEngine @0x174 ("datpack version engine", from dndclient.log)
  - gameId @0x178 ("datpack version game")
- The claim says this header is "identical to AC". The code does not say that. The offset and the general shape (block size, free list, B-tree root) do match AC, but that comparison is the claimant's inference.

**Directory node (DatDirectory.cs)**
- At the node offset, the code first checks that 2 dwords are zero. If they are not, it silently returns, which suggests a block-chain header.
- Next come 62 pairs of (uint32 size, uint32 offset), 496 bytes in total.
  - Traversal stops when size != the parent's size, offset == 0, or offset == 0xCDCDCDCD.
- Next come 61 file entries of 32 bytes each (8 dwords): unknown1, fileType/flags, fileId, fileOffset, size1, timestamp (unix), unknown2, size2.
- There is no explicit entry count. The list ends at the first entry with fileId == 0 or offset == 0.
- Constants: MAX_FILES=61, MAX_DIRS=62.
- This structure differs from AC's directory node (AC has an explicit count and 24-byte entries), so "identical to AC" holds only for the header.

**Compression**
- CompressionType = FileType & 0xFF: 0 Uncompressed, 1 Maximum, 2 Unknown, 3 Default.
- Compressed entries are read from data at fileOffset+8: 4 header bytes, then zlib data of size1 bytes starting at offset+12.
  - The inflated payload starts with fileId (uint32) followed by a small unknown uint32.
- Uncompressed entries: at offset+8 come fileId (uint32) and size (uint32), with the data at offset+16.
- The reader assumes file data is contiguous. It does not follow block chains, so fragmented or multi-block files will probably read wrong. Do not copy this behaviour.

**Content sniffing (DatFile.GetActualFileType)**
- RIFF…WAVE → Wave.
- OggS with dword2==512 and dword3==0 → Ogg.
- Dword0 equal to 'DXT1'/'DXT3'/'DXT5'-style FourCC values, or dword3 equal to the FourCCs 'DXT1' (0x31545844), 'DXT3', 'DXT5' → that DXT type.
- First 2 bytes 0x789C or 0x789A → Zlib.

**Other**
- DdoFileIdMap: 0x0A000000–0x0AFFFFFF are audio files (DDO).
- DxtUtil.cs contains a DXT1/3/5 software decompressor.
how_to_use:
Use as reference only. Read it for the format, then write our own code from a written spec. Do not depend on it or port it.

- **License:** AGPL-3.0 is strong copyleft. Copying or porting its code would make our project AGPL, which may not suit the license we pick.
- **Not authoritative:** it is DDO-specific, unfinished and inactive since 2018, and it contains guesses ("unknown" and "guess?" fields). It also does not follow block chains.
- **What it is good for:** cross-checking the facts above (header at 0x140, the 62-subdir/61-file B-tree node, 32-byte entries, the compression flag in the low byte of the flags field, zlib payloads that start with the file id). Check these against real LOTRO .dat files and against more complete LOTRO tools such as LotroCompanion/lotro-tools and jmspashett datool before writing the clean-room reader.
- **Confidence:** the repo was verified by clone; its LOTRO applicability is inferred, not stated by the repo.
- **Correction to the claim:** cite the upstream Mogwai-TheFurry/DatExplorer rather than the Endevir fork.

label: verify:Mogwai-TheFurry/DatExplorer (DDO)
actual_description: A small C# (.NET WinForms) explorer for Turbine-engine .dat archives, aimed at DDO (repo topics: dat, ddo, dungeons-and-dragons, lotro). It has no README. The solution has three projects: Mogwai.DDO.Explorer (core library), Mogwai.DDO.Explorer.UI (WinForms tree view, filters, export, DXT preview with ZoomBox) and Mogwai.DDO.Explorer.Tests. There are 12 commits, all between 2017-08-25 and 2018-01-24, so the repo has been dormant since early 2018. It has 6 stars and 6 forks. It is a read-only viewer and exporter. last_activity: 2018-01-24 (last commits were "move to AGPL" and "Delete LICENSE"). Earlier history: 2017-08-25 initial commit, the license was changed to BSD the same day, and DXT preview and export were added on 2017-08-29.
license: AGPL-3.0-only (the LICENSE file at HEAD is the GNU AGPL v3 text). In 2017-08 the history briefly carried a BSD license ("updated to BSD license"), then switched to AGPL on 2018-01-24.
key_facts:
I read the source through raw.githubusercontent.com. Cloning was not possible because the local disk was full (ENOSPC).

HEADER (DatDatabase.cs): reading starts at 0x140 and covers 15 uint32 values, all little-endian:
- 0x140 magic
- 0x144 blockSize
- 0x148 fileSize
- 0x14C fileVersion
- 0x150 unknown
- 0x154 firstFreeBlock (the author marks this as a guess)
- 0x158 lastFreeBlock
- 0x15C freeBlockCount
- 0x160 rootOffset (root directory)
- 0x164–0x170 four unknown values, all zeros
- 0x174 "datpack version engine"
- 0x178 "datpack version game" (named _gameId; both labels come from dndclient.log)
The claim about 0x174 and 0x178 is CONFIRMED.

DIRECTORY NODE (DatDirectory.cs, DatConstants.cs):
- Seek to the node offset and read two uint32 values. If either is nonzero the node is skipped. This matches the usual 8-byte block header: a next-block pointer plus a second word.
- Then comes DIR_BLOCK_SIZE = 62 × (2 × uint32) = 496 bytes of (size, offset) pairs. Iteration stops when the size is not equal to the parent's block size, or the offset is 0 or 0xCDCDCDCD.
- Then comes FILE_BLOCK_SIZE = 61 × 32 bytes = 1952 bytes of file entries (MAX_FILES = 61, MAX_DIRS = 62).
- The claimed "62×8" means 62 directory pointers of 8 bytes each. That is CONFIRMED.
- The code never reads an explicit file-count field. It stops at the first entry with fileId == 0 or offset == 0. The real format probably has a count word that this code misses.

FILE ENTRY (DatFile.cs, 32 bytes):
- +0 Unknown1
- +4 FileType
- +8 FileId
- +12 FileOffset
- +16 Size1
- +20 Timestamp (Unix epoch)
- +24 Unknown2 (likely the version/iteration)
- +28 Size2
The compression level is (FileType & 0xFF), mapped to the enum Uncompressed = 0, Maximum = 1, Unknown_Value_2 = 2, Default = 3. CONFIRMED.

DATA READ (UI/Form1.cs):
- Compressed: read 4 bytes at FileOffset + 8, then Size1 bytes at FileOffset + 12, then zlib-inflate with Ionic.Zlib.ZlibStream.UncompressBuffer, then skip 8 bytes of the inner header.
- Uncompressed: read 8 bytes at FileOffset + 8. The length is the uint32 at header + 4, and the data starts at FileOffset + 16.
- The code does NOT follow block chains. It reads contiguous bytes from FileOffset, so it is wrong for any file that spans fragmented blocks. Do not copy this behaviour.

CONTENT SNIFFING:
- 'RIFF' means WAV.
- 'OggS' with dword2 == 512 and dword3 == 0 means Ogg.
- FourCC 'DXT1'/'DXT3'/'DXT5' at offset 0 or 8.
- First uint16 equal to 0x789C or 0x789A means zlib.
- The texture payload starts with height (uint32) then width (uint32), followed by raw DXT data.
- DxtUtil implements software DXT1/3/5 decoding, and DdsFile converts DDS to BMP. DXT decoding is CONFIRMED.

FILE IDS: DdoFileIdMap gives the DDO ID range 0x0A000000–0x0AFFFFFF as AudioFiles.
lotro_relevance: medium. The code targets DDO, but DDO and LOTRO share the same Turbine dat container format (the repo itself carries the "lotro" topic). That makes it a useful second witness for the header at 0x140, the directory and B-tree node layout, and the 32-byte entry layout. It covers nothing above the container layer: no meshes, no DIDs/properties, no networking. It also lacks block chaining and fragmentation handling.
how_to_use:
Use as reference-only, through clean-room spec extraction. Do not copy or port the code, and do not depend on it. The HEAD license is AGPL-3.0, and copying code would force AGPL network-copyleft on our client unless the project chooses AGPL itself. Its main value is as an independent cross-check of facts that other LOTRO tools should also confirm (header offsets 0x140–0x178, 62 directory pointers plus 61 file entries of 32 bytes, compression byte = FileType & 0xFF, zlib framing at FileOffset + 8/+12, texture layout of height, width, then DXT data). Write those facts into our own format spec and test them against the user's own .dat files.

Do not take its block handling as correct. It ignores the next-block chain, the inner sizes are partly guesses, and fields are labelled "unknown". Prefer a maintained LOTRO-specific source (for example the LOTRO Companion / lotro-tools dat readers) as the primary reference, and use this repo only to corroborate.

DXT decoding is generic, well-known math, so implement it ourselves (or use a permissively licensed library such as bcdec) rather than taking DxtUtil.

The original claim is accurate: every listed item was confirmed in source. Overall confidence in the claim: verified-by-fetch (source read file by file).

label: verify:Endevir/DatExplorer (fork of Mogwai)
canonical_url: https://github.com/Mogwai-TheFurry/DatExplorer (upstream original; https://github.com/Endevir/DatExplorer is an unmodified mirror fork)
actual_description: Endevir/DatExplorer exists and is a GitHub fork of Mogwai-TheFurry/DatExplorer, a small C# .NET WinForms explorer for Turbine .dat archives. The solution is Mogwai.DDO.Explorer.sln with three projects: Mogwai.DDO.Explorer (core library), Mogwai.DDO.Explorer.UI, and Mogwai.DDO.Explorer.Tests. The upstream repo is tagged with the topics dat, ddo, dungeons-and-dragons and lotro. The fork has 12 commits, last dated Jan 24, 2018 ("move to AGPL"), and the commit page shows only Mogwai-TheFurry as author. It has no README and no description. Endevir (who also owns the Elanor "LotRO Rusification Project" app, LOTRO-Enchanced-text-patcher and a jtauber/lotro fork) is linked to the Russian LOTRO translation effort, so that part of the claim holds. Two corrections to the claim: the fork adds no Endevir work, so it is not a separate tool from the Russian team, and the original author's tool is the one to cite. Upstream has 6 stars and 6 forks and appears inactive since 2018. I fetched the GitHub HTML pages and raw source files directly. The api.github.com JSON calls returned 403, and I could not clone because the local disk was full (ENOSPC).
license: AGPL-3.0
last_activity: 2018-01-24 (commit 748ecee "move to AGPL"; earlier commits run Aug 25-30, 2017: export support, DXT preview and bitmap export, tree sorting)
key_facts:
Read directly from raw source files in Mogwai.DDO.Explorer/:
- DatDatabase.cs: the header starts at file offset 0x140 and is 15 uint32 fields (60 bytes), in this order:
  - 0x140 magic
  - 0x144 BlockSize
  - 0x148 FileSize
  - 0x14C FileVersion
  - 0x150 unknown
  - 0x154 FirstFreeBlock
  - 0x158 LastFreeBlock
  - 0x15C FreeBlockCount
  - 0x160 RootOffset (offset of the root directory node)
  - 0x164-0x170 three unknown uint32s (zero)
  - 0x174 DatpackEngineVersion
  - 0x178 GameIdVersion
- DatConstants.cs: MAX_FILES=61 and MAX_DIRS=62. DIR_BLOCK_SIZE = 2*4*62 = 496 bytes and FILE_BLOCK_SIZE = 8*4*61 = 1952 bytes.
- DatDirectory.cs: a directory node starts with two uint32s that must both be 0. Then come up to 62 subdirectory entries of (uint32 size, uint32 offset); parsing stops when an offset is 0 or 0xCDCDCDCD. After that come up to 61 file entries of 32 bytes each.
- DatFile.cs: each 32-byte file entry is laid out as:
  - +0 Unknown1
  - +4 FileType
  - +8 FileId
  - +12 FileOffset
  - +16 Size1
  - +20 Timestamp
  - +24 Unknown2
  - +28 Size2
- Compression level is (FileType & 0xFF), mapped by the CompressionType enum: 0 Uncompressed, 1 Maximum, 2 Unknown, 3 Default. The real content type is found by sniffing magic bytes: DXT textures, Ogg Vorbis, WAVE and zlib.
- DatReader.cs is a plain FileStream/BinaryReader wrapper with no block-chain following or decompression. Data is read as offset plus length, so multi-block files and compressed payloads are only partly handled.
- DdsFile.cs and DxtUtil.cs decode DXT textures to bitmaps.
- DdoFileIdMap.cs and KnownFileType.cs (with FileIdRangeAttribute and FileExtensionAttribute) map file-ID ranges to types. They are DDO-oriented but the same scheme applies to LOTRO, since both games use the same Turbine dat engine.
how_to_use: Use it for reference only. Do not depend on it, port it, or copy code, because AGPL-3.0 is incompatible with a permissively licensed project and the code is small, old, incomplete and DDO-focused. Treat it as one more independent confirmation of the Turbine dat container layout. The facts worth using are the header at 0x140, the 62-subdirectory/61-file B-tree directory nodes, the 32-byte file entries, and the compression flag in the low byte of FileType. Cross-check these against other sources, such as LotroCompanion/lotro-dat-utils, the Asheron's Call / ACE DatLoader, and the Russian team's LotroDat C++ library, then write an independent spec in our own words. Cite the upstream Mogwai-TheFurry/DatExplorer, not the Endevir fork, which adds nothing. The Endevir account is still a useful lead to the Russian LOTRO translation tooling (Elanor, the text patcher, and the related LotroDat work), which deserves separate verification. Confidence is high that the repo exists and is licensed as claimed (verified by fetch). The claim that it is the Russian team's own fork with changes is overstated: it is an unmodified fork.

label: verify:Ghidra RecoverClassesFromRTTIScript.java
actual_description: A prototype Ghidra script in the C++ category (about 1650 lines on master). It uses MSVC RTTI structures, and also GCC typeinfo, to recover class hierarchies, inheritance types, vftables, constructors and destructors, and class data types. It also names virtual functions. When a PDB is present it uses the PDB to fill in member names and types. Without one, it infers member types from decompiler p-code. Its helper classes live in the `classrecovery` package next to it, in ghidra_scripts/classrecovery/ (for example, RTTIWindowsClassRecoverer.java returned HTTP 200). The header describes it as a prototype: the names and layout of the data types it creates may change. It also says Windows recovery is more complete than GCC recovery.
license: Apache-2.0
how_to_use: Use it as a tool only, as an analyst-side helper inside Ghidra. Do not depend on it or port it into the reimplementation. Run it on a legally obtained lotroclient(64).exe to get the class hierarchy, vftable layouts and ctor/dtor lists. That analysis informs a clean-room spec, for example class and subsystem names, object model and serialization class layouts. Nothing it produces should be copied verbatim into project code. Keep the analysis team (dirty room) separate from the implementation team, or at least keep the spec-writing step separate, and record the separation. Ghidra's Apache-2.0 license is no problem for tool use. The legal risk lies in how the decompiled output is used, not in the script. Run it on a freshly auto-analyzed program, as the script's notes recommend. Optional companions in the same folder are ApplyClassFunctionSignatureUpdatesScript.java and ApplyClassFunctionDefinitionsUpdatesScript.java. Caveat: I did not check the claim that lotroclient64.exe contains RTTI, because I had no binary to inspect. MSVC emits RTTI by default (/GR), so it is plausible. To confirm, look for '.?AV' type-descriptor strings in the exe before relying on this script.
key_facts:
- The URL is correct: raw.githubusercontent.com returned HTTP 200 for the script on master. The repo LICENSE is Apache License 2.0, and the file header is an Apache-2.0 notice ("IP: GHIDRA").

label: verify:lotro-freecam-toolkit (NeuralFoundry)
actual_description: The repo exists. - Target module is lotroclient64.exe (64-bit). The tool moves the engine's existing FlightCameraController onto the camera stack; the character does not move.
- Subsystems named: FrillEngine (grass/detail objects; struct grew by 0x18 bytes between builds 4900 and 4901), SmartBox (landscape provider handling surface requests and residency), AsyncCache (resource streaming with completion hooks for landblock surfaces).
- AsyncCache land type IDs: 0x11 LandblockData, 0x2e LandblockInfo, 0x2f LandblockBlockmap, 0x29 LandblockProperties, 0x1a EntityGroup, 0x64 KynmapLandblock.
- Geometry: a landblock is 160 units across, split into 16 sectors of 10 units. Terrain draws in three bands: full detail to 224 sectors (14 blocks) by default, a native medium band to 384 sectors (24 blocks), then distant imposters. Streaming uses 3x3 source groups, with a cap of about 185 retained sources at default range.
- Engine variable globals: STATIC_PVS_FLAG, ALLOW_LODS_FLAG, MATERIAL_DETAIL, OBJECT_DRAW_DISTANCE, LANDSCAPE_DRAW_DISTANCE, TEXTURE_FILTERING, ANISOTROPIC_QUALITY, GRAPHICS_MEMORY_USAGE.

Its value to a clean-room client is architectural knowledge: subsystem names (FrillEngine, SmartBox, AsyncCache), the AsyncCache data type IDs for landblock resources (worth cross-checking against the dat-file DIDs), and how landscape streaming and LOD work (16 sectors per 160-unit landblock; near, medium and imposter bands at 14 and 24 blocks; 3x3 streaming groups). label: verify:Palantir Edition (PalantirTools)
actual_description: "The repository for The Lord of the Rings Online (LOTRO) - Palantir Edition." It contains no source code. It adds field-of-view controls (vertical and base FOV via gamepad), a fly-camera mode (F3), a custom GUI (F2) and an unload key (F1). - Login-queue keys: WorldQueue.LoginQueue.URL=https://gls.ddo.com/GLS.AuthServer/LoginQueue.aspx, with TakeANumber parameters "command=TakeANumber&subscription={0}&ticket={1}&ticket_type=GLS&queue_url={2}" and LeaveQueue parameters "command=LeaveQueue&subscription={0}&context={1}&ticket_type=GLS&queue_url={2}".

- GetDatacenters: POST /GLS.DataCenterServer/Service.asmx with SOAPAction "http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS/GetDatacenters", namespace http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS.
  - The response is Datacenter{Name, Worlds[World{Name, LoginServerUrl, ChatServerUrl ip:2900, StatusServerUrl ...StatusServer.aspx?s=<internal ip>, Order, Language}], AuthServer, PatchServer patch.ddo.com:5015, LauncherConfigurationServer}.
  - LoginServerUrl reads "(invalid service specified)". The real login and queue URLs come from the StatusServerUrl query, whose response format is not documented.
- LoginAccount: POST https://gls-auth.ddo.com/GLS.AuthServer/Service.asmx with SOAP <LoginAccount><username/><password/><additionalInfo/></LoginAccount>. The server needs a weak TLS cipher (the author had to use curl --ciphers DEFAULT@SECLEVEL=1).
  - Failure: soap:Fault with faultcode BIS, "No Subscriber Formal Entity was found.", detail result 0x8004C002.
  - Success: LoginAccountResult{Subscriptions[GameSubscription{Game, Name, Description, ProductTokens[string], CustomerServiceTokens, Status, BillingSystemTime, AdditionalInfo}], Ticket}.
- Patching: POST /stateless2 to patch host port 5015 with Content-Type application/x-www-form-urlencoded. The server identifies as Microsoft-HTTPAPI/2.0 and replies with Content-Type "binary".
  - The first reply is 128 opaque bytes. Later requests start with hex 6d 01 00 80 04 '3des' 80 00 00 00 ..., which suggests 3DES-encrypted payloads with a length-prefixed cipher name.
  - The author did not decode any of it, and the 70 KB responses are omitted.
GAME/CHAT (protocol/game.md):
- Speculative, by the author's own account: UDP traffic, separate chat and game connections, and an assumption that compression is used.
- The login packet has ASCII markers at rough offsets: 0x41 "061004_", 0x48 "netver:", 0x55 "didver:", 0x91 the subscription name (UTF-16), and from 0xC8 the login token to the end of the packet.
- The 2-byte packet "identifiers" (00 33, 00 3A, 02 C4, 02 5D) are guesses. The author says they likely don't know the Turbine/AC-lineage UDP header (sequence, flags, checksum).
- The chat message layout is a rough sketch: a length-prefixed UTF-16 username and channel, marker bytes 04 08, and the message.
- Nothing on the DAT format, crypto keys, or checksums.
how_to_use:
Use it only as a reference, and treat the facts as clean-room protocol observations. The repo has no license, so do not copy its text verbatim into the project. Protocol facts such as endpoint names, SOAP schemas and argument templates are interoperability data and can be restated in our own words in the spec.
What it is good for:
- A sanity check for the launcher/GLS flow, which uses the same Turbine GLS stack as LOTRO's gls.lotro.com: GetDatacenters, then LoginAccount, then the StatusServer query, then the login queue, then launching the client with -a/-h/--glsticketdirect/--chatserver/--rodat on/--gametype/--authserverurl/--glsticketlifetime.
- A hint that the patch protocol (stateless2, port 5015, 3DES-wrapped) is binary and encrypted.
What it is not good for:
- The UDP game protocol. Its notes there are guesswork and should not be trusted. Prefer the Asheron's Call emulator lineage (ACE / ACEmulator protocol docs) and the LOTRO/DDO launcher projects OneLauncher, PyLotRO and lotro-launcher, which implement GLS and the client arguments in source.
The claim's "verified-by-fetch" confidence holds for existence and content. The value it implies is overstated for anything past the launcher stage.

label: verify:bethington/ghidra-mcp
actual_description: Ghidra MCP Server (v7.0.0 in pyproject.toml and pom.xml; the CHANGELOG lists v7.0.0 as unreleased). It has two parts. The first is a Java Ghidra plugin that also runs as a headless server, and it serves an HTTP API on 127.0.0.1:8089. The second is a Python bridge (`uv run bridge-mcp-ghidra`) that exposes that API as MCP tools. The bridge supports three transports: stdio (the default), streamable-http, and sse (deprecated). The project advertises 253 tools covering decompilation, xrefs and the call graph, strings, imports/exports, creating structs, unions and enums, batch renaming, commenting and retyping, script management, P-code emulation, a live debugger over TraceRmi, cross-binary function-hash documentation transfer, and Ghidra Server version control. It was originally derived from LaurieWired/GhidraMCP (Apache-2.0), per the NOTICE file. Correction to the claim: the server is NOT read-only. It has full write access. "Read-only allowlist" is only a README recipe: a minimal set of 4 GET-only tools (get_metadata, list_methods, get_entry_points, decompile_function) that you can allowlist in your MCP client. "Multi-program routing" is real: there is a program= selector on calls, and GHIDRA_MCP_REQUIRE_PROGRAM_SELECTORS=1 turns on strict routing. Built against Ghidra 12.1.3 (pom.xml property ghidra.version=12.1.3). Requires Java 21 and Python 3.10+.
license: Apache-2.0
last_activity: 2026-09-29 (HEAD d66702c, "docs(claude): drop two test paths removed with tests/performance (#552)"); active, with dependabot and other feature branches
key_facts:
- Java plugin HTTP API on localhost:8089. Python bridge CLI flags: --transport stdio|streamable-http|sse, --mcp-host/--mcp-port, --lazy/--no-lazy (env GHIDRA_MCP_LAZY).
- Lazy tool groups: only listing, function and program are loaded on connect. search_tools, list_tool_groups, load_tool_group and check_tools let an agent find and load the rest, which keeps Claude Code's context small.
- GHIDRA_MCP_REQUIRE_PROGRAM_SELECTORS=1 rejects any program-scoped call that has no program= selector. Use this when the LOTRO client exe and its DLLs are open together.
- The full surface writes to the database (renames, retyping, struct creation, script execution). Its "convention enforcement" auto-fixes and rejects names (Hungarian notation, PascalCase).
- Cross-binary SHA-256 function-hash matching carries documentation across binary versions. This helps with LOTRO's frequent client updates (32-bit vs 64-bit lotroclient.exe, patch versions).
- The P-code emulator and TraceRmi debugger (dbgeng on Windows) are included.
- Headless/Docker mode is available for batch analysis.
- Ghidra 12.1.3 ships Jython as an optional extension, so .py ghidra_scripts need it installed.
- The NOTICE credits LaurieWired/GhidraMCP as the origin.
how_to_use:
Use it as an external dev tool only. Do not depend on it, vendor it, or ship it in the reimplementation. The Apache-2.0 license is compatible with any use, but nothing from it needs to go into our codebase. It fits the "dirty room" (spec-extraction) side of a clean-room process: a reverse engineer uses Claude Code + Ghidra + this MCP on their own legally obtained lotroclient.exe to work out file formats (DAT btree/file headers, DID types, property/enum tables), network message layouts, and UI/layout formats, and writes those up as prose specs. A separate "clean" implementation side then writes code from the specs only. Caveats:
(1) Decompiler output and renamed Ghidra databases for LOTRO contain or derive from SSG's copyrighted code. Never commit them, or decompiled snippets, to the project repo.
(2) The LOTRO EULA/ToS forbids reverse engineering. Rely on interoperability exceptions (e.g. 17 USC 1201(f), EU Software Directive Art. 6) and get legal advice. Do not attach the debugger to a live game connected to official servers (anti-cheat/ToS).
(3) For agent safety, run with strict program selectors and a read-only allowlist when the goal is spec extraction only, because the default surface is write-capable.
Alternatives to compare: LaurieWired/GhidraMCP, the original and much smaller project.

label: verify:ghidriff
actual_description: The claim is accurate. ghidriff is a "Ghidra Binary Diffing Engine": a Python 3 command-line tool that uses pyghidra (JPype) to run Ghidra headless on two binaries. It finds the functions that were added, deleted and modified between them. Results are saved as JSON and rendered as Markdown, with optional side-by-side HTML. It also produces "meta diffs" covering binary strings, called and calling functions, and binary metadata. Its main purpose is patch diffing, and it is also published on PyPI as `ghidriff`.
license: GPL-3.0-only (the LICENSE file is the GNU GPL v3 text; setup.cfg says "GPL-3.0 license" with the classifier "GNU General Public License v3 (GPLv3)")
language: Python (3.10 or newer; drives Ghidra, which is Java, through pyghidra and JPype)
last_activity: 2026-05-11. The shallow clone's HEAD is commit 4f5d895f, "Merge pull request #141 from clearbluejar/ghidra12-dev-refresh", so it was updated for Ghidra 12. It is actively maintained.
how_to_use: Use it as an external tool only, on the reverse-engineering side of the clean room. Do not vendor it, link it or copy its code into the project: it is GPL-3.0, and it is not needed at runtime. Suggested use: when Standing Stone Games ships a new client build (lotroclient.exe / lotroclient64.exe), run `ghidriff old.exe new.exe` to find functions that changed. Likely targets are message serialization, DID/property tables and the DAT reader. That shows which parts of the published format/protocol spec need re-checking. Legal caveat: the diff output contains decompiled original code. It must stay with the reverse-engineering team and never enter the project repo. Only clean-room prose specs written from it (field layouts, opcode meanings) should pass to implementers. Running it on the client relies on interoperability exemptions such as EU Software Directive Art. 6 and DMCA 1201(f), even though the EULA forbids reverse engineering, so keep it optional and documented in the RE workflow docs. It is not part of the build. Pin a version (1.0.0 or later) together with a compatible Ghidra release (11 or 12) and a JDK, or use its Dockerfile or devcontainer.

label: verify:pyghidra-mcp
actual_description: A Python command-line MCP (Model Context Protocol) server that exposes Ghidra's ProgramAPI/FlatProgramAPI through pyghidra/jpype. It is headless-first: one long-running streamable-HTTP server keeps the Ghidra project loaded. It can also drive a live Ghidra GUI (--gui, which needs an HTTP transport). It ships a separate HTTP client, pyghidra-mcp-cli, and is published on PyPI as pyghidra-mcp and as a Docker image at ghcr.io/clearbluejar/pyghidra-mcp. The README presents it as an alternative to LaurieWired/GhidraMCP. Everything in the claim checks out: it is Python; the README recommends headless streamable-http; the README gives `claude mcp add --transport http pyghidra-mcp http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp`; and its .mcp.json example uses "type": "http" with "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp".
license: Apache-2.0
language: Python (>=3.10); depends on pyghidra>=2.2.1 and jpype; dev stubs ghidra-stubs>=11.3.2
last_activity: 2026-09-25 (HEAD 323fbdb, merge of PR #121 'fix/stdio-ctrl-c-exit'); pyproject version 0.2.7
key_facts:
Checked by shallow-cloning the repo on 2026-10-03 and reading README.md, LICENSE and pyproject.toml.

Setup and running:
- Requires the GHIDRA_INSTALL_DIR environment variable to point at a local Ghidra install.
- The console entry point is pyghidra-mcp = pyghidra_mcp.server:main.
- Transport options are -t/--transport [stdio|streamable-http|sse|http]. The default is stdio, SSE is deprecated, and `http` is an alias for streamable-http.
- Defaults are host 127.0.0.1 and port 8000, and the endpoint is http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp.
- GUI mode is `pyghidra-mcp --gui --transport streamable-http --project-path project.gpr`.

Claude Code configuration:
- Command: `claude mcp add --transport http pyghidra-mcp http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp`
- .mcp.json entry: {"mcpServers":{"pyghidra-mcp":{"type":"http","url":"http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp"}}}

Tools the README lists (about 40):
- import_binary: takes a path and recursively imports a whole directory, keeping its structure.
- list_project_binaries and list_project_binary_metadata: the metadata covers architecture, compiler, format, analysis metrics and hashes.
- decompile_function: batch decompiles a list of targets. Flags can attach callees, strings and xrefs, and timeout_sec is applied per target.
- search_code: semantic vector search (ChromaDB embeddings) or literal search over decompiled pseudo-C.
- search_strings and search_symbols_by_name (the latter supports regex).
- list_xrefs, read_bytes and set_comment, with types decompiler, plate, pre, eol, post and repeatable.
- Callgraph tools and rename/edit tools.

Caveat: string and semantic indexing on the MCP side can finish later than Ghidra's own analysis.
how_to_use:
Use it as an external development tool only, not a dependency. Do not vendor or link it into the client codebase; developers install it separately (`uvx pyghidra-mcp` or Docker). Apache-2.0 would allow redistribution, but the client gains nothing from it.

Its use in the project is agent-assisted reverse engineering: Claude Code queries a headless Ghidra project over HTTP. Because the server is long-running, the 10-60 s Ghidra startup per query goes away.

Clean-room process (the legal requirement):
- Only the "dirty" analysis side may use this on the user's own legally obtained LOTRO client binaries (lotroclient.exe / lotroclient64.exe and the DLLs).
- That side writes prose and spec descriptions of formats and protocols, for example .dat archive structure, DID/property layouts and the network message framing.
- The implementation side writes code only from those specs.
- Never commit decompiler output, renamed symbol dumps or Ghidra project files (.gpr/.rep) to the repo.
- Keep the Ghidra project outside the repo, or add it to .gitignore.
- Flag the EULA/ToS reverse-engineering clauses for legal review, since they vary by jurisdiction (interoperability exceptions under EU Software Directive Art. 6 and 17 U.S.C. 1201(f)).

Suggested repo setup: commit an optional .mcp.json with the "type": "http" entry shown above, so contributors who run the server locally get it automatically.

label: verify:Pharos / OOAnalyzer (CMU SEI)
actual_description: The Pharos Static Binary Analysis Framework from CMU SEI (CERT). It is built on LLNL's ROSE compiler infrastructure for disassembly, CFG and instruction semantics. It ships these tools: OOAnalyzer (C++ class and method recovery using Prolog rules; CCS 2018 paper "Using Logic Programming to Recover C++ Classes and Methods from Compiled Executables"), ooprolog, APIAnalyzer, CallAnalyzer, FN2Yara, FN2Hash, PathAnalyzer and dumpmasm. The Ghidra import plugin that used to be in Pharos now lives in CERTCC/kaiju.
license: BSD-3-Clause-style custom "BSD (SEI)" license (adds a CMU/SEI non-endorsement clause; bundled third-party components have their own licenses). There is no exact SPDX match; it is closest to BSD-3-Clause.
language: C++ (C++17, ROSE/Boost) with Prolog rules (SWI-Prolog, formerly XSB)
last_activity: HEAD commit 782492f on 2026-08-03 ("Change contact from Cory Cohen to Ed Schwartz"). The repo is not archived and has several branches (itanium, arch-test, cfcpic, add-workflow-dispatch-trigger). Its Dockerfile is based on ubuntu:noble.
key_facts:
The repo and tool exist and match the claim. I cloned it and read README.md, LICENSE.md, tools/ooanalyzer/ooanalyzer.pod, share/prolog/oorules/README.md and the Dockerfile.

- **What the README says it supports:** "The current version of the tool only supports analysis of 32-bit x86 executables compiled by Microsoft Visual C++." The ooanalyzer.pod adds: "64-bit Windows executables may work somewhat, but have not been tested extensively."
- **Output and Ghidra import:** results go out as JSON and are imported into Ghidra with the CERTCC/kaiju plugin. The old in-tree Ghidra plugin was removed.
- **Large binaries:** oorules/README.md recommends a multi-step workflow: partition with the partitioner, then extract facts, then run ooprolog with SWI-Prolog tabling. It warns that disassembly can need up to 1000x the executable's size in RAM, because ROSE builds many objects per instruction. A client executable of tens of MB would therefore need tens of GB of RAM or swap, and the runtime is long.
- **Build:** heavy. It needs ROSE, built against the same Boost, plus SWI-Prolog, Z3, yaml-cpp, libxml2 and capstone. The supported way is the Docker image or scripts/build_prereqs.bash.

**The claim is overstated.** It describes OOAnalyzer as "usable on the still-shipped 32-bit lotroclient.exe", and that part is outdated. Web search results from late 2025 to 2026 (gamersunchained, massivelyop, containsmoderateperil) say Standing Stone Games discontinued the legacy 32-bit LOTRO client with Update 45.3. It went offline on 2025-08-27, and the 32-bit worlds closed on 2025-08-31. Only lotroclient64.exe is current. My direct fetches of those articles were blocked (HTTP 403/429), so this rests on search snippets: moderate-to-high confidence.

The claimed license ("BSD-style") and language ("C++/Prolog") are accurate.
how_to_use:
Use it as a local analysis tool only. Run it on the analyst's machine, preferably through the official Docker image. Never vendor it into the project or link it into the reimplementation.

It suits a dirty-room or analysis team that recovers class hierarchies, vtables and method-to-class assignments from a client binary the analyst owns legally. That team turns the results into written specs (object layouts, virtual interfaces) for clean-room implementers. They should not copy decompiled code across.

Caveats:
- **32-bit vs 64-bit:** the only current client is 64-bit, where OOAnalyzer is officially untested ("may work somewhat"). Run it on an old 32-bit lotroclient.exe from a legacy install the analyst owns, if one is available, or treat 64-bit results with caution.
- **Cost:** RAM and runtime for a client of this size will be high. Use the staged partition, then facts, then ooprolog workflow.
- **Alternatives:** compare its output with Ghidra's own RTTI/class recovery, or with a Ghidra C++ class analyzer script, since MSVC RTTI may already give class names.

The BSD (SEI) license allows free use. Just don't use the CMU/SEI names to endorse anything.

label: verify:dmorcellet GitHub (delta-* common libs)
actual_description:
This is the personal GitHub account of Damien Morcellet, the author of LOTRO Companion. It holds 16 public repos. The named ones exist and are generic Java/Maven utility libraries under groupId com.dam.delta4j. There are no LICENSE, NOTICE or pom <licenses> entries in any of them.
- delta-common-ui: "Common UI-related utilities", 137 .java files, about 196 commits, last commit 2026-09-15.
- delta-json: 5 .java files, last commit 2024-11-24.
- delta-downloads: 12 .java files, last commit 2025-04-20.
- delta-sound-player: 69 .java files, last commit 2025-04-01.
- delta-updates-manager: 57 .java files, last commit 2025-04-08. It depends on delta-downloads and delta-common:1.15.
- lotro-test-utils: the repo page exists (HTTP 200), but `git ls-remote` returns no refs, so it is empty and has no code.

The other repos on the account are delta-common-l10n, delta-launcher, delta-kickstarter, delta-misc, delta-utils-statistics, delta-genea, delta-genea-webapp, euler, xwing-cheat-utility and the dmorcellet profile repo.

The LOTRO-specific code is NOT on this account. github.com/dmorcellet/lotro-core, lotro-companion, lotro-tools and lotro-data return 301 redirects to the LotroCompanion organization (https://github.com/LotroCompanion), which has 19 repos: lotro-companion, lotro-core, lotro-tools, lotro-maps, lotro-data, lotro-data-extractor, lotro-jukebox(-core), lotro-values, lotro-icons, lotro-items-db, lotro-maps-db, lotro-companion-distrib, and others.

The claim that "lotro-dat-utils is NOT public" is CONFIRMED. `git ls-remote` on dmorcellet/lotro-dat-utils needs authentication (it is private or does not exist), it is absent from the LotroCompanion org, and lotro-companion's pom.xml uses it only as a binary dependency: com.dam.delta4j:delta-lotro-dat-utils:11.12. delta-common (com.dam.delta4j:delta-common:1.15/1.19) is also not public, and neither are delta-lotro-memory:6.8 or delta-lotro-maps:4.6 under that name.
license: none/unknown. The claim of "Apache-2.0 (per NOTICE)" is UNVERIFIED and very likely wrong. None of the cloned delta-* repos has a LICENSE or NOTICE file or a <licenses> element in pom.xml. GitHub shows no license for delta-common-ui. The LotroCompanion org shows no license on any repo. lotro-companion's README and pom.xml have no license statement. My guess (not confirmed) is that the "NOTICE" came from the vendored apache-ant-1.10.1 folder in LotroCompanion/lotro-companion-distrib, which would be Ant's own Apache notice, not the project's. Under default copyright, this code is all-rights-reserved.
how_to_use:
Reference only, and in practice mostly avoid. The libraries this claim names are generic Java helpers: Swing UI, JSON, HTTP downloads, a sound player and an app update manager. None of them reads LOTRO .dat files or models anything about the game client. With no license, they cannot be legally copied or ported, and we would not want Java Swing or update-manager code in a client reimplementation anyway.

The useful LOTRO knowledge lives in the LotroCompanion org instead. lotro-core and lotro-tools hold the property and DID-based data models. lotro-data-extractor and lotro-jukebox are also there. Those repos also have no visible license, so they should be read for clean-room spec extraction only, never copied.

The key DAT-reading library (delta-lotro-dat-utils) is closed source. It ships only as a jar inside the LOTRO Companion distribution. Decompiling it would be a legal and ethical gray area, so do not rely on it. Get DAT and container format details from other projects, such as Turbine DAT readers for DDO/AC/LOTRO, with their licenses checked first.

Possible exception: delta-sound-player might show how LOTRO sounds (OGG/WAV pulled from client_sound.dat) are played. I did not inspect it because the scratch disk filled up. Even if it does, it would be at most a reference. A good next step is to contact the author (Damien Morcellet) about licensing if any of his code turns out to matter.
