label: verify:BinDiff (open source)
actual_description: BinDiff is Google's (formerly zynamics) open-source tool for comparing disassembled binaries. It finds identical and similar functions across two binaries using call-graph and flow-graph matchers (MD-index, prime signatures, hashes, string refs, loop entries and others in match/). It ports function names, comments and local names between disassemblies and highlights changed functions. The core engine is C++. The visual diff UI and the zylib utility library are Java. Integrations: IDA Pro/Home 9.4+ (Tier 1), IDA Freeware 9.4+ (Tier 2), Binary Ninja 3.5+ and Ghidra 10+ (both Tier 4, work in progress). Disassembly is read through BinExport exporter plugins (google/binexport, a separate repo that the build expects at ../binexport).

how_to_use: Use it as an external tool only. Do not vendor it or link it into the client. It is useful for reverse-engineering work on the user's own legally obtained LOTRO client binaries (lotroclient.exe / lotroclient64.exe, which change with every patch). Analysts can carry their function names, comments and struct annotations from one client build to the next, and see which functions changed after a patch, for example in the network protocol or the DAT loader. For a clean-room setup, keep it with the 'dirty' RE team that writes specs. Its output (match databases, annotated IDBs or Ghidra projects) holds information derived from the original binary and must never go into the reimplementation repo. Only the written specifications go to the implementers. The license is fine for tooling use. With Ghidra, the free route, support is only Tier 4: export both builds with the BinExport Ghidra extension, then run the bindiff CLI or UI on the .BinExport files. IDA 9.4+ gives the best experience. Use the v8 prebuilt packages from the releases page, or build from master, which is active (2026).

- xrefs, which can include callers and callees

how_to_use:
Use it only as a tool for analysis, never as a code dependency of the client. It is a good MCP bridge for AI-assisted reverse engineering of the LOTRO client binaries (lotroclient.exe / lotroclient64.exe) in Ghidra. Headless mode and multi-program support make it useful for batch work.

Keep it on the "dirty room" side of the clean-room process. Analysts or agents use it to work out file formats (the DAT archive and its record layouts), network protocols and engine behaviour. They write that knowledge up as specs. The reimplementation is then built from those specs alone. Decompiled output must never be pasted into the project's repository.

The MIT license allows free use, and since we would only run it, never ship it, the license puts nothing on our project. It can stand in for, or run alongside, LaurieWired/GhidraMCP; pick whichever has more tools or works better with the MCP client.

label: verify:jtauber/lotro
actual_description: James Tauber's "code for exploring LOTRO data files". It is a small set of Python 2 scripts: dat.py (DatFile/Directory B-tree reader), clidat.py (CLI with header/block/file_block/directory/list/find_file commands), surface.py (texture extraction to PNG), sound.py (WAV/OGG extraction), cell.py and extract_cells.py (landblock heightmaps rendered to a hill-shaded PNG), anim.py ("first pass at trying to understand anim format"), local.py (localized images/strings), png.py (a pure-Python PNG writer) and utils.py (hexdump and dword helpers). The repo has 42 commits, 17 stars and 7 forks. The README is a single line. Real development ran from July 2012 to January 2013. The last commits, dated 2014-07-15, are only PEP8 and whitespace changes. The claim is accurate except one detail: the format knowledge dates from 2012, not 2014.
license: none/unknown (no LICENSE file in the repo tree, so all rights are reserved by default)
how_to_use: Use as reference only, for clean-room spec extraction. Do not copy or port the code: it has no license, so it is all-rights-reserved and we cannot vendor or relicense it. Its value is as a short, readable statement of the facts of the DAT container (offsets, struct layouts, magic values, the compression flag). Facts are not copyrightable, so write those facts into our own format spec and then implement from the spec (one person reads the code, another implements). It is also useful as a cross-check against richer, licensed tools such as LotroCompanion/lotro-tools and the dat-export tools. Caveat: it reflects the 2012-era 32-bit DAT format. Current LOTRO clients (64-bit, post-2019 updates) may use changed superblock or directory layouts, so verify every field against real current data files before relying on it. It is Python 2 (print statements, integer `/`), so running it needs python2 or a trivial port for private experiments only. Verification note: the local disk was full (ENOSPC), so I could not clone the repo. I checked it by fetching the GitHub page, the commit history and the raw source files (dat.py, surface.py, sound.py, cell.py, clidat.py, utils.py, README.md), and I am confident in the result.
key_facts:
Facts read from the raw source:

**Superblock (dat.py)**
- Reads the first 1024 bytes.
- Asserts dword@0x101 == 0x4C50 ('PL') and dword@0x140 == 0x5442 ('BT').
- block_size@0x144, file_size@0x148 (asserted equal to the on-disk size), version@0x14C, version_2@0x150, free_head@0x154, free_tail@0x158, free_size@0x15C, root directory_offset@0x160.

**Directory node (B-tree)**
- At the node offset: 8 zero bytes.
- Then up to 62 subdirectory pointers of 8 bytes each (<LL block_size, dir_offset). A zero block_size ends the list.
- Entry count is a u32 at node+0x1F8 (8*63). The pointer list is truncated to count+1.
- After the count come `count` file entries of 0x20 bytes, each <LLLLLLLL: unk1 (flags; the low byte is 0x03 when compressed and 0x02 when not), file_id, file_offset, size1, timestamp (unix), version, size2, unk2. Entries with size1 == 0 are skipped.
- Lookup is a binary search on file_id within the node, recursing into subdir_ptrs[l] on a miss.
- In-order traversal visits the subtree for child i, then file entry i.

**File data block**
- At file_offset there is a 16-byte header <LLLL: 0, 0, file_id, length.
- Compressed: detected when the u16 at +0x0C == 0xDA78 (the zlib 78 DA header). Read size1+8 bytes, skip 12 bytes (8-byte block header plus a 4-byte decompressed length), then zlib.decompress. The decompressed length equals the u32 at +0x08.
- Uncompressed: read size1+8 bytes and skip 8.

**Surfaces (client_surface.dat)**
- After the 8- or 12-byte prefix, a 24-byte header: id, unk, width, height, format, data_len.
- Formats: 0x14 RGB24, 0x15 ARGB/RGBA32, 0x1C 8-bit grayscale, 0x1F4 JPEG, and FourCC DXT1/DXT3/DXT5 (0x31545844 / 0x33545844 / 0x35545844).

**Sound**
- 16-byte header <LLLL (0, 0, file_id, size1-0x10), followed by a raw RIFF/WAV or OggS payload.

**Cells (client_cell_N.dat)**
- Landblock file_ids are in the ranges 0x8001xxxx / 0x8002xxxx. Other ranges seen but not decoded: 0x2701/0x2702xxxx, 0x8021/22, 0x8041/42, 0x8051/52.
- Content header <LLLL: file_id, then 0 or 0x00200000+file_id, then 0, then 0x441.
- Heightmap: 0x441 = 33x33 u16 heights. The full content size is 0x1168.

**Other**
- anim.py asserts the compressed flag but only partly decodes the format.
- History: the first commit was 2012-07-14, "find file by id" was added 2012-08-10, and the heightmap work-in-progress was committed 2013-01-03.
last_activity: 2014-07-15 (PEP8/whitespace only; last substantive work 2013-01-03, most format work July-August 2012)

label: verify:lotro-fov (mklinik)
actual_description: Cheat Engine tables by Markus Klinik that change the LOTRO third-person camera field of view, written to help with motion sickness caused by the narrow default FOV. Files: lotro-3rd-person-FOV-32bit.CT, lotro-3rd-person-FOV-64bit.CT, lotroclient-fov-work-in-progress.CT, README.md, LICENSE and a doc/ folder with screenshots and developer notes. I checked it by WebFetch of the repo page, the README, the LICENSE, the commit history and both .CT files. The local git clone and the API call could not run because the scratch disk was full (ENOSPC). The claim is accurate apart from the license field: it says "see repo", but the repo uses MIT. The README is unsure of the character-select factor ("60 (I think)"), so the claim's "about 60" is right to hedge.
license: MIT
last_activity: 2020-11-05. All 15 commits were made on 2020-11-04 and 2020-11-05, and the repo has had no activity since. The pointer offsets are tied to client builds from November 2020 and are now almost certainly out of date.
key_facts:
- FOV model, according to the README: the client multiplies the aspect ratio (for example 1.777777 for 16:9) by a per-scene factor. The factors are about 60 for character select (the README says "60 (I think)"), 45 for in-game third person, and unknown for first person. 3D character portraits are a separate scene with their own value.
- The README says the value lives in a nested object that moves every time the scene changes or the game restarts. It is reached through a base pointer plus 4 indirections.
- How the value was found: scan memory for floats between 44.999999 and 45.000001, then keep only the values that stay constant during gameplay.
- 64-bit table: base "lotroclient64.exe"+26E5240, offsets 18, 70, 0, 10 (hex), value type float.
- 32-bit table: base "lotroclient.exe"+17d94a0, offsets 10, 68, 0, C (hex), value type float.
- Both tables bind Ctrl+PageUp and Ctrl+PageDown to change the value by ±5. The saved values in the tables (85 and 95) are the author's own modified settings, not the game's defaults.
- The README warns to use the hotkeys only in third-person mode while in the game, or memory gets corrupted.
- The repo contains no game code and no assets.
how_to_use: Reference only. The useful part is behavioral: in-game third-person FOV is 45 × aspect ratio and character select uses about 60 (unconfirmed). That is small enough to restate in our own camera spec and code, and the MIT license allows it anyway. The memory offsets are of no use to a clean-room client. They are tied to 2020 client binaries and reflect the original program's internal layout, so we should not copy them into our docs or code. If an exact FOV match matters, check the 45/60 factors and how the aspect ratio is applied by comparing screenshots from the real client side by side. Do not depend on this repo or port it.

label: verify:ddolauncher (n0la / Florian Stinglmayr)
actual_description: A small, unmaintained Python 3 command-line launcher for Dungeons & Dragons Online, not LOTRO. It is one script, ddolauncher.py, plus setup.py for cx_Freeze. It reads TurbineLauncher.exe.config, queries the Turbine GLS datacenter SOAP service, logs in with LoginAccount, waits in the world queue (TakeANumber), then starts dndclient.exe with the GLS ticket. It can log in several accounts at once, run under Wine, and run the patcher. It does not reimplement any part of the game client, so the claim's kind "client-reimpl" is wrong. The repo also has a dumps/ folder with three real captured server responses: getdatacenters.txt, login.txt (username and ticket replaced with LOGINID/TICKETID) and queue.txt. The repo has one branch, master, and one pull request ref, refs/pull/1/head.
license: BSD-2-Clause
last_activity: Last commit 2016-10-10 ("Fix spelling in README.txt", Florian Stinglmayr, 2a989586). The code dates from 2012-2013. The GitHub API was rate-limited, so archive status and star count were not checked.
key_facts:
Checked by cloning the repo and reading LICENCE.txt, README.txt, ddolauncher.py and dumps/*. Location: ~/.cache/tessera/clones/ddolauncher

License:
- LICENCE.txt is the standard 2-clause BSD text, "Copyright (c) 2012, Florian Stinglmayr".
- The source header reads "Copyright 2012 - 2013 Florian Stinglmayr" and "Copyright 2013 Scott Winburn".
- README says "two clause BSD licence".

Protocol facts (Turbine GLS, which LOTRO also uses):
1. Config: TurbineLauncher.exe.config, appSettings keys "Launcher.DataCenterService.GLS" (the datacenter URL) and "DataCenter.GameName".
2. GetDatacenters:
   - SOAP 1.1 POST over HTTP port 80, namespace http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS, SOAPAction "http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS/GetDatacenters", body `<game>NAME</game>`.
   - The response is GetDatacentersResult/Datacenter, which holds Name, Worlds/World, AuthServer, PatchServer ("patch.ddo.com:80") and LauncherConfigurationServer (a ...server.config.xml URL).
   - Each World holds Name, LoginServerUrl (shows "(invalid service specified)" in the dump), ChatServerUrl (ip:2900), StatusServerUrl (StatusServer.aspx?s=<internal ip>), Order and Language.
3. StatusServer: GET the StatusServerUrl. The XML has a `<loginservers>` field and a `<queueurls>` field, each a ';'-separated list. The script uses the first entry as the client's -h host and as the queue URL.
4. LoginAccount:
   - SOAP POST over HTTPS to the AuthServer URL (.../GLS.AuthServer/Service.asmx), SOAPAction "http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS/LoginAccount", fields username, password and an empty additionalInfo.
   - The response is LoginAccountResult, which holds Subscriptions/GameSubscription and Ticket.
   - GameSubscription holds Game, Name (the subscription/account name passed as -a), Description, ProductTokens/string[], CustomerServiceTokens, Status, BillingSystemTime and AdditionalInfo.
5. World queue:
   - Form POST to https://gls.ddo.com/GLS.AuthServer/LoginQueue.aspx with "command=TakeANumber&subscription=..&ticket=..&ticket_type=GLS&queue_url=..".
   - The XML reply `<Result>` holds Command, HResult (0x hex), QueueName (GUID), QueueNumber, NowServingNumber, LoginTier and ContextNumber.
   - The script polls every 2 s until QueueNumber <= NowServingNumber.
6. Client command line (dndclient.exe): `-h <loginserver> -a <subscription name> --glsticketdirect <ticket> --chatserver "<ip:2900>" --language English --rodat on --outport 5201 (+1 per extra instance; the client binds this port) --gametype DDO --supporturl ... --supportserviceurl ... --authserverurl ".../Service.asmx" --glsticketlifetime 21600`.
7. Patching: `rundll32.exe PatchClient.dll,Patch <patchserver> --highres --filesonly --language <lang> --productcode <game>`, run once and then again with --dataonly instead of --filesonly.

All endpoints are DDO hosts from 2012 (gls.ddo.com, gls-auth.ddo.com, tss.turbine.com) and are probably out of date. LOTRO's equivalents differ (lotroclient.exe, LOTRO game names and servers).
how_to_use: Use as a reference only, ideally alongside newer LOTRO-specific launchers (OneLauncher, Pylotro). The license would allow porting, since 2-clause BSD only requires keeping the copyright notice, but the code is small, made for DDO, from 2012, and written in old Python 2/3 style with `is` used for comparisons and old ssl.wrap_socket calls, so there is little worth porting. Its value is the documented login flow and the real captured XML responses. Use them to write the spec and test fixtures for our launcher/login module and for any local mock GLS server built for testing, adapting them to LOTRO (lotroclient.exe and LOTRO GLS endpoints). Before relying on endpoint URLs or arguments, check them against a current LOTRO launcher. The claim gets most things right: it exists, it is Python, it is BSD by Florian Stinglmayr, it has dumps of all three responses, and it calls the patcher through rundll32. Two corrections: the kind should be "launcher", not "client-reimpl", and the game is DDO, not LOTRO, although both run on the same Turbine GLS system. The license is exactly BSD-2-Clause, with Scott Winburn as an extra copyright holder in the source header.

actual_description: PyLotRO is a Linux/macOS game launcher for LOTRO and DDO, written in Python with PyQt4. It is not a client reimplementation, so the claim's kind "client-reimpl" is wrong. It logs in through Turbine GLS SOAP, reads world status, joins the world queue, runs the patcher (patchclient.dll via rundll32 under Wine or CrossOver) and starts the original lotroclient.exe under Wine. The GitHub repo nwestfal/pylotro is a fork of Lynx3d/pylotro (GitHub marks it isFork, parent Lynx3d/pylotro) and already contains every upstream commit. It has 66 commits. Its last commit is 19c0609 on 2021-04-19, "Update certificate chain after game update 29.5"; the one before is 2020-02-12, "Added option to Game Settings to select game client", v0.27. It has 8 stars and 3 forks and is not archived, but it is effectively dormant. Original author: Alan Jackson (AJackson), based on his earlier LotROLinux and on SNy's CLI launcher. The Launchpad page https://launchpad.net/pylotro exists: registered 2009-04-07, maintainer Alan Jackson, licence GNU GPL v3, code at lp:pylotro (old Bazaar), last announcement PyLotRO 0.1.6. Most later work moved to the OneLauncher project, which is not verified here.
license: GPL-3.0-or-later
last_activity: 2021-04-19 (last commit on master, 19c0609). Upstream Lynx3d/pylotro HEAD 143b38e is already contained in it.
how_to_use: Use as reference only, by writing a spec from it. Do not copy code into a project that may not be GPL. It is GPL-3.0-or-later (COPYING is GPLv3, and source headers say "either version 3 ... or any later version"). Copying code is fine only if our launcher component is itself GPL-3-compatible. It has nothing on rendering, the .dat format or the game protocol. Its value is a working, readable record of the pre-game bootstrap flow: GLS SOAP login, the launcher config keys, the world queue, and the client command-line argument template. A reimplemented client needs that flow to get a GLS ticket and the login/chat server addresses. The code is old (PyQt4, a pinned CA chain) and the endpoints may have changed since SSG's 2021+ updates, so check it against a current, maintained launcher such as OneLauncher before relying on it. Note that it is a fork mirror, so cite Lynx3d/pylotro or launchpad.net/pylotro as the origin. Fix the claim: kind should be "launcher", not "client-reimpl".
key_facts:
Details below come from the cloned source, mainly ~/.cache/tessera/clones/nwestfal-pylotro/PyLotROLauncher/PyLotROUtils.py.
(1) Datacenter lookup is a SOAP 1.1 POST using namespace http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS. It sends GetDatacenters with a <game> parameter and SOAPAction http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS/GetDatacenters. The service URL comes from the key "Launcher.DataCenterService.GLS" in TurbineLauncher.exe.config (dndlauncher.exe.config for DDO). The response gives realms (worlds) with fields such as ChatServerUrl and a login-queue URL, plus the patch server and the launch config server.
(2) Login is a LoginAccount SOAP call with <username>, <password> and an empty <additionalInfo>, SOAPAction .../GLS/LoginAccount. The response has a <Ticket> element (the GLS ticket) and subscription or account entries.
(3) The launcher config XML (appSettings <add key=...>) carries these keys: DataCenter.GameName, Patching.ProductCode, WorldQueue.LoginQueue.URL, WorldQueue.TakeANumber.Parameters, URL.NewsFeed, URL.NewsStyleSheet, Launcher.NewsFeedCSSUrl, GameClient.Arg.{crashreceiver, DefaultUploadThrottleMbps, bugurl, authserverurl, supporturl, supportserviceurl, glsticketlifetime}. It also has the game-client argument template and the 32-bit, legacy and x64 client filenames; the x64 client runs from the "x64/" subdirectory.
(4) World queue: the launcher posts TakeANumber parameters to the queue URL with the account and ticket, then loops until the returned queue number is no greater than the "now serving" number.
(5) Client launch (StartGame.py) fills the template by substituting {SUBSCRIPTION}, {LOGIN} (login server), {GLS} (ticket), {CHAT} (chat server), {LANG}, {GLSTICKETLIFETIME}, {SUPPORTURL} and others. This is the exact set of inputs a reimplemented client must accept from a launcher.
(6) Patching (PatchWindow.py) runs `rundll32.exe patchclient.dll,Patch <patchServerURL> --language <lang> --productcode <code> --filesonly` and then runs it again without --filesonly to patch the .dat files. Files are patched twice because patchclient.dll can patch itself.
(7) TLS: it ships a pinned CA bundle at PyLotROLauncher/certificates/ca_certs.pem, updated at game update 29.5 (2021).
(8) It also handles a local game-client override in TurbineLauncher.exe.config (2017 commit).

label: verify:themixednuts GhidraMCP
actual_description:
A Ghidra extension written in Java that runs an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server inside Ghidra over streamable HTTP, at http://127.0.0.1:8080/mcp by default. Its gradle.properties describes it as "A Ghidra extension implementing the Model Context Protocol (MCP) by running an embedded MCP server." The repo is real and active. A shallow clone on 2026-10-03 showed HEAD 3f1d389 "chore: prepare 0.9.0 release" from 2026-09-22, and dependabot branches are open. The claim of "about 30 tools" is out of date. The current README lists 14 consolidated MCP tools:
- Analysis: analyze, inspect, script_guidance
- Editing: annotate, functions, symbols, data_types, memory, delete
- Debugging: debugger
- Projects: project, batch_operations
- Version Tracking: vt_sessions, vt_operations

Earlier versions may have exposed more, finer-grained tools. It also offers:
- MCP resources: ghidra://programs, and per program: info, functions, symbols, datatypes, memory, imports, exports, strings, rtti, listing/{address}, function/{address}/decompile.
- Prompts: analyze_function, analyze_vtable, compare_binaries, find_vulnerabilities, map_data_structures, rename_analysis, triage_binary.
license: MIT
how_to_use:
Use as an external tool only, not something the project depends on or ports. It is a developer workstation aid for agent-assisted reverse engineering in Ghidra.

Its legal fit for a clean-room LOTRO project is narrow:
- Use it only on the "dirty" side of a clean-room split, where an analyst studies the client binaries (for example lotroclient.exe / lotroclient64.exe) that the analyst owns legitimately.
- Use it mainly to document data formats and protocols: DAT file structures, property/DID layouts, network message layouts. The RTTI/vtable views and the analyze_vtable and map_data_structures prompts suit MSVC C++ class recovery.
- Only written specifications (no decompiled code) should reach the clean implementation side.
- Never commit or redistribute decompiler output, Ghidra project databases or symbol exports.

The MIT license allows free use, and nothing from it ships in the client. Pin the GhidraMCP version to the matching Ghidra version, because each release is tied to one Ghidra version (0.9.0 needs Ghidra 12.1.4).

Alternatives to compare include LaurieWired/GhidraMCP (Apache-2.0, a Python bridge) and the newer GhidraMCP forks. This one has the advantage of running inside Ghidra as an embedded HTTP server, with no Python bridge.

label: verify:DDO-ML (traversc)
actual_description: The repo exists. It is DDO-ML, a GUI launcher for Dungeons & Dragons Online written in AutoIt3, used for multi-account login, saved and encrypted passwords, and auto-selecting a character. It is not a client reimplementation, so the claim's kind "client-reimpl" is wrong. The right kind is launcher / login-protocol reference. It contains src/ddolauncher.au3, an AutoIt port by MIvanIsten (Maturicz Iván) of Florian Stinglmayr's Python ddolauncher (github.com/n0la/ddolauncher, 2012), plus DDO-ML.au3 (the GUI), ddoclient_wrapper.au3 and _XMLDomWrapper.au3. Prebuilt .exe files are committed to the repo. HEAD is 2e96f98, dated 2025-07-15, "hotfix for update 74.1" (changelog 1.5.3.1), and tag v1.2.0.0 also exists. The repo page shows about 14 stars. The claim's details check out against the source: the queue POST URL-encodes the ticket and queue_url, and the 2025 README lists the 64-bit server names Moonsea [EU], Shadowdale [US] and Thrane [US], with old servers renamed to "X [Old]". Calling it "active" is a stretch: there is one hotfix commit in 2025, and the previous release before it was in 2020.
license: none/unknown (there is no LICENSE file. The README says source is included for self-compilation but asks people "do NOT widely distribute a modified executable without my permission", so in effect it is all-rights-reserved. The upstream n0la/ddolauncher license was not checked here.)
how_to_use: Reference-only, as clean-room protocol documentation. Because there is no license and redistribution is explicitly restricted, do not copy the code. It is also AutoIt and Windows/MSXML-specific, so it would not be worth porting anyway. It is useful as a second, independent confirmation of the Turbine GLS login / world-queue handshake that LOTRO shares with DDO: the same GLS SOAP namespace, the same TakeANumber queue and the same client command-line arguments. A LOTRO launcher or login module can be written from the protocol facts below. For a license-compatible reference that targets LOTRO itself, prefer OneLauncher or PyLotro, or n0la/ddolauncher after checking its license. Fix the claim's kind to "launcher/login-protocol reference", not client-reimpl.
key_facts:
All of the following come from reading src/ddolauncher.au3 at HEAD 2e96f98:
1) Bootstrap. Read ddo.launcherconfig, or fall back to TurbineLauncher.exe.config, from the game directory. Take appSettings key "Launcher.DataCenterService.GLS" (the GLS datacenter SOAP URL) and key "DataCenter.GameName".
2) GetDatacenters. SOAP POST with SOAPAction http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS/GetDatacenters (namespace http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS). Parse //GetDatacentersResult/*, then for each datacenter read Worlds/* with child elements Name, LoginServerUrl, ChatServerUrl, Language and StatusServerUrl. The datacenter also provides the auth server URL and the launcher config URL (configserver).
3) World status. Plain GET on StatusServerUrl, which returns XML. //loginservers is a ';'-separated list (use the first entry as the host) and //queueurls is a ';'-separated list (use the first entry as the world queue_url). An empty response means the world is down; the code then sets the host to 0.0.0.0.
4) Launcher config. GET configserver and read appSettings keys "Game.Version", "GameClient.Arg.glsticketlifetime" (default 21600), "WorldQueue.LoginQueue.URL", and "GameClient.WIN32.Filename", "GameClient.WIN32Legacy.Filename" or "GameClient.WIN64.Filename". The 64-bit exe lives under the x64\ subfolder. Which one is used depends on UserPreferences.ini [Launcher] GameClientType: 1 = Win32, 2 = Win32Legacy, 3 = Win64. The supporturl and supportserviceurl args were removed in DDO Update 51.2.
5) LoginAccount. SOAP POST to the auth server with SOAPAction http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS/LoginAccount and body <LoginAccount xmlns="http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS"><username/><password/><additionalInfo/></LoginAccount>. From the response read //Ticket and //Subscriptions/GameSubscription, each with Game, Name and Description. Pick the subscription whose Game matches DataCenter.GameName, or whose Description matches the user's choice, and use its Name as the account name.
6) World queue. Form-encoded POST to WorldQueue.LoginQueue.URL with body "command=TakeANumber&subscription=<subName>&ticket=<urlenc ticket>&ticket_type=GLS&queue_url=<urlenc world queue_url>". The code sends the header Content-Type: text/xml; charset=utf-8 even though the body is form-encoded. The URL encoder escapes every byte except [A-Za-z0-9-_.]. The response has hex fields //HResult, //QueueNumber and //NowServingNumber. The client polls every 2 seconds until QueueNumber <= NowServingNumber.
7) Client command line. <exe> -h <loginserver> -a <subscriptionName> --glsticketdirect <ticket> --chatserver <ChatServerUrl> --language <lang> --rodat on --gametype <GameName> --authserverurl <authserver> --glsticketlifetime <n> [--outport <port>].
8) DDO Update 74.1 (July 2025) added 64-bit-only servers Moonsea [EU], Shadowdale [US] and Thrane [US], and renamed the legacy servers to "Argonnessen [Old]" and similar, plus "Cormyr [US]".
last_activity: 2025-07-15 (commit 2e96f98 "hotfix for update 74.1" by Maturicz Iván / MIvanIsten). The release before that was 1.5.3.0 on 2020-12-01.

label: verify:ACUnreal
actual_description:
Asheron's Call (AC1, Throne of Destruction era) .dat asset exporter/importer for Unreal Engine 5 (UE 5.3/5.5; README still says 5.3). An editor plugin plus a commandlet (ACUnrealExportResources) export AC .dat content to FBX, T3D, WAV, PNG and DXT, then run scripted imports that rebuild the Dereth landscape (r16 heightmap tiles), landblocks, scenes and materials inside the UE editor. The game module is very thin: a Character/GameMode/PlayerController, about 130 lines at most per file, for walking around the imported world. There is no networking, protocol or gameplay code. Calling it an "AC client prototype" overstates it. It is an asset pipeline for viewing the world in Unreal.

Verified by GitLab API and a shallow clone. Project id 14194458, created 2019-09-07, 4 stars, 1 fork. Branches: master, sceneryfixes, ue54. The newest commit (5ea4d0c) is from 2025-05-15, "Landscape1 hole mask UV tiling correction". Recent commits are UE 5.5 migration plus Setup/Scene scaling fixes.
license: MIT (Copyright (c) 2019 Jason Eubank). The bundled decompress.c is also MIT (Benjamin Dobell 2009 / Matthaeus Chajdas 2012-2015). Separately, Unreal Engine's EULA covers any build.
language: C++ (Unreal Engine 5 modules), one C file
last_activity: 2025-05-15 (master commit 5ea4d0c; GitLab last_activity_at 2025-05-16)
key_facts:
Source checked: Source/ACUnrealDatTools/{Public,Private}/*, about 7.4k lines in total.

1. **Dat header**
   - Read at file offset 0x140 for ToD-format dats (client_cell_1.dat, client_portal.dat, client_highres.dat, client_local_English.dat). Older retail dats use 0x12C. ToD-format is chosen by filename.
   - Fields in order: Format magic 0x00005442 ("BT"), BlockSize (256 or 1024), FileSize, Version (1/2/3 for ToD; 0x768 for old).
   - ToD only: Identifier (0, 1 or 0x69466948).
   - Then: FreeBlockHead, FreeBlockTail, FreeBlockCount, RootDirectoryOffset.
   - ToD only: NewLRU, OldLRU, bUseLRU (u8 + 3 pad), MasterMapID (0 or 0x25000000), EnginePackVersion (0x6E portal, 0x16 cell), GamePackVersion, VersionMajor[16], VersionMinor.
   - This "BT" block-filesystem family is the same Turbine lineage as LOTRO's dats, which also put the header at 0x140 with magic 0x5442. The LOTRO-specific fields and entry layout differ, though, and LOTRO adds zlib-compressed entries. ACUnreal has no decompression of dat entries.

2. **Block chains**
   - Each block starts with a u32 offset to the next block (0 ends the chain), followed by BlockSize-4 bytes of payload.

3. **Directory B-tree node**
   - Layout: u32 Offsets[62] (child nodes; Offsets[0]==0 means a leaf), then u32 EntryCount, then Entries[62].
   - ToD entry = {Flags, Identifier, Offset, Size, Time, Version}, 24 bytes. The node is 1740 bytes for ToD and 1020 for old.
   - Lookup is a linear scan for the first entry id >= target, then recursion into Offsets[Index].

4. **AC resource-ID high byte types**
   - 0x01 Model(GfxObj), 0x02 Setup, 0x03 Animation, 0x04 Palette, 0x05 ImgTex, 0x06 ImgColor (RenderSurface), 0x08 Surface, 0x09 MotionTable, 0x0A Sound, 0x0D Environment, 0x12 Scene, 0x13 Region, 0x20 SoundTable, 0x22 EnumMapper, 0x32 ParticleEmitter, 0x33 PhysicsScript, 0x34 PhysicsScriptTable.
   - These are AC-specific. LOTRO uses different DID class ranges.

5. **Per-type parsers**
   - Model/GfxObj, Setup, Region, Scene, Surface, Palette, ImgTex, Sound, Environment, Cell/landblock (ACUnrealCellFile.cpp, 330 lines) and Landscape (823 lines: height tables, terrain textures, hole masks).
   - Writers: FBX (custom ASCII FBX writer), T3D and CSV.

6. **decompress.c is a DXT1/3/5 texture decoder**, not a dat or archive decompressor. The claim implies otherwise.

7. **The claim's other points check out.** It lists Portal/Cell/Surface/Setup/Region/Landscape tools and FBX/T3D exporters, and those are present. ExportResources.sh runs the UE editor commandlet headless with -nullrhi.
how_to_use:
Reference only.

The MIT license would legally allow porting, but the code is tied to Unreal (FArchive, TArray, check(), UE_LOG). It targets AC1's dat format and object types, not LOTRO's. A LOTRO engine should not depend on Unreal (EULA, size, and a custom engine is closer to the original client).

Useful as a cross-check:
- (a) the shared Turbine "BT" dat block-chain and B-tree directory layout (header at 0x140, magic 0x5442, 62-slot nodes, next-block-pointer chains). Compare it against LOTRO-specific readers such as LotroCompanion/lotro-tools and datexport-derived code to see what changed between AC and LOTRO.
- (b) how the older AC engine laid out its asset types (GfxObj/Setup/Surface/Region/landblock). Some of that lineage survives in LOTRO.
- (c) an example of an "import user-supplied dats into a modern engine at runtime or import time, never redistribute" pipeline. That fits our legal model.

If we copy any snippet, keep the MIT notice. The bundled DXT decoder is MIT, but our project should use a maintained library (bcdec, or GPU-native BCn) instead.

Do not cite it as a "client reimplementation". It has no networking, protocol or gameplay code.

label: verify:lotro-analyzer (bwgypyth)
actual_description: The repo exists. It is "A web based analyzer for lotro packets" by bwgypyth (author email bwgypyth@gmx.net; package com.blogspot.bwgypyth.lotro). GitLab project id 248573 in the "lotro" group, which also holds lotro/unpacker. It is a small Java servlet/JSP web app, built with Maven as a WAR. Users upload raw packets as hex strings, sort them into PacketGroups, and add named Analyses. An Analysis is made of AnalysisEntries, each marking a byte range (start/end) with a name, an HTML description and colors. This gives colored byte-range markup of each packet. Packets and groups can be exported as JSON or binary (application/octet-stream) and imported back as JSON. Storage is JPA/Hibernate 5.2 through the JNDI datasource jdbc/lotroDS. It started as a Google App Engine app; AppEngine support was dropped in the last commit (2016-09-25). The repo contains no packet data or captures, and no capture or proxy code. Corrections to the claim: development was mostly in 2013 (85 commits, all by bwgypyth, 2013-03-09 to 2013-10-13), plus one commit in 2016. It is not a 2016 tool. The license is not "none stated": every Java file carries an MIT license header (Copyright (c) 2013 bwgypyth), though the repo has no top-level LICENSE file. It has no README.
license: MIT (in per-file source headers, "Copyright (c) 2013 bwgypyth"; no top-level LICENSE file)
how_to_use: Use as reference only, as a UI and data-model idea for a community packet-annotation corpus. Its data model is: packet group, then packet (hex), then a named analysis, then byte-range entries with name, description and colors. The MIT license would allow porting, but the code is not worth it: it is outdated Java EE/JSP built for 2013-era AppEngine, the default protocol annotations are commented out, and it ships no data. A modern project would do better with Kaitai Struct or ImHex patterns, or a Wireshark Lua dissector, plus a git-versioned corpus of user-captured pcaps or hex dumps. One idea worth copying is storing annotations as JSON byte ranges next to raw captures. The few protocol hints in it come from one person's 2013 guesses (see key_facts) and are unconfirmed. Do not rely on them, and check them against the current client's traffic. Distributing captured packets is generally low risk, but the corpus should not include account credentials or session keys.
key_facts: Verified by git ls-remote (HEAD 68e41c5c, master), the GitLab API (created 2015-04-25, i.e. migrated there; last_activity 2016-09-25; 0 stars, 0 forks; public), and a shallow-then-full clone. Model classes: Packet {String data (hex, uppercased, whitespace stripped, column length 16777216), name, group, analyses}; Analysis {packet, name, entries ordered by start asc, end desc}; AnalysisEntry {name, start, end, description, color, foregroundColor}; PacketGroup {name, description, packets}. Servlets: /packet_upload, /import/packet (JSON packet_data plus group_key), packet and group export (JSON or binary). Unverified 2013 guesses at the LOTRO UDP packet header, from the commented-out AnalysisFactory defaults: the header spans bytes 0x00-0x13 (20 bytes); 0x00-0x01 is a "Communication ID"; 0x02-0x03 is the "Size of payload data"; 0x04-0x07 is a "Root command" (flags); 0x08-0x0B is "Number of all packets sent in this session" (sequence); data starts at 0x14. If byte 0x04 (hex chars 8-10) == 0x08, there is 6 bytes of extra data at 0x14-0x19. If it == 0x0B, there is 0x12 (18) bytes at 0x14-0x25. A "subcommand" occupies 3 bytes at 0x14+offset. This layout matches the general shape of the Asheron's Call/Turbine UDP header (sequence, flags, checksum, id, time, size), but offsets need checking against modern captures.
language: Java 8 (Servlet 3.1 / JSP / JPA-Hibernate 5.2 / org.json / Guava; jQuery front-end)
last_activity: 2016-09-25 (commit "Drop appengine support"); before that, 2013-10-13

label: verify:lotro-gls (bwgypyth)
actual_description: "An authentication meta server" (GitLab project id 248567, created 2015-04-25, last activity 2016-10-29, 0 stars, 0 forks, no README). It is a Visual Studio/MonoDevelop solution (GLS.sln) for two ASP.NET 3.5 .asmx SOAP web services, both stubs that return hardcoded data. GLS.AuthServer has LoginAccount(username, password, additionalInfo), which returns a UserProfile; it ignores the credentials and always gives the same hardcoded ticket. It also has RefreshTicket(ticket), which returns its input unchanged. GLS.DataCenterServer has GetDatacenters(game), which returns Datacenter[] with one hardcoded world. In total it is about 150 lines of meaningful C#. Commits are all by bwgypyth <bwgypyth@gmx.net>: the initial commit is dated 2010-04-07, there were tidy-ups in 2015-04 and the last commit (3c0fa6d, "Drop GLS.userprefs") is from 2016-10-29. Abandoned. Sibling projects in the same 'lotro' GitLab group: lotro/server ("Code written by tAmMo to capture, encrypt and decrypt packages", activity 2020-03), lotro/analyzer (web-based LOTRO packet analyzer, 2016), lotro/htdocs ("htdocs necessary for the meta server", 2015) and lotro/unpacker (source of lotrounpacker.ucoz.com, 2020). lotro/server and lotro/analyzer are probably more useful for networking than gls is. VERDICT ON CLAIM: the name, URL, owner, language and kind are accurate. Overstated: (1) "proof that the official launcher and client accept a custom meta server". The repo has no README, notes or test evidence. World.LoginServerUrl is literally "(invalid service specified)", so it never got a client to a login server. At most it suggests the launcher's GLS discovery can be pointed at a custom endpoint, and that is unverified. (2) "license: none stated" is slightly wrong. There is no LICENSE file, but World.cs (one file only) has an HPND-sell-variant/X11-style permissive notice ("Copyright 2008-2009 bwgypyth", left over from a Red Hat template). All other files have no license.
license: none (no LICENSE file); only GLS.DataCenterServer/World.cs carries an HPND-sell-variant style permission notice (Copyright 2008-2009 bwgypyth); everything else is unlicensed / all rights reserved by default
how_to_use: Reference only; do not copy. Most of the repo has no license. The long WebMethod/WebService Description strings appear to be copied verbatim from Turbine's own WSDL, so they are Turbine-authored text and should not go into our tree. label: verify:LOTRO-Tools / lotro-server (tAmMo, maintained by bwgy
actual_description:
The repo is "LOTRO-Tools" (README title). The GitLab project description is "Code written by tAmMo to capture, encrypt and decrypt packages". bwgypyth runs it. It is a C# solution with these parts:
- liblotro: a big-endian reader/writer, Decrypt.cs, Encrypt.cs, HelperMethods.cs (RSA + RC4) and data/ tables.
- Protocol: about 40 packet classes covering the Payload/PayloadHeader/session-setup handshake (SYNACK, Synchronize, Acknowledgment, OldClientVersion, WrongGLSTicket, Terminate, ConfirmSequence, DoubleLoginNOK, CharaData and others).
- A UDP Server (ports 9000/9001) with XML account and character files.
- LOTROendecrypt and LOTROendecryptClient command-line tools.
- LOTROPacketCaptureAndAutoDecryption, a SharpPcap/WinPcap sniffer that auto-decrypts.
- A WPF PacketBrowser contributed by Ananta Das.
- LOTRO-Investigation.pdf, v0.2 "Riders", dated 22 Jan 2013, by tAmMo.
- Helper/Helper.dll, a 237 KB closed .NET (Mono/.NET PE32) assembly.

CHANGELOG milestones: 14.03.2013 "Client working til character creation screen. Checksum working". 17.03.2013 "can create a pseudo character (sometimes)".

Git history:
- The first commit is from 2012-03-11. Most work was done 2012–2013, with WPF browser commits in Apr 2015.
- Commits on 2017-02-26/27 moved to NuGet.
- The last commits are 2020-03-02 by bwgypyth: "Convert to .NET core", "Add mock implementation of checksum generation". The HEAD commit is 5ce7a7a.
- The GitLab project was created 2015-04-25. Last activity 2020-03-01. 3 stars, 4 forks.
- A sister repo, gitlab.com/lotro/unpacker, holds source for the lotro-unpacker from lotrounpacker.ucoz.com.
license: none/unknown. There is no LICENSE or COPYING file, and no copyright headers in the source. The README only says "Use source and exe's on your own risk... Please feel free to share, comment, mod and optimize", which is not a license grant. Treat it as all rights reserved.
how_to_use:
reference-only (clean-room spec extraction). Use it to write a protocol spec document: header layout, handshake sequence, the shape of the bit-tree decompression, and the RSA/RC4 session-key flow. Then implement from that spec.
- Do not copy code. There is no license.
- Do not ship or depend on Helper.dll. It is a closed binary, and decompiling it to lift the checksum algorithm creates provenance risk.
- Do not redistribute liblotro/data/table_* or Helper/data/*_raw. The source says these tables were dumped from the running client's memory, so they are derived from copyrighted client data. Our implementation should extract equivalent tables at runtime from the user's own legally obtained client or data files.
- Do not use liblotro/data/private or public. These are a project-generated RSA keypair that was "used to inject the public key into the client", which means patching the client binary. A faithful legal client reimplementation is the reverse direction anyway: we need the client side of the handshake (server public key, RSA-encrypt the session key), and the private server key cannot be recovered. Do not ship patched binaries or keys from this repo.
- The protocol is from the 2012–2013 Riders of Rohan era. Expect drift against current live servers.

Corrections to the claim:
1. "The 0xBADD70DD header checksum formula" overstates it. The constant and a partial additive formula exist in PayloadHeader.calcChecksum (a private method that is never called). The real header and data checksum tables live in the closed Helper.dll (updateChecksumTable / generateInitialChecksumTable / generateChecksumFromHead). The liblotro/Checksum.cs in the repo is a 2020 mock that returns 0.
2. "Flag constants" overstates it. There are only raw 4-byte "Action" identifiers per packet class, such as Synchronize = 00 00 04 00. They are not named flag constants.
3. "Furthest public LOTRO server prototype" is plausible but I could not verify it.
4. The claimed 2013 date is accurate for the character-creation milestone. Repo activity runs 2012–2020.
key_facts:
Verified against the cloned source in ~/.cache/tessera/clones/lotro-server. Paths below are relative to that clone.

**Packet header** (Protocol/Generic/PayloadHeader.cs and the PDF, all fields big-endian):
- u16 SessionID
- u16 DataLength
- 4-byte Action/identifier
- u32 SequenceNumber
- u32 Checksum
- u32 ACKNR (temporary session or ack number)
- The header is 0x14 (20) bytes in session. During session setup it is 22 bytes, because the packet starts with an extra 0x0000 prefix.
- Constant 0xBADD70DD appears as `private const UInt32 defaultValue = 0xBADD70DD;`.
- calcChecksum sums little-endian u32 words of the reversed header, plus 0xBADD70DD plus 0x00140000, and returns 0 - (sum - word1). This method is dead code. Live checksums go through the closed Helper.dll, using generateChecksumForHeader(SessionID, DataLength, Action, Seq, Checksum, ACKNR).

**Encryption flag in packet bytes 0–2:**
- If bytes 0–1 are 0x0000, the packet is unencrypted (handshake).
- If byte 2 is 0x00, the packet is not encrypted. That padding byte is skipped.
- The first 2 bytes (the session ID) are never transformed.

**"Decryption"** (liblotro/Decrypt.cs) is really Huffman-style bit-tree decoding:
- Data is processed in 4-byte blocks, with the first 4 bits of the first block skipped.
- The bit order is reversed. A jump table [state, bit] walks the tree; a negative entry plus an offset (16372 for client, 16125 for server) indexes a lookup list of output byte strings.
- There are separate client and server tables. A comment says they were "extracted from hex dump when the client is running", not found in the exe.
- Table files: liblotro/data/table_jump_client (130968 B), table_jump_server (128992 B), table_lookup_client (205027 B), table_lookup_server (201323 B).

**Handshake** (PDF, sections 2–3):
- The first client packet is unencrypted. It carries a length-prefixed client version string (e.g. "061004_netver:7537; didver:926CD8E3-2984-4CA9-9C6B-6DF2C8EB6BC3"), a u32 Unix timestamp, and the UTF-16 account name.
- It also carries a 128-bit session key, RSA-1024 encrypted (the last 128 bytes, byte-reversed, PKCS#1 v1.5; see extractSessionKeyFrom1stClientPacket).
- The account name and GLS ticket are RC4-encrypted with that session key.
- The server replies with a temporary session key and two 32-bit checksum seeds. The client echoes the reversed session key and builds the checksum table.
- Later the server sends character data and then the world server IP/port, and the client reconnects to the world server.
- SYNACK contains the constant 16 bytes DA 82 CF 61 37 12 45 85 9C 4E 1C 6D 01 F1 62 BB.
- Wireshark capture filter used: "not broadcast and not multicast and udp and not port 53 and not port 9200".

**Other facts:**
- The server listens on UDP 9000 (login) and 9001 (world) in config.xml.
- liblotro/data/private is a project-generated RSA private key, not the real server key. The README says it was used to inject the public key into a patched client. The CHANGELOG later claims "no patched client needed".
- The PDF targets the Riders of Rohan client, Jan 2013.
language: C# (.NET Framework, converted to .NET Core in 2020; the PacketBrowser is WPF)
last_activity: 2020-03-02 (last commit by bwgypyth: README rename, mock checksum, .NET Core port); substantive RE work 2012-03 to 2013-03; PacketBrowser 2015-04

label: verify:LOTRO-Investigation.pdf v0.2 (tAmMo, Jan 2013)
actual_description:
I confirmed this is a real 15-page PDF (709,527 bytes; Microsoft Word 2010 export, created 2013-02-20). Its title page reads "LOTRO Investigation v0.2 (Riders)", dated "Januar 22 2013", with the subtitle "Gathering information for building a private LOTRO server". The only listed author is tAmMo, and its changelog says "22.01.2013 Update packets to Riders Version". It lives in the GitLab repo lotro/server, whose description is "Code written by tAmMo to capture, encrypt and decrypt packages". bwgypyth maintains the repo: initial commit 2012-03-11, the PDF was updated to Riders of Rohan on 2013-03-02, and the last commit (port to .NET Core) is dated 2020-03-02. GitLab reports last_activity_at as 2020-03-01 UTC, which is the same evening (the commit has a +0100 offset). The blob and raw URLs both return HTTP 200, and git ls-remote works (HEAD 5ce7a7a).

What the PDF actually contains:
1. A short Wireshark workflow with the capture filter "Not broadcast and not multicast and udp and not port 53 and not port 9200", using Follow UDP Stream and a CreatePacketsFromWiresharkHexDump tool.
2. A communication flow written as prose only.
3. Annotated hex dumps of the 1st and 2nd client packets and the 1st and 2nd server packets. It also has a "client confirms server session" packet, and a ping/ack packet that appears under section 3.4.2 "Client confirm/request last/next sequence packet" but is captioned "Figure 12: Server pong packet".
4. A Document Attachments page that points to the C# source in the same repo.

The claim is mostly accurate but slightly overstated:
- RSA is never named. The text says a 128-bit session key block is encrypted with a 1024-bit public key (it miswrites "Clients Public Key"), and that the "Account name + GLS Ticket Block is RC4 encrypted with the Session Key".
- The world-server referral is only two prose sentences ("When user joins world, server sends ip and port of world server"). There is no packet layout for it.
- Many fields are marked "(???)" or "Unknown". The 2nd server packet is mostly unexplained ("The other values are unknown to me").
- The handshake description is partial.
license: none/unknown (no LICENSE file in the repo; the PDF has no license statement; the AssemblyInfo.cs files have only default Visual Studio copyright attributes; the README says "Please feel free to share, comment, mod and optimize", which is not an actual license)
how_to_use:
Use the PDF for reference only, as a clean-room source of facts about the protocol. Its observations about packet structure are uncopyrightable facts, and we can restate them in our own protocol spec, citing the PDF.

Do not copy the PDF's text, figures or code. Do not copy or port the repo's C# code, Helper.dll, or the data/table_*_client_raw files, which look like data dumped from the client binary. None of it has a license.

The PDF describes the 2012/2013 Riders of Rohan protocol with client version string 061004_netver:7537. Expect the live protocol to differ, so treat every field as a hypothesis and confirm it against our own captures.

It is only useful for protocol and networking work, not for the client renderer or DAT parsing. Its main value is:
- the header layouts (22 bytes during session setup, 20 bytes in session),
- the order of the handshake,
- the pointers to the checksum-table seeds.

The repo's Protocol/ and liblotro/ code is a better source of detail than the PDF, but its license problem is the same.
key_facts:
- UDP payload is a header followed by zero or more data objects. The header is 22 bytes during session setup (it starts with 00 00) and 20 bytes otherwise.
- Header fields, in order:
  - session ID (u16 big-endian, e.g. 0x942A, 0x0A50)
  - data-part length (u16 BE)
  - flags/"identifier" (u32, e.g. 00 01 00 00, 08 00 00 02, 00 00 40 00)
  - sequence number (u32 BE)
  - 32-bit checksum of the data part
  - temporary session number / ack.
- 1st client packet (unencrypted), session ID 0:
  - length-prefixed client version string "061004_netver:7537; didver:926CD8E3-2984-4CA9-9C6B-6DF2C8EB6BC3"
  - a u32 length of the remaining data
  - an unknown field
  - a u32 timestamp in Unix seconds (stored byte-swapped)
  - the account name as UTF-16LE with a 1-byte length prefix.
- The PDF text says the 128-bit session key block is encrypted with a known 1024-bit public key that only the server's private key can decrypt. The account name + GLS ticket block is RC4-encrypted with that session key. RSA is not named explicitly.
- 1st server packet (unencrypted) contains:
  - a session token/key (the client must echo it back byte-reversed)
  - the session ID the client should use from now on (e.g. 0x0A50)
  - two 32-bit base values that seed the server and client checksum tables
  - a constant.
- 2nd client packet echoes the reversed key back. That establishes the session.
- From the 2nd server packet on, traffic is encrypted. That packet contains the client's IP as a UTF-16 string and data objects with length-prefixed indicators. Most of it is unknown.
- Login/auth relies on a prior web-service (GLS) authentication. The server later sends account and character data. When the player enters the world, it sends the world server's IP and port, and the client opens a new connection to it. This part is prose only.
- The repo README says the shipped private key is not the real one. It was generated so a patched public key could be injected into the client. Per the 2013-03-14 CHANGELOG, the checksum later worked without a patched client, and their server reached the character creation screen.
language: PDF (English, by a German author); the accompanying repo is C# (.NET, ported to .NET Core in 2020)
last_activity: Repo: last commit 2020-03-02 (+0100) by bwgypyth, matching GitLab last_activity_at 2020-03-01T22:31Z. PDF: v0.2 dated 2013-01-22, PDF creation date 2013-02-20, last committed 2013-03-02.

label: verify:lotro-unpacker (gitlab mirror)
actual_description: A public GitLab project in the "lotro" group ("Miscellaneous code around lotro"), described as "Source for the lotro-unpacker from http://lotrounpacker.ucoz.com/". It is a Visual Studio solution with two small Windows .NET 4.0 console apps by "Dancing_on_a_rock_hacker", copyright 2011-2013: (1) lotro-unpacker / DAT_UNPACKER v1.3.2, about 900 lines of C#, and (2) localedata-extractor / LOCALDATAEXTRACTOR v1.0, about 108 lines. The repo has only 2 commits, both dated 2013-10-04 by bwgypyth ("Initial import" and "Add changelog and readme"). HEAD is 5d7162f39f7d446a2634e0e6e91e2ba307a1ec24 on master. The project was created on GitLab in 2015-04, and the API shows last_activity 2020-02-01. The code looks decompiled (ILSpy-style artifacts such as `(IntPtr)i / sizeof(void)` and nested if/else chains made from switch statements), so it is probably not the author's original source. The DAT reader does not parse the .dat format itself. It is a P/Invoke wrapper around Turbine's own proprietary DatExport.dll (which ships with the game) and zlib1T.dll. Neither DLL is in the repo. The claim is accurate on the URL, the C# language, the missing license and the description. Its "verified-by-fetch" confidence holds up. One nuance: the "unpacker" here only wraps Turbine's DLL and is not an independent DAT parser.
license: none/unknown (no LICENSE file; AssemblyInfo says "Copyright © 2011-2013 Dancing_on_a_rock_hacker"; all rights reserved by default)
last_activity: Commits dated 2013-10-04 (only 2 commits); GitLab project last_activity_at 2020-02-01
key_facts:
Verified by shallow-cloning the repo and reading all of its source files.

DatExport.dll API (from the P/Invoke signatures in lotro-unpacker/DatExport.cs):
- `OpenDatFileEx2(handle, fileName, flags, out didMasterMap, out blockSize, out vnumDatFile, out vnumGameData, out ulong datFileID, StringBuilder datIdStamp[64], StringBuilder firstIterGuid[64])`. It returns -1 on failure.
- Also exported: `CloseDatFile`, `GetNumSubfiles`, `GetSubfileCompressionFlag(handle, did)`, `GetSubfileSizes(handle, out did, out size, out iteration, offset, count)`, `GetSubfileVersion(handle, did)` and `GetSubfileData(handle, did, buf, writeOffset, out version)`.

Open flags (DCOF_*):
- UseLRU=1, Expandable=2, ReadOnly=4, Create=8, CreateIfNeeded=16, OptionalFile=32, FreeThreaded=64, LoadIterations=128, Journalled=256, SkipIndexCheck=512.
- The unpacker opens files with 130 (Expandable|LoadIterations), adding ReadOnly (4) when read-only.

Each subfile has these metadata fields:
- DataID (32-bit file id)
- size
- iteration
- version
- compression flag

Compressed subfiles:
- The first 4 bytes are the uncompressed length as a little-endian uint32.
- The rest is a zlib stream, decompressed with uncompress().

The DID is printed as 8 hex digits, and the top 3 hex digits act as a category/type prefix.
- 0x0A0xxxxx is sound: an 8-byte header, then RIFF (wav) or OggS (ogg).
- 0x040xxxxx is Havok packfile data: the magic 57 E0 E0 57 appears at offset 8. The code returns the extension "hkx", although the readme says "hks".
- 0x050xxxxx is also Havok: the same magic at offset 17.
- 0x410xxxxx and 0x411xxxxx are textures:
  - JPEG: an FF D8 FF marker at offset 24, after a 24-byte header.
  - DXT: an ASCII "DXT1", "DXT3" or "DXT5" fourcc at offsets 16-19. Width and height are int32s at offsets 8 and 12 (header 16 bytes for DXT1, 24 bytes for DXT3 and DXT5). The tool builds a 128-byte DDS header around the data.
  - Otherwise the texture is treated as uncompressed 24-bit RGB with a 24-byte header.
- 0x25xxxxxx (in client_local_*.dat) holds localization string tables.

String-table layout (localedata-extractor/Program.cs):
- Header: int32 fileId, int32 unknown, byte, then a count in a 1–2-byte varint.
- The varint format: if the high bit (0x80) is set, the value is ((b ^ 0x80) << 8) | next byte.
- Each entry has:
  - int64 token/key
  - int32 nStrings, then that many strings. Each string is a varint char-count followed by UTF-16LE text.
  - int32 nArgRefs, then that many int32 values
  - byte nArgStringGroups. Each group is an int32 count followed by that many varint-prefixed UTF-16LE strings.

dictionary.bin is the tool's own cache of int32 id/version pairs and is not a game format.

The sibling projects in the same GitLab group are probably more relevant to this project than the unpacker, but they were not verified here:
- gitlab.com/lotro/server: "Code written by tAmMo to capture, encrypt and decrypt packages", last activity 2020-03
- gitlab.com/lotro/gls: "An authentication meta server", 2016
- gitlab.com/lotro/analyzer: "A web based analyzer for lotro packets", 2016
- gitlab.com/lotro/htdocs: htdocs for the meta server
how_to_use:
Reference-only. Do not depend on it or port it. There are three reasons:
1. There is no license. The code is all-rights-reserved and appears to be decompiled from a binary, so copying it is legally unsafe.
2. It does not implement the DAT container format at all. It calls Turbine's proprietary DatExport.dll, which a clean-room project must not ship or require.
3. It is Windows/.NET 4.0 x86 only and has been dormant since 2013.

What is worth recording, as facts in a clean-room spec, is these interoperability details:
- the DID category prefixes (0x0A0 sound, 0x040/0x050 Havok, 0x410/0x411 textures, 0x25 strings)
- the texture header layout (width and height at offsets 8 and 12, a DXTn fourcc at offset 16, header sizes of 16 or 24 bytes)
- compressed subfiles carrying a uint32 uncompressed length followed by a zlib stream
- the localization string-table layout and its 1–2-byte varint
- the DatExport flag and metadata vocabulary (blockSize, vnumDatFile, vnumGameData, datIdStamp, firstIterGuid, iteration, version), which hints at which fields exist in the real DAT header

Re-verify these against actual .dat files and against better-maintained, licensed DAT readers before relying on them. Separately, follow up on the sibling gitlab.com/lotro/server, gls and analyzer repos, which look more relevant to the network protocol and login side.

Its files are DatExport.cs, DatFile.cs, DatFileInitParams.cs, FileDictionary.cs, Options.cs, Program.cs, Subfile.cs, SubfileCollection.cs and SubfileEnumerator.cs. (2) localedata-extractor: a small tool that parses exported locale .bin string tables into LocalData.txt. Both projects have readme.txt and changelog.txt. The code looks decompiled (ILSpy-style names such as num, array, text2, binaryReader, and deeply nested if/else chains), so this is probably not the author's original source. The same "lotro" GitLab group also has lotro/server (tAmMo's packet capture/encrypt/decrypt code), lotro/analyzer (web packet analyzer), lotro/gls (auth meta server) and lotro/htdocs. The claim is accurate: the repo exists, is C#, states no license, and includes the changelog/readme and the DID-to-folder naming.
license: none/unknown (no LICENSE file in tree; AssemblyInfo copyright 2011-2013 Dancing_on_a_rock_hacker; code appears decompiled from the original binary, so redistribution rights are doubtful)
last_activity: Commits 2013-10-04 (only 2 commits); GitLab project last_activity_at 2020-02-01
how_to_use: Use as reference only, by extracting the facts it shows into our own spec. Do not depend on it or port it, for three reasons. First, it has no license and looks like decompiled output of someone else's binary. Second, it does not parse .dat files itself: it P/Invokes Turbine's proprietary datexport.dll (OpenDatFileEx2 etc.), which a clean-room project cannot ship or require, so it says nothing about the on-disk .dat B-tree or block layout. Third, it is Windows/.NET only. What it is good for: (a) cross-checking the subfile payload conventions below (zlib size prefix, per-category header offsets, DDS header synthesis from Turbine texture headers); (b) the DID hex-prefix category convention; (c) an early look at the locale string-table encoding, which should be cross-checked against LotroCompanion/lotro-tools and other maintained parsers. For actual .dat parsing, prefer a native .dat reader from other projects. Treat the details below as second-hand facts to re-verify against real data files.
key_facts:
Read from the source via GitLab raw URLs. The tree was listed via the API. Local cloning failed because the disk was full (ENOSPC), so everything was fetched over the web.
- DatExport.cs P/Invokes into DatExport.dll:
  - OpenDatFile (EntryPoint "OpenDatFileEx2"; handle, fileName, uint flags, ...)
  - CloseDatFile(handle)
  - GetNumSubfiles(handle)
  - GetSubfileSizes(handle, out did, out size, out iteration, offset, count)
  - GetSubfileVersion(handle, did)
  - GetSubfileCompressionFlag(handle, id) -> byte
  - GetSubfileData(handle, did, IntPtr buf, writeOffset, out version)
  - It also P/Invokes zlib1T uncompress().
  - There are nine DCOF open flags (DcofCreate .. DcofUseLRU).
- Compressed subfiles start with a 4-byte little-endian uncompressed size. The zlib stream begins at offset 4.
- The output path uses the DID formatted as "X8". Folders nest by the first, first two and first three hex digits: data\<datname>\{d0}XXXXXXX\{d0d1}XXXXXX\{d0d1d2}XXXXX\. The 3-hex-digit prefix acts as the file "category"; the readme says the first 3 digits are catalog info and the last 5 are the real file id.
- Magic checks used for typing (payload offsets):
  - WAV: "RIFF" at offset 8.
  - OGG: "OggS" at offset 8.
  - Havok HKX: bytes 57 E0 E0 57 at offset 8 for category 0x040, and at offset 17 for category 0x050.
  - JPEG: FF D8 FF at offset 24 for categories 0x410/0x411 (texture categories).
- DDS rebuild for categories 0x410/0x411:
  - Width and height are taken from payload bytes 8-15.
  - The format code is the byte at offset 19: '1' -> DXT1, '3' -> DXT3, '5' -> DXT5, otherwise uncompressed A8R8G8B8.
  - A 128-byte "DDS " header is synthesized. Exact flag bytes came via an AI summary and should be re-checked.
- Unpacker type filter flags: 1=WAV, 2=OGG, 4=JPG, 8=DDS, 16=HKS, 256=RAW.
- dictionary.bin stores DID+version so only changed files are re-extracted on later runs. The readme says memory stays under 100 MB.
- localedata-extractor .bin layout:
  - Header: int32 id, int32 unknown, 1 unknown byte, then a varint string count.
  - Varint rule: if the first byte has 0x80 set, value = ((b ^ 0x80) << 8) | next byte.
  - Each entry: 8 skipped bytes, int32 count of string pieces, and each piece is a varint length plus UTF-16LE chars.
  - Then an int32 count of skipped int32s, then a byte count of nested string groups.
  - Output lines look like "[HEX_ID][HEX_INDEX] - text".
- The changelog runs from v1.0 to v1.3.2: DXT texture export, report/compare tools, a 64-bit rebuild, .NET 4.0, and Havok animation detection in 1.3.2.

actual_description: The claim is accurate. "Lotro Resources" is a uCoz site run by "Dancing_On_A_Rock_Hacker" and is the original home of DAT_UNPACKER and LOCALDATAEXTRACTOR. Both are Windows console tools written in C#/.NET 4.0 that extract files from Turbine .dat archives (LOTRO and DDO). On 2017-12-30 the author posted a "Source code" entry: a zip with the source of both tools plus 4 text files describing formats. The Files catalog lists 3 entries: DAT UNPACKER TOOL 1.3.2 (7057 downloads), LOCALDATAEXTRACTOR 1.0, and "Source code, documentation" (192.6 KB). license: GPL-3.0-or-later. Every .cs file carries a GPLv3 "or any later version" header, "Copyright(C) 2011-2012 Dancing_on_a_rock_hacker". how_to_use: Use it as reference only. Read its notes, and do not copy its code unless the project itself is GPL-3.0-or-later. The tool does not parse the .dat container itself. It calls Turbine's proprietary DatExport.dll through P/Invoke (OpenDatFileEx2, GetNumSubfiles, GetSubfileSizes, GetSubfileData, GetSubfileVersion, GetSubfileCompressionFlag, CloseDatFile) and the game's zlib1T.dll. So it teaches nothing about the on-disk DAT B-tree or block layout, and a clean-room reader must not depend on DatExport.dll. The useful parts are the post-extraction facts: the compressed-subfile envelope, the DID-prefix categories, the header offsets used to detect embedded wav/ogg/jpg/DXT/Havok data, and the 4 short format descriptions (0x19, 0x25, 0x28 and 0x40 DID classes). Treat these as hints and confirm each one against current data, since they date from 2011-2017 and the formats have since changed. LotRO Companion's lotro-dat / LotroCompanion tools are better maintained sources for the same information. Cite this site as prior art in docs and clean-room notes. The Wayback copy is a good fallback if the uCoz site goes down; the CDX index shows snapshots from 2012 to 2025-09.
key_facts:
Read from the source zip (src/UNPACKER/LOTRO_UNPACKER/*.cs, src/LOTROLOCALDATA/.../Program.cs, src/FORMATS/*.txt):
- How it opens DATs: DatExport.dll OpenDatFileEx2(handle, fileName, flags, out didMasterMap, out blockSize, out vnumDatFile, out vnumGameData, out ulong datFileID, datIdStamp[0x40], firstIterGuid[0x40]). It passes flags 130 (0x82), or 0x86 for read-only. DCOF flag constants: UseLRU=1, Expandable=2, Create=8, CreateIfNeeded=0x10, SkipIndexCheck=0x200. It allows at most 0x40 open handles. It walks subfiles with GetSubfileSizes(handle, out did, out size, out iteration, offset, count).
- Compressed subfile, when GetSubfileCompressionFlag is set: the first 4 bytes are the decompressed length (little-endian uint32), followed by a zlib stream (size-4 bytes), which is passed to zlib uncompress().
- File category is the first 3 hex digits of the 8-hex-digit DID. Output goes to data\<dat>\1XXXXXXX\12XXXXXX\123XXXXX\<DID>.ext.
- Type detection by category and offset: 0A0 means sound, with an 8-byte header and then RIFF (wav) or OggS. 040 means Havok, with magic 57 E0 E0 57 at offset 8 (header 8). 050 means Havok with the magic at offset 17 (header 17). The tool saves these as .hkx; the changelog calls them .hks. 410/411 means an image: a JPEG SOI (FF D8 FF) at offset 24 means a 24-byte header. The text "DXT" at offset 16 with a byte 0x31/0x33/0x35 at 19 means DXT1/3/5, and the tool synthesizes a 128-byte DDS header. Changelog 1.3.0.1 notes that the width and height order in the Turbine texture header had been swapped. Non-DXT textures get an uncompressed RGB/ARGB DDS header (pixel format flags 0x40, 24-bit).
- 0x25XXXXXX localization string table, from client_local_*.dat: uint32 DID, uint32 1, byte type, then a count stored as a byte, or as a 15-bit big-endian value when the high bit 0x80 is set (this "VLE" length encoding is used everywhere in the format). Each entry is: uint64 hash/token, uint32 nPieces, then nPieces strings (VLE length in UTF-16 code units, then UTF-16LE text), uint32 nArgs and nArgs uint32 values, byte nVarGroups, and per group a uint32 count of VLE-length UTF-16 strings.
- 0x19XXXXXX: uint32 masterFileID, uint32 count, then records {uint32 index; byte len; char[len] group_name; uint32 recordID; uint32 link_to_40XXXXXX; uint32 type1, type2; uint32 link_to_42XXXXXX; uint32 type3, type4; byte[15] unk; uint32 link_to_78XXXXXX; byte unk; uint32 unk; uint32 link_to_40XXXXXX; uint32 0xFFFFFFFF; uint32 unk}.
- 0x28XXXXXX: masterFileID, then repeated blocks {byte type1; VLE count; (uint32 index, uint32 fileID)*; byte type2; VLE count; (uint32 index, byte len, char[len] description)*}.
- 0x40XXXXXX: masterFileID; byte type; byte count (6 if type==4); uint16 unk; byte unk; count x uint32 link_to_41XXXXXX; uint32 0; uint32 0x0F.
- Code size: about 1.6k lines of C# in total. Last release 1.3.2.0 (2012-06-17); source published 2017-12-30. Contact named in the headers: dancingonarockhacker@gmail.com.
language: C# (.NET Framework 4.0), Windows-only; P/Invoke to native DatExport.dll and zlib1T.dll
last_activity: Last news post 2017-12-30 (source code release); last tool release 1.3.2.0 on 2012-06-17. The site is still online (footer says © 2026). The latest Wayback snapshot is 2025-09.

actual_description:
LOTRO Companion is a Java desktop app by Damien Morcellet for managing characters, simulating gear and stats, and browsing a lore database. Its LOTRO .dat reading code sits in a separate library jar, delta-lotro-dat-utils. I checked the following:
(1) The SourceForge files page exists and lists lotro-companion-24.10.0.49.6.zip (265.0 MB, released less than a day before 2026-10-03), along with folders 16/, loredb/, patchs/, jukebox/ and tiles/.
(2) The current lotro-data-extractor pom.xml on GitHub depends on com.dam.delta4j:delta-lotro-dat-utils:11.12, delta-lotro-core:24.10 and delta-common:1.19. Version 11.12 and the 24.10 core line match the claim.
(3) The older distribution repo, LotroCompanion/lotro-companion-distrib, ships lib/delta-lotro-dat-utils-11.0.jar. This shows the dat-utils jar is bundled inside the distribution.
(4) github.com/LotroCompanion/lotro-dat-utils returns 404. That repo does not appear in the LotroCompanion org's repo list or in dmorcellet's personal repos, so the dat-utils source is not public, as the claim says.
I could NOT check the bytecode details the claim lists (superblock, B-tree, extent/fragment reads, DID routing, WState/WLib classes). The local sandbox disk was full (ENOSPC), so I could not download the 265 MB zip or run javap. Those details are still unverified by me.
license: Apache-2.0 (declared at the distribution level). The SourceForge project page lists "Apache License V2.0". lotro-companion-distrib/lotro-companion/doc/LICENSE.txt is the Apache License 2.0 text. NOTICE.txt states that the delta jars are by Damien Morcellet (copyright 2011-2023), and it is the Apache 2.0 attribution notice for the distribution. The claim's "unclear" is overstated: the jars are distributed under Apache-2.0. Two cautions remain. The dat-utils source code is not published. how_to_use:
Treat it as a reference implementation and an oracle for checking our own dat reader. Do not vendor it.
- Apache-2.0 legally allows using, redistributing and even modifying the binary jar with attribution. Even so, porting decompiled code would be hard to justify in a project that markets itself as clean-room, and decompiled output is poor-quality source anyway.
- Recommended split: one person reads the jar's public API and class and field layouts (javap -p -c), plus the PUBLISHED Apache-licensed callers in github.com/LotroCompanion/lotro-core, lotro-data-extractor and lotro-tools. That person writes a format spec. A separate implementer writes our reader in our own language from that spec.
- Use the jar at development time only, as a test oracle: run it against the user's own dat files and compare its output (DIDs, decoded properties, string tables, images) with our reader's output.
- Pin the version (11.12 with core 24.10) because the format code follows live patches.

actual_description:
The claim is accurate and comes from a fetched page, but it is miscategorized. LotROLinux was a GTK#/Glade GUI launcher written in Mono (C#) by Alan Jackson ("AJackson", SourceForge user spherelance) for running the Windows LOTRO and DDO clients under Wine or CrossOver on Linux and Mac OS X. It is not a client reimplementation. It logs the user in, fetches realm and queue information, runs Turbine's own patchclient.dll through rundll32 under Wine, and then starts the original lotroclient.exe.

I fetched the 2008-02-08 Wayback snapshot. It shows "LOTRO Launcher for Linux / Graphical Launcher for Linux", says the GUI launcher is "written using Mono", and links to SNy's CLI launcher (bmx-chemnitz.de/~mfr/LOTRO). The archived download page also lists an Ubuntu PPA (ppa.launchpad.net/ajackson-bcs) and a LotROMac .app build.

The SourceForge project "lotrolauncher" (group_id 200627, created 2007-07-08, GPLv3) has its external homepage set to lotrolinux.com. Its file releases run from July 2007 (0.4) to 0.9.8 in January 2009. The SourceForge metadata now lists Python/Qt, because the same project later hosted PyLotRO by the same author. That makes the "ancestor of PyLotRO" part of the claim correct; OneLauncher grew out of PyLotRO, so "ancestor of OneLauncher" is plausible but I did not verify it here. The AUTHORS file says "Based on CLI launcher for LOTRO (C) 2007-2008 SNy". I did not verify the claim that it was the "first" Linux launcher, and SNy's CLI script came first in any case.

I downloaded and read the LotROLinux-0.9.8.tar.bz2 source. COPYING is GPLv3, and the file headers say "GPL v3 or later".
license: GPL-3.0-or-later
how_to_use:
Treat it as reference only, mainly for history. The GPLv3 code could be ported, but it is not worth porting: it targets Mono 1.x and GTK#, and it describes the 2007-2009 GLS login flow, which Turbine and SSG have since changed (modern launchers such as OneLauncher handle the current flow).

Its main use for this project is documenting the launcher-to-client handoff:
- the GLS SOAP calls for datacenters, login and tickets
- launcher.config keys, including GameClient.ArgTemplate
- the world login queue

That handoff tells us what a reimplemented client must accept on its command line.

For the launcher component itself, use OneLauncher, which is actively maintained and GPL, as the reference. Do not copy LotROLinux code into a project with a non-GPL license; extract the protocol facts in clean-room form instead.

The claim's "kind" should be changed from "client-reimpl" to "launcher".
key_facts:
All of the following comes from reading the LotROLinux 0.9.8 source:

- **Datacenter request (GLSDataCentre.cs):** a SOAP POST with header `SOAPAction: "http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS/GetDatacenters"` and body `<GetDatacenters xmlns="http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS"><game>{gameName}</game></GetDatacenters>`.
- **Datacenter response:** a `<Datacenter>` element containing:
  - `<Worlds>`, a list of worlds, each with Name, ChatServerUrl and StatusServerUrl
  - `<AuthServer>`, `<PatchServer>` and `<LauncherConfigurationServer>`
  - The response is cached as GLSDataCenter.config.
- **Where the datacenter service URL and game name come from (BaseConfig.cs):** the keys "Launcher.DataCenterService.GLS" and "DataCenter.GameName" in the game's TurbineLauncher.exe.config (DDO falls back to dndlauncher.exe.config).
- **Login (AuthenticateUser.cs):** a SOAP POST with header `SOAPAction: "http://www.turbine.com/SE/GLS/LoginAccount"` and body `<LoginAccount><username/><password/><additionalInfo/></LoginAccount>`.
  - The response contains Subscriptions/Game entries with Name, Description and Status (Active), plus a Ticket.
  - It is cached as GLSAuthServer.config.
  - The code installs an override that accepts any SSL certificate (SecureHTTPOverride).
- **Launcher configuration (WorldQueueConfig.cs):** launcher.config is read from the LauncherConfigurationServer. Its appSettings keys are:
  - GameClient.Filename and GameClient.ArgTemplate
  - URL.NewsFeed, URL.NewsStyleSheet and URL.AlertsStyleSheet
  - WorldQueue.LoginQueue.URL and WorldQueue.TakeANumber.Parameters
  - LauncherConfig.DateTime and Patching.ProductCode
- **Realm status (Realm.cs):** an XML document fetched from the world's StatusServerUrl. It includes a "queueurls" list (one is picked at random) and login server lists.
- **World queue (JoinWorldQueue.cs):** a form-urlencoded POST of the TakeANumber parameters, built from the account, the URL-encoded ticket and the queue URL. The XML response has HResult (0x00000000 means success), QueueNumber and NowServingNumber. In 0.9.7 the queue step is skipped when no queue URLs are returned.
- **Game launch (StartGame.cs):** the client is started with GameClient.ArgTemplate filled in from the account, the ticket and other values, under wine, CrossOver Games or CrossOver Office, with the WINEPREFIX and WINEDEBUG environment variables set.
- **Patching (PatchWindow.cs):** `rundll32.exe patchclient.dll,Patch <patchServerUrl> --language <lang> --productcode <code>`, run first with `--filesonly` and then with `--dataonly`, adding `--highres` when high-resolution textures are enabled. Under CrossOver it uses `--bottle <name> --workdir <dir> --`.
- **Settings:** stored in LotROLinux.config, with keys such as Game.Directory, Wine.Prefix, Realm, Language, HiRes and PatchClient.
- **Historical Wine notes from the how-to pages:** Windows version set to 2000, Direct3D UseGLSL and VideoMemorySize registry values, and UserPreferences.ini entries AllowFakeFullScreen=False and FullScreen=True (the how-to says the ini lives under ~/The Lord of the Rings).

The source has no .dat archive, rendering or network-protocol code beyond the launcher-level HTTP/SOAP calls above.

Local copy: ~/.cache/tessera/clones/lotrolinux/
language: C# (Mono 1.x, GTK#/Glade); later the same SourceForge project hosted the Python/Qt PyLotRO
last_activity: Last LotROLinux (Mono) release: 0.9.8, 2009-01-12 on SourceForge. The Wayback snapshot is from 2008-02-08, and the download page was captured 2008-12-18. The lotrolinux.com domain now serves unrelated spam pages (2020-2021 captures).
