actual_description: Verified by downloading the 30-page PDF and reading every page. It is "Order Granting Motion for Preliminary Injunction (ECF No. 38)" in Daybreak Game Company LLC v. Kristopher Takahashi and Alexander Taylor, Case No. 3:25-cv-01489-BAS-BLM, U.S. District Court for the Southern District of California. It was filed 09/19/25 as Document 66 (PageID.1688-1717) and signed by Chief Judge Cynthia Bashant. "The Heroes' Journey" (THJ) was a for-profit EverQuest emulator (EQEmu-derived server plus a modified retail client). Daybreak brought it to suit. The claim's "ECF 66, 2025-09-19" is correct. One thing the claim leaves out: the case has since ended. A web search found a Joint Consent Motion filed 2026-03-18 (ECF 104, fetched and confirmed by title and date) and reports of a "Final Judgment and Permanent Injunction Upon Consent" with a confidential monetary settlement. There was no appeal, so this order has no appellate review. It is an unpublished, non-binding district-court ruling made under the preliminary-injunction "likelihood of success" standard, not a final merits decision.
license: none/unknown (US federal court record; public domain as a government work, 17 U.S.C. 105)
how_to_use:
Use it as a reference-only legal source. This is the most on-point recent ruling against MMO emulators and it should shape the project's legal design rules. Each part of the claim checked against the text:

(1) Sega distinguished for asset use: ACCURATE (pp. 9-10). The defendants called their code "fan-written, clean-room, reverse engineered, open-source." The court said Sega covers copying done only to reach functional elements. THJ instead used "character models, environmental textures, spell effects, and user interface elements nearly wholesale."

(2) Server authentication held a TPM: ACCURATE (pp. 16-17). Account verification, subscription validation and access authorization, plus continuous in-session authorization checks, were held to "effectively control access" under 1201(a)(3)(B). The court relied on MDY v. Blizzard.

(3) Client redirection counts as circumvention even without touching Daybreak's servers: ACCURATE (pp. 17-18). Editing eqhost.txt to point from everquest.com to projecteq.net, and bypassing login in eqlsClient.ini, was held likely circumvention. The court was "skeptical of a reading of the statute that would impose a requirement of attempted or direct interaction with the copyright holder's servers." It also found 1201(a)(2) trafficking likely, because the install guide shows the product is designed to circumvent.

(4) Telling users to copy client files is volitional infringement: ACCURATE (p. 15). The install step had users copy the Steam EverQuest client (app 205710) into a THJ folder. The court held this "instigat[es] third-party infringement" and meets the volitional-conduct requirement for direct infringement.

(5) Fair use, estoppel and laches rejected: ACCURATE (pp. 14, 19-25). All four fair-use factors went against the defendants. Estoppel failed even though Daybreak had tolerated emulators and had a written agreement with Project 1999. Laches failed because Daybreak's cease-and-desist letters showed it was not sleeping on its rights.

The claim leaves out several caveats. This is a preliminary injunction, not a merits ruling. It is not precedential. The case settled in March 2026. The facts were extreme: a commercial operation earning about $100k a month, with 234 Daybreak files modified, 4,215 inserted and 66 deleted. A bond of $1,000,000 was set. The injunction also reached the GitHub repos and personal liability for the LLC founders (pp. 4-5, 30).

Design rules this implies for the LOTRO client project:
- Never ship or point users to modified original assets or patched files.
- Never ship a patcher or launcher whose purpose is to redirect the retail client or bypass its login.
- Never connect to SSG/Daybreak servers or emulate their authentication.
- Write install instructions that only read data files the user already owns, in place.
- Stay non-commercial, with no donations tied to access.
- Expect 1201 claims to be the main risk even for an engine that is clean-room in the Sega sense.

Wording to use in project docs: "district court preliminary injunction, later superseded by a consent judgment; persuasive, not binding." Do not call it established law.
key_facts:
Caption: Daybreak Game Company LLC v. Takahashi & Taylor, S.D. Cal. No. 3:25-cv-01489-BAS-BLM. ECF 66, filed 2025-09-19, 30 pages, Chief Judge Cynthia Bashant. It grants ECF 38, Daybreak's Supplemental Motion for Preliminary Injunction; the hearing was 2025-08-12.

Claims raised: 17 USC 106 copyright infringement; DMCA 1201(a)(1) and (a)(2); Lanham Act 1125(a); UCL; breach of contract. The court reached only copyright and DMCA (fn. 3).

Copying: the expert report (Garry Kitchen, para. 149) found THJ altered 234 copyrighted files, inserted 4,215 and deleted 66, and used the audiovisual asset library. Side-by-side exhibits showed Lady Vox, zone architecture and race-selection UI icons.

Volitional conduct: the install guide had users copy the Steam EverQuest Rain of Fear client (GAME_APP_ID 205710) into a THJ folder. The court cited Perfect 10 v. Giganews and VHT v. Zillow.

DMCA TPMs: (a) server-side account verification, subscription validation and access authorization; (b) continuous in-session authorization checks. Circumvention: the eqhost.txt redirect from everquest.com to projecteq.net, and the login bypass in eqlsClient.ini. The court cited Bungie v. AimJunkies: "Bypassing a password to access a file is the type of circumvention the DMCA was intended to prevent." It rejected the argument that no circumvention occurs because emulators never contact Daybreak's servers.

Defenses rejected: Sega v. Accolade is "not controlling" because the defendants copied expressive assets, not only functional elements. Fair use failed on all four factors (commercial use, not transformative, copied the "heart" of the work, market harm). Estoppel failed even with the Project 1999 written agreement cited, because the reliance and ignorance elements were not met. Laches failed because of cease-and-desist history and a 2024-12-12 email that went to junk mail.

Irreparable harm: about 30,000 THJ users and a population correlation, plus YouTube comments from users who quit retail EverQuest.

Bond and scope: bond set at $1,000,000 (Daybreak had asked for $5,000) because THJ revenue was about $100k a month. The injunction covers THJ "or any similar software that infringes Daybreak's copyrights," heroesjourneyemu.com, github.com/The-Heroes-Journey-EQEMU, "operating any server emulation software that enables unauthorized access" to EverQuest, and the EVERQUEST mark. Founders were held personally liable as the "moving, active, conscious force" behind the LLC (Another Quest LLC).

Later history (search, not fully read): ECF 104 is a Joint Consent Motion dated 2026-03-18. It is reported to have led to a Final Judgment and Permanent Injunction Upon Consent with a confidential settlement payment. No appeal. A massivelyop.com report also mentions Daybreak pursuing an additional THJ admin.
last_activity: ECF 66 filed 2025-09-19; case later resolved by Joint Consent Motion (ECF 104) filed 2026-03-18, reportedly leading to a consent final judgment and permanent injunction.

label: verify:THJ Order compelling arbitration / denying stay of PI
actual_description: Daybreak Game Company, LLC v. Kristopher Takahashi et al., No. 3:25-cv-01489-BAS-BLM (S.D. Cal.), ECF No. 84, filed 10/30/25, 12 pages, signed by Chief Judge Cynthia Bashant. The full title is "ORDER: (1) GRANTING DEFENDANTS' MOTION TO COMPEL ARBITRATION (ECF No. 61); AND (2) DENYING DEFENDANTS' EX PARTE MOTION FOR AN ADMINISTRATIVE STAY OF PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION (ECF No. 75)". The case concerns "The Heroes' Journey" (THJ), an EverQuest emulator / private server. I fetched the PDF and read all 12 pages, so the claim is accurate. One correction to the claim: the court did not decide that the IP claims belong in arbitration. Because the EULAs incorporate the AAA rules, the court sent the threshold question of arbitrability to the arbitrator and paused the court case (FAA section 3) until the arbitrator rules. The preliminary injunction (ECF 66, granted 9/19/25) stays in force while that happens. The court ordered a joint status report by 1/30/2026 or within one week of the arbitrator's decision, whichever comes first.
license: none/unknown (US federal court order; judicial opinions are not copyrightable under the government edicts doctrine, so it is effectively public domain)
how_to_use:
Use as reference only, for legal-risk analysis in the project's LEGAL.md or risk notes. It is not a technical resource and not legal advice. Lessons for a LOTRO client reimplementation:
(1) Daybreak's claims against THJ rested on the defendants using the original client and its assets. THJ required players to install the RoF EverQuest client, modified its executable, and allegedly copied code and assets, including the RoF EULA text itself. The court treated any developer who accesses or uses the game software as bound by the EULA. So contributors who have accepted the LOTRO/SSG EULA are probably bound by its no-reverse-engineering and no-derivative-works terms. This supports a strict clean-room process: specs written by people separate from the implementers, no copying of original code or assets, and users supply their own .dat files.
(2) Court-adopted language: an EULA binds anyone "accessing, downloading and/or using the Software and/or any Game(s)", and later EULAs supersede older ones under California contract law. Contributor exposure therefore follows whichever EULA version is current.
(3) Even with arbitration compelled, the IP injunction stayed in place. IP claims against a server or client project can halt it quickly, before any decision on the merits.
(4) Running or connecting to official servers, or bypassing protections (DMCA section 1201 was pleaded), sharply raises risk. Keep the project an offline/data-viewer client plus a separately built server.
Cite it together with the PI order (ECF 66) and the later judgment and filings (e.g. ECF 104), which matter more for the substantive copyright and DMCA analysis than this procedural order.
key_facts:
- Complaint filed 6/14/2025. It asserts 9 claims: direct copyright infringement; inducement of copyright infringement; DMCA section 1201; federal trademark dilution (Lanham Act 1125(c)); federal unfair competition (1125(a)); California trademark dilution (Bus. & Prof. Code 14330); breach of contract; California UCL (17200); and unjust enrichment.
- PI motion filed 6/14/25 (ECF 5); hearing 8/12/25; PI granted 9/19/25 (ECF 66). Motion to compel arbitration filed 8/22/25 (ECF 61). Ex parte motion to stay the PI pending appeal filed 9/23/25 (ECF 75).
- Waiver: the court found no waiver. Defendants moved about 2 months after the complaint, and their PI opposition had already said they would seek arbitration (Armstrong v. Michaels Stores, 59 F.4th 1011).
- Which EULA controls: the RoF EULA (effective 12/2/2008) has a California forum-selection clause and says: "You may not copy...distribute...modify or create derivative works... You may not reverse engineer, disassemble or decompile the [RoF] Software." The amended EULAs (Feb 2018 and June 2022) add AAA consumer arbitration. Under Suski v. Coinbase, the later agreements prevail where they conflict. The court said "[A]ny Game(s)" includes older client versions, so the amended EULAs cover the defendants' conduct after 2018.
- The amended EULAs' "Excluded Disputes" carve-out covers "any Dispute relating to the infringement, misappropriation and/or other misuse of intellectual property rights other than patent rights (including...injunctive relief)". Such disputes may go to court in D. Del. or S.D. Cal. However, because the EULAs incorporate the AAA rules (R-7(a)), arbitrability itself is delegated to the arbitrator (Brennan v. Opus Bank; Henry Schein v. Archer & White), so the court did not decide whether the IP claims are arbitrable.
- Stay of the PI denied under Rule 62(c) and the Hilton v. Braunskill factors. Lost work product from "an activity which has been shown likely to be infringing" deserves "little equitable consideration."
- Section IV: compelling arbitration does not affect the PI. A court may keep interim relief in place to preserve the status quo (Toyo Tire v. Continental Tire, 609 F.3d 975). The case is stayed pending the arbitrator's decision on arbitrability.
- Facts recited in the order: THJ required the RoF client, modified its executable to reach unauthorized servers, and its source code was publicly posted on GitHub in June 2025. Plaintiff's expert is Garry Kitchen.
- Related docket entries: ECF 104.0 and 104.1 exist on CourtListener. Press (TweakTown, Aftermath, MassivelyOP) reports that THJ later lost the copyright suit and shut down, with an injunction covering heroesjourneyemu.com and github.com/The-Heroes-Journey-EQEMU. I did not verify those later outcomes from primary documents.
- Verification note: I fetched the PDF with WebFetch (302 KB) and read all 12 pages. Bash was unavailable (ENOSPC, disk full), so I could not use curl or pdftotext.
last_activity: Order dated/filed 2025-10-30; status report due by 2026-01-30; later docket entries (e.g. ECF 104) exist

actual_description: A real federal case: Daybreak Game Company LLC v. Kristopher Takahashi, Alexander Taylor and Does 1-20. U.S. District Court, S.D. Cal., Case No. 3:25-cv-01489-BAS-BLM, before Chief Judge Cynthia A. Bashant. Daybreak sued the operators of The Heroes' Journey (THJ), a for-profit, donation-funded EverQuest emulator server built on EQEmu. CourtListener/RECAP hosts the filings. I read three of the PDFs myself. Every date in the claim checks out: complaint and PI motion 2025-06-14 (ECF 1, ECF 5); PI granted 2025-09-19 (ECF 66); order compelling arbitration and denying a stay of the PI 2025-10-30 (ECF 84); joint motion for consent judgment and permanent injunction filed 2026-03-18 (ECF 104); and the court's order granting it on 2026-03-19 (ECF 105), with the Final Judgment and Permanent Injunction entered separately.
license: none/unknown (U.S. federal court filings; court-authored orders are public domain, and party filings are public records)
how_to_use:
Use this as a legal reference only. Read it as the latest, closest precedent for what an MMO publisher will sue over and what a court will order. It does not decide LOTRO's case: there was no trial and no finding of fact or law, it settled with no admission, and the arbitration ruling depended on the EULA. It still matters because Daybreak (EverQuest) is in the same Enad Global 7 corporate family as Standing Stone Games (LOTRO).

Lessons for the project's legal policy:
(1) Never ship, copy, or embed original client code or assets. Daybreak's argument against arbitration rested on THJ having "literally stole[n] the RoF EULA along with other portions of Daybreak's code" and modifying the RoF client executable.
(2) Avoid anything that circumvents authentication or reaches official servers. The DMCA §1201 claim is the key one, and the injunction separately bans software that "circumvents authentication mechanisms."
(3) Do not monetize at all, including "donations." The damages proxy was the publisher's lost revenue, and press coverage contrasts for-profit THJ with the non-profit P99 and Quarm.
(4) Avoid publisher trademarks in the project name and branding. Federal and California dilution claims were brought.
(5) Note the scope of the injunction text in ECF 104. It covers "operating any server emulation software that enables access to any of Daybreak's online games, including... software that ... replicates server functionality, or facilitates access outside of Daybreak's authorized distribution channels." It also orders the defendants' GitHub repos (github.com/The-Heroes-Journey-EQEMU) taken down. This is a consent decree binding only these defendants, but it shows the remedy a publisher in the same group will ask for.
(6) EULA arbitration clauses can push such disputes into arbitration (ECF 84).

The project should cite the RECAP PDF URLs directly; they are stable and fetchable. The HTML docket page blocks automated fetches.
key_facts:

- ECF 84 background lists the complaint (ECF 1) as filed 2025-06-14, with 9 counts: direct copyright infringement (17 USC 101 et seq.); inducement; DMCA 17 USC 1201; trademark dilution 15 USC 1125(c); federal unfair competition 1125(a); Cal. dilution B&P 14330; breach of contract; Cal. UCL B&P 17200; unjust enrichment.
- PI history per ECF 84: motion filed 2025-06-14 (ECF 5), opposition 2025-07-30 (ECF 50), hearing 2025-08-12 (ECF 58), PI granted 2025-09-19 (ECF 66).
- The arbitration fight was over which EULA governed. Defendants relied on the 2018/2022 EverQuest EULAs ("any dispute," including arbitrability). Daybreak relied on the Rain of Fear client EULA, arguing that THJ requires the RoF client, modifies the RoF executable, and copied the RoF EULA and code.
- ECF 104 (filed 03/18/26, 5 pp): joint motion for consent judgment and permanent injunction. Damages are set in a confidential settlement and enforceable only on material breach; each side bears its own fees; no admission. Counsel: Dentons for Daybreak, Morgan Lewis for defendants. It enjoins (a) THJ or any similar infringing EQ emulator; (b) the heroesjourneyemu.com site; (c) repos including github.com/The-Heroes-Journey-EQEMU; (d) any server emulation software for Daybreak games, including auth circumvention or replicated server functionality; (e) EverQuest marks; (f) other infringing use.

actual_description: The Daybreak Game Company LLC End User License Agreement, "Last Updated on April 24, 2026". I fetched it with WebFetch and again with raw curl (76 KB HTML) on 2026-10-03. One agreement covers every Daybreak game ("Each of our games is offered pursuant to this Daybreak End User License Agreement"). license: none/unknown (proprietary legal text, Daybreak Game Company LLC; it is a contract, not a software license for this project)
how_to_use:
Use as reference only. It is the binding contract that applies to any contributor who installs or plays LOTRO, so the project's legal policy (LEGAL.md / CONTRIBUTING) must be designed around it.

1. **Clean-room separation.** Section 4.2 bans contract-wise reverse engineering of the client and its "file formats". The only exception is "to the extent that this restriction is expressly prohibited by applicable law", for example EU Software Directive 2009/24/EC Art. 6 (decompilation for interoperability) and US DMCA §1201(f). That makes the separation important. Spec writers who have accepted the EULA should rely on already-published third-party format documentation (existing community tools and wikis) and on interoperability exemptions. Implementers work only from written specs.

2. **Server-protocol emulation is the biggest exposure.** Sections 4.3, 4.4 and 4.5 ban protocol emulation, packet sniffing, unauthorized connections and decrypting client-server traffic. These terms bind the person who accepted the EULA, not the code, but the project should:
   - make offline/local viewing and play of user-supplied .dat files the core scope;
   - never connect to official servers;
   - never ship decryption keys or captured traffic;
   - get qualified legal advice before attempting any network protocol work.

3. **Asset use.** Section 4.1 (no derivative works or redistribution) and section 4.7 (no incorporating Game Assets into any product) support the OpenMW-style model: users supply their own .dat files and nothing copyrighted is distributed.

4. **Housekeeping.**
   - Contributors should not run this project's tools while the official client is running, because section 5 lets Daybreak monitor the system for third-party programs.
   - Delaware law (section 11) and mandatory arbitration with a class-action waiver (section 12, no opt-out wording found) apply to EULA disputes. Copyright claims could still come up separately.
   - Re-check the "Last Updated" date regularly and keep a dated copy of the text in project legal notes.

This is not legal advice. Have a lawyer review the project's legal policy.

license: none/unknown (proprietary legal document, (c) Daybreak Game Company LLC; this is a contract, not a software license)
how_to_use:
Use it as a reference only, for the project's legal-risk analysis and for writing its rules. It is a contract that binds anyone who accepted it (anyone with a LOTRO account). Copyright law alone would not bind non-users this way. The practical consequences:

(1) Contributors who hold LOTRO accounts accept §13 (and §10/§12): no reverse engineering, decompiling, disassembling or modifying the client. They also accept §7.1: no creating or distributing "utilities, emulators or other software tools related to any Daybreak Game(s)" without written permission. This bans more than server emulators, and the wording is broad enough to reach a reimplemented client and even data-file viewers. So the clean-room split matters. People who study the original binaries or network traffic should be kept apart from people who write code. Better still, rely on published third-party documentation and existing open-source format work instead of new disassembly. Whether this contract term can be enforced against interoperability work, or is overridden by it, depends on the jurisdiction: in the EU, Software Directive Art. 6 and Art. 8 make interoperability decompilation rights non-waivable; in the US, DMCA §1201(f) and the fair-use precedents Sega v. Accolade and Sony v. Connectix exist, but contract terms can still override them (Bowers v. Baystate). Get a real lawyer's opinion before going further.

(2) Under §12 the original client may not be "used as a stand-alone game" or "used in connection with non-Daybreak game servers". That clause covers Daybreak's own client software. It does not directly cover independent code. However, combined with the §7.1 ban on playing on unauthorized servers, it means any private-server or offline mode carries ToS risk for users who hold accounts. Design the project so it works without connecting to Daybreak servers and without shipping or patching Daybreak code.

(3) §14.4 forbids using "the name of any Daybreak Game(s) in any Fan Site name, domain name or App name". The project name, repo name and domain therefore must not contain "LOTRO" or "Lord of the Rings Online". The name could also raise separate Middle-earth Enterprises/Tolkien trademark problems. Pick a neutral codename and use the game's name only as a nominative description.

(4) §25 sets binding individual arbitration and a class-action waiver, and §24 sets governing law and jurisdiction. Both matter for contributors who are bound by the contract.

Do not quote large parts of the text into the repo. Link to it and record the date you accessed it, because Daybreak can revise it unilaterally ("Last Updated" legend; continued use counts as acceptance). Also review the separate EULA at daybreakgames.com/eula, which this check did not cover.

label: verify:EFF bnetd case archive (briefs)
canonical_url: https://www.eff.org/document/opening-brief-defendants-appellants (PDF: https://www.eff.org/files/filenode/Blizzard_v_bnetd/20050112_Opening_Brief_of_Defendants.pdf; the lowercase URL in the claim also resolves to the same PDF). Case index: https://www.eff.org/cases/blizzard-v-bnetd
actual_description: This is the real Opening Brief of Defendants-Appellants in Davidson & Associates, Inc. d/b/a Blizzard Entertainment and Vivendi Universal Games v. Internet Gateway, Inc., Tim Jung, Ross Combs and Rob Crittenden. It was filed in the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit as No. 04-3654, on appeal from E.D. Mo. Case No. 4:02CV498 CAS (Judge Charles A. Shaw). Counsel were Day Casebeer Madrid & Batchelder, Thompson Coburn, and Jason Schultz of the EFF. I fetched the PDF (576.6 KB) and read the cover, the Summary of the Case and the table of contents. The EFF case page also links the reply brief, the appellees' brief, amicus briefs (CCIA/OSAIA, Consumers Union/Public Knowledge, IEEE-USA, IP law professors; and on the other side ESA/RIAA/MPAA, SIIA, Data Tree), the oral-argument audio, and the 8th Circuit ruling of 1 Sept 2005.
license: none/unknown (US court filing; the brief's text is generally treated as public record, and EFF hosts it with no explicit license)
how_to_use: Use as reference only, as legal background for the project's LEGAL.md / clean-room policy. Do not cite it as support that the project is legal. These defense arguments LOST: the 8th Circuit affirmed for Blizzard in Davidson & Assocs. v. Jung, 422 F.3d 630 (8th Cir. 2005). It held that the EULA/ToU ban on reverse engineering was enforceable and not preempted by copyright law. It also rejected the 17 U.S.C. 1201(f) interoperability defense, because circumventing the CD-key check enabled unauthorized play and the circumvention was not 'solely' for interoperability. Lessons for the LOTRO project: (1) agreeing to SSG's EULA/ToS while reverse-engineering the client or protocol may create contract liability no matter how strong a fair-use argument is, so keep clean-room roles separate and prefer documentation from people who never agreed to the terms, or from existing public specifications. (2) Never bypass or emulate authentication or DRM (login, ticket/session-key checks, subscription or entitlement checks), and never make it possible to use the game without a legitimate account or data. (3) Keep the client loading only user-supplied data and ship no assets. Read this brief together with the 8th Circuit opinion and the appellees' brief to get both sides. Get real legal counsel before any public release.
key_facts:
The claimed URL exists and serves a real PDF (application/pdf, 576.6 KB). On the EFF site the filename is capitalized as 20050112_Opening_Brief_of_Defendants.pdf, and the lowercase form in the claim also resolved. Docket: 8th Cir. No. 04-3654; district case E.D. Mo. 4:02CV498 CAS.

Issues framed in the Summary of the Case:
- Whether mass-market shrinkwrap/clickwrap licenses enforced under state law can outlaw fair use despite the Copyright Act of 1976 and the DMCA.
- Whether the public can rely on the DMCA's reverse-engineering exemptions.

Argument outline from the table of contents:
- II: a state breach-of-contract claim conflicts with federal fair-use protections (conflict preemption, "full purposes and objectives", "stands as an obstacle").
- III.A: 1201(f) reverse-engineering-for-interoperability defense:
  - "sole purpose" requirement: access to Battle.net mode was solely for interoperability;
  - free distribution of bnetd does not defeat the defense;
  - bnetd was an independently created program;
  - the district court found infringement without analysis.
- III.B: no prima facie DMCA case:

Use it as a legal reference only, not as code. The claim's confidence of "verified-by-fetch" is accurate: the URL exists and has the text described. There are limits on what (f) covers, though:

(3) The findings can be shared only to make an independently created program interoperate, and only if that does not infringe copyright or break other laws. The exact wording below comes from LII through a second WebFetch prompt that asked for the text word for word. A small model produced that extraction, so check the wording against uscode.house.gov before putting it in project documents.
- §1201(f)(1): "Notwithstanding the provisions of subsection (a)(1)(A), a person who has lawfully obtained the right to use a copy of a computer program may circumvent a technological measure that effectively controls access to a particular portion of that program for the sole purpose of identifying and analyzing those elements of the program that are necessary to achieve interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs, and that have not previously been readily available to the person engaging in the circumvention, to the extent any such acts of identification and analysis do not constitute infringement under this title."
- (f)(2), summarised: a person may build the technological means to circumvent, for the (f)(1) purpose or to make an independently created program interoperate, as long as this does not infringe.
- §1201(f)(3): "The information acquired through the acts permitted under paragraph (1), and the means permitted under paragraph (2), may be made available to others if the person referred to in paragraph (1) or (2), as the case may be, provides such information or means solely for the purpose of enabling interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs, and to the extent that doing so does not constitute infringement under this title or violate applicable law other than this section."
- §1201(f)(4): "For purposes of this subsection, the term 'interoperability' means the ability of computer programs to exchange information, and of such programs mutually to use the information which has been exchanged."
- (a)(3)(A) defines "circumvent a technological measure" as to "descramble a scrambled work, to decrypt an encrypted work, or otherwise to avoid, bypass, remove, deactivate, or impair a technological measure, without the authority of the copyright owner." The fetch result cut this off after "without authority", so the ending of that quote should be confirmed against the official text.
- (a)(3)(B): a measure "effectively controls access" if, in the ordinary course of its operation, it requires information, or a process or treatment, applied with the copyright owner's authority in order to gain access to the work.
- (a)(1)(C) sets up the triennial rulemaking by the Librarian of Congress. The resulting exemptions are codified at 37 CFR 201.40.

label: verify:Directive 2009/24/EC Art. 5, 6, 8 (legislation.gov.uk
canonical_url: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2009/24/article/6/adopted (mirror; the official authentic text is on EUR-Lex: https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/24/oj). Sibling pages that were also fetched and checked: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2009/24/article/5/adopted and https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2009/24/article/8/adopted
actual_description: The UK National Archives' (legislation.gov.uk) copy of Directive 2009/24/EC on the legal protection of computer programs. The pages are labelled "This is the original version (as it was originally adopted)." I fetched all three article pages with WebFetch on 2026-10-03; the curl attempt failed because the local disk was full. What each page says: Art. 5(1) allows use and error correction by a lawful acquirer. Art. 5(2) protects the right to make a back-up copy. Art. 5(3) quote: "The person having a right to use a copy of a computer program shall be entitled, without the authorisation of the rightholder, to observe, study or test the functioning of the program in order to determine the ideas and principles which underlie any element of the program if he does so while performing any of the acts of loading, displaying, running, transmitting or storing the program which he is entitled to do." Art. 6(1) allows reproduction and translation of code (decompilation) where this is "indispensable to obtain the information necessary to achieve the interoperability of an independently created computer program with other programs". It has three conditions: (a) the acts are done by the licensee or another person with a right to use the program, (b) the interoperability information was not previously readily available, and (c) the acts are limited to the parts of the program needed for interoperability. Art. 6(2) says the information obtained may not be: (a) used for goals other than interoperability, (b) given to others unless necessary for interoperability, or (c) "used for the development, production or marketing of a computer program substantially similar in its expression, or for any other act which infringes copyright". Art. 6(3) is the Berne three-step test limit. Art. 8, second paragraph, quote: "Any contractual provisions contrary to Article 6 or to the exceptions provided for in Article 5(2) and (3) shall be null and void." Every element of the claim was confirmed verbatim.
license: Legislation text is public law. legislation.gov.uk content is reusable under the Open Government Licence v3.0. The EU-origin text is also © European Union and may be reused under the EUR-Lex reuse policy (Decision 2011/833/EU). Quoting it in project docs is fine.
how_to_use:
Use as a reference legal source for the project's LEGAL.md and its clean-room policy. It is not code. Quote Art. 5(3), 6 and 8 verbatim and cite EUR-Lex (eli/dir/2009/24/oj) as the authentic source; legislation.gov.uk is a convenient mirror. Caveats for the project:
(1) Art. 5(3) only covers observing, studying and testing while doing acts you are licensed to do (loading, running and so on) by someone with a right to use a copy. Contributors doing dynamic analysis must own a legitimate LOTRO install. Article 8 makes EULA/ToS clauses against 5(2), 5(3) and 6 void in the EU, but only for those exceptions. Article 8 also preserves trade-mark, trade-secret, unfair-competition and contract law, so trademark use ("LOTRO", "Lord of the Rings") and anti-cheat or ToS issues for connecting to live servers are not resolved by this directive.
(2) Art. 6 decompilation must be "indispensable" for the interoperability of an independently created program, which fits a client that talks to SSG's servers and reads user-supplied .dat files. Decompilation is limited to the parts needed. The information obtained must not be passed on except where necessary for interoperability, which argues for a written spec and a firewalled clean-room implementer split. It also must not be used to build a program "substantially similar in its expression": the project must not copy code structure or expression, but reproducing behaviour and protocol is allowed. Art. 6(3) (the three-step test) is an extra limit.
(3) The /adopted pages show the original 2009 text. For UK contributors after Brexit, cite CDPA 1988 ss. 50A–50C and 296A (the UK implementation) rather than the directive itself. For US contributors this directive does not apply; Sega v. Accolade, Sony v. Connectix and DMCA 1201(f) are the relevant law.
(4) Interoperability with a server-side service is legally less tested than file-format interoperability. This is general information, not legal advice.
key_facts: Directive 2009/24/EC codifies 91/250/EEC and is still in force in the EU. The articles relevant here are Art. 5(3) (observe/study/test, cannot be overridden by contract per Art. 8), Art. 6 (decompilation for interoperability, with conditions 6(1)(a)-(c) and limits 6(2)(a)-(c), including "substantially similar in its expression"), and Art. 8 paragraph 2 (contract terms contrary to Art. 6, 5(2) or 5(3) are null and void). Art. 8 paragraph 1 keeps patent, trade-mark, unfair-competition, trade-secret and contract law intact. Recital 15 (not fetched) gives the interoperability rationale. Under the CJEU's SAS Institute v World Programming (C-406/10), functionality, programming languages and data file formats are not protected as expression; this is useful support for reimplementing the .dat formats and protocol behaviour, but it should be checked separately. The legislation.gov.uk URL pattern for other articles is /eudr/2009/24/article/N/adopted.
last_activity: Original version as adopted, OJ L 111, 5.5.2009; the legislation.gov.uk pages were live when fetched on 2026-10-03

label: verify:UK CDPA 1988 s.50B / s.50BA / s.296A
actual_description: Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (UK), as amended. All three URLs were fetched on 2026-10-03 and the claim holds. s.50B "Decompilation": a lawful user may convert a low-level program into a higher-level form, and copy it as part of doing so, only when this is necessary to get the information needed to build an independent program that interoperates with the decompiled program or another program. s.50BA "Computer programs: lawful users": a lawful user may observe, study or test how a program works, to find its underlying ideas and principles, while loading, displaying, running, transmitting or storing it as they are entitled to. s.296A "Avoidance of certain terms": contract terms are void where they restrict (a) necessary back-up copies, (b) decompilation that meets the s.50B(2) conditions, or (c) observing, studying or testing under s.50BA. s.296A came in on 1993-01-01 (SI 1992/3233 reg.11); (1)(c) was substituted on 2003-10-31 (SI 2003/2498 reg.15(4)). It implements Software Directive 91/250/EEC, now 2009/24/EC Arts 5(3), 6 and 9, and remains retained UK law after Brexit.
license: Open Government Licence v3.0 (legislation.gov.uk text; Crown copyright)
how_to_use:
reference-only. Cite it as the legal basis in the project's LEGAL/clean-room policy. Do not treat it as general permission. Limits that matter for this project:
1. s.50B only allows decompiling when it is NECESSARY. Under s.50B(3)(a), the right does not apply if the information is already "readily available", so black-box observation (s.50BA), packet captures and published community format docs come first.
2. Information obtained by decompiling may not be passed to anyone who does not need it (s.50B(3)(c)). In practice, decompiler output and annotated disassembly must never go into the public repo. Only specs written by the "dirty" side, describing behaviour and formats, may cross to the "clean" implementers.
3. The new client must not be "substantially similar in its expression" to the original (s.50B(3)(d)). That means no copied code, no mechanically translated code, and no copied tables or strings that are themselves protectable expression.
4. Each person doing the work must be a "lawful user", meaning a licensed LOTRO account or install.
5. s.296A voids EULA/ToS terms against these acts only. It does NOT cover other ToS breaches, such as connecting to the official servers with a third-party client, which could breach contract or lead to account bans. It also does not cover circumvention of technological protection measures (CDPA ss.296–296ZF), database right (Copyright and Rights in Databases Regulations 1997), or trade marks (LOTRO, Turbine, SSG, Middle-earth Enterprises / Tolkien Estate).
6. The .dat contents are data and media assets, not "computer programs", so these sections do not cover copying them. They support only the OpenMW-style model where users load their own lawfully obtained files.
7. These are UK-only rights. Pair them with the equivalent EU (Directive 2009/24/EC Arts 5(3)/6/9) and US (DMCA 17 USC 1201(f), Sega v. Accolade, Sony v. Connectix) sources, matched to where contributors live.
Relevant case law: SAS Institute v World Programming [2013] EWHC 69 (Ch) and CJEU C-406/10 hold that functionality, programming languages and data file formats are not protected as expression, which supports reimplementing the .dat formats and protocol.
key_facts:
Exact wording that matters (fetched):
- s.50B(1)–(2): decompiling is permitted only if "it is necessary to decompile the program to obtain the information necessary to create an independent program which can be operated with the program decompiled or with another program ('the permitted objective')", and only if the information "is not used for any purpose other than the permitted objective".
- s.50B(3): the conditions fail if the lawful user:
  (a) has the information "readily available";
  (b) does not confine decompiling to necessary acts;
  (c) supplies the information to anyone it is not necessary to supply it to; or
  (d) creates a program "substantially similar in its expression" or does any act restricted by copyright.
- s.50B(4) and s.50BA(2): any contract term against the permitted act is irrelevant because "by virtue of section 296A, void".
- s.50BA(1): a lawful user may "observe, study or test the functioning of the program in order to determine the ideas and principles which underlie any element of the program" while doing the acts of "loading, displaying, running, transmitting or storing the program which he is entitled to do".
- s.296A(1)(a)–(c): voids terms that restrict back-up copies, s.50B decompilation, and s.50BA observe/study/test.
- Note: legislation.gov.uk lists the s.50BA heading as "Computer programs: lawful users", not "Observing, studying and testing".
last_activity: s.296A(1)(c) last substituted 2003-10-31 (SI 2003/2498); text current as fetched 2026-10-03

actual_description: The LoTROInterface forum thread "Skinning the LOTRO UI". It has 31 posts, from 9 Feb 2007 to 14 Apr 2009. Cairenn opened it by reposting Turbine's skinning documentation. The claim is accurate, with one correction: it is official Turbine content reposted on a community forum, not an official page.
license: none/unknown (forum post; Turbine-authored content reposted, no license stated)
how_to_use: Use it as reference only, for a clean-room spec. Write down the format facts (where skins live, the SkinDefinition.xml schema, TGA/JPEG with alpha, the crop and sizing behaviour) in our own words. Do not copy the forum text. For the ArtAssetID dictionary: treat it as a list of names (functional identifiers that are needed for compatibility). Build our own table, and where possible check the names against the user's own .dat files. Do not paste the forum's list in wholesale. Why it matters: the real client lets users override UI art by ArtAssetID from <documents>\ui\skins\<SkinName>\SkinDefinition.xml. A faithful reimplementation should keep this system so existing community skins (e.g. on lotrointerface) load unchanged. It also tells us that our UI layer needs a string-keyed art-asset registry that local files can override. It says nothing about .dat formats, rendering or networking, so it is medium relevance (UI and modding compatibility only).
key_facts:
Note: two WebFetch passes confirmed the content. Raw curl could not be used because the scratch disk is full (ENOSPC).

Location: skins go in "<documents>\ui\skins", one subdirectory per skin. <documents> is the folder holding UserPreferences.ini (at the time, "My Documents\The Lord of the Rings Online").

To activate: open Options (Ctrl-O), click "User Skins", then pick the skin from the "Current User Skin" droplist. The thread says the game must be relaunched when a skin is added or changed. A later note says only SkinDefinition.xml changes need a restart, and image edits can be reloaded.

Scope: you can only replace selected media. A full UI replacement is not allowed.

SkinDefinition.xml format:
- Root element <opt>.
- <SkinName Name="..."/> sets the display name.
- One or more <Mapping ArtAssetID="..." FileName="..."/> elements, each mapping an internal image ID to a file path relative to the skin folder.
- Example: <Mapping ArtAssetID="LetterBoxBottom" FileName="letterbox_bottom_red.tga"/>.

Images:
- 32-bit TGA (RGB plus alpha) is the main format; JPEG also works.
- Alpha is honoured, so visible areas must be opaque.
- An image larger than its slot is cropped from the top-left.
- A Mapping that points to a missing file shows a grid pattern, which people used to work out sizes.
- The bottom toolbar is 1074x85 px.
- No official tool gives the dimensions.

ArtAssetID dictionary: the original post lists roughly 250+ string IDs with _normal/_pressed/_rollover state suffixes. Examples: accomplishment_journal_normal, bag_inventory, bag1..bag4, button_autoattack_*, chat_back, chat_entry_focussed, LetterBoxBottom, titlebar_X_2. A 2009 post by cipher_nemo expanded it to 500+ IDs, including runes, traits, housing and item advancement.

The thread mentions no tools for extracting the default art from the .dat files.

label: verify:Chorizite.DatReaderWriter (NuGet)
actual_description: A real NuGet package that ships the Chorizite/DatReaderWriter C# library. The nuspec describes it as "an open-source library for reading and writing .dat files used by the game Asheron's Call". It reads and writes the end-of-retail Asheron's Call (AC) .dat files (client_portal.dat, client_cell_1.dat, client_local_English.dat, client_highres.dat). It supports full BTree seek, insert, remove and range queries, caching and an async API, and targets net8.0, netstandard2.0 and net48. Its only dependencies are DotNet.Standard.Common, System.Buffers, System.IO.Pipelines, System.Memory and ZLibDotNet. A companion package, Chorizite.DatReaderWriter.Extensions 1.1.1, adds write helpers. The claim's "Packaged DRW 2.1.x" is accurate: versions 2.1.0 through 2.1.9 exist. The library is for Asheron's Call only. It does not support LOTRO, and a grep of the source finds no LOTRO references.
license: MIT
last_activity: NuGet 2.1.9 published 2026-08-29 (release note: "fix bsp parsing", PR #71). GitHub HEAD a40acb4 "Bump version" was committed on 2026-08-29. Release history: 1.0.0 (2025-05-14), 2.0.0 (2026-01-31), then 2.1.0 through 2.1.9 between Feb and Aug 2026. About 10.5k total downloads.
key_facts:
Checked against the NuGet API, the nuspec and a shallow clone of the source (nuspec repository commit a9345f24; clone HEAD a40acb4):
- License: LICENSE.txt is MIT, "Copyright 2024 ACClientLib". The NuGet license expression is also MIT.
- Code generation: DatReaderWriter/dats.xml drives a source generator (DatReaderWriter.SourceGenerator) that produces the DBObj and Type classes. This is a schema-driven way to describe dat object layouts.
- DatHeader (Lib/IO/DatHeader.cs) is 400 bytes, in this order:
  - char[256] Version string
  - byte[64] Transactions
  - int32 Magic = 0x00005442 (RETAIL_MAGIC, "BT")
  - int32 BlockSize (1024 by default when creating)
  - int32 FileSize
  - uint32 DatFileType
  - uint32 SubSet
  - int32 FirstFreeBlock, LastFreeBlock, FreeBlockCount
  - int32 RootBlock
  - int32 NewLRU, OldLRU, UseLRU
  - int32 MasterMapId
  - int32 EngineVersion, GameVersion
  - Guid MajorVersion (16 bytes)
  - uint32 MinorVersion
- Blocks: each block starts with a 4-byte next-block pointer, leaving BlockSize-4 bytes of payload. On free-list chains the pointer has the high bit 0x80000000 set. The first block offset is ceil(400/BlockSize)*BlockSize.
- DatBTreeNode is 1720 bytes: 62 int32 branch offsets (MAX_BRANCHES), then int32 fileCount at offset 248, then 61 file entries (MAX_FILES).
- DatBTreeFile is 24 bytes: uint16 Flags, uint16 Version, uint32 Id, int32 Offset, uint32 Size, uint32 RawDate (unix time), int32 Iteration. Files longer than BlockSize-4 span ceil(Size/(BlockSize-4)) blocks.
- Block access comes in two variants: StreamBlockAllocator and MemoryMappedBlockAllocator.
- DatCollection opens the Portal, Cell, Local and HighRes databases together and resolves cross-references by object ID (e.g. Region 0x13000000).
- Zlib (ZLibDotNet) is used for compressed entries.
- Caveat: LOTRO's .dat files come from the same Turbine lineage and share the block, free-list and B-tree design. However, LOTRO's header fields, entry sizes and object types differ, so these exact layouts cannot be assumed to match LOTRO. They need to be checked against LOTRO-specific tools (e.g. LotroCompanion/lotro-dat-utils style readers) and real LOTRO dat files.
how_to_use:
Use it as a reference only, not as a dependency. The NuGet package reads Asheron's Call dats only, so it cannot open client_gamelogic.dat, client_surface.dat, client_mesh.dat or the other LOTRO files without changes. The MIT license allows reading, porting or adapting the code with attribution. Two parts are worth studying because LOTRO's Turbine archive format is related:
1. The block-allocator, free-list and B-tree read/write logic, as a design reference for our own LOTRO dat layer, once the LOTRO-specific layouts are checked against real files.
2. The dats.xml plus source-generator approach to declaring object schemas.
If our toolchain is .NET, it could also be forked for a LOTRO variant, keeping the "Copyright 2024 ACClientLib" MIT notice. Do not describe it as LOTRO-capable in project docs. The claim is accurate on existence, language, license and version, but "for tooling" overstates its usefulness to LOTRO, since it is an Asheron's Call library.

label: verify:SEI blog: Using OOAnalyzer with Ghidra
canonical_url: https://www.sei.cmu.edu/blog/using-ooanalyzer-to-reverse-engineer-object-oriented-code-with-ghidra/ (legacy alias: https://insights.sei.cmu.edu/sei_blog/2019/07/using-ooanalyzer-to-reverse-engineer-object-oriented-code-with-ghidra.html). The tooling it describes now lives at https://github.com/CERTCC/kaiju, with the analyzer at https://github.com/cmu-sei/pharos.
actual_description: The claim checks out. The URL returns HTTP 200 and the page is "Using OOAnalyzer to Reverse Engineer Object Oriented Code with Ghidra" by Jeff Gennari, CMU SEI blog, published July 15, 2019. It announces the OOAnalyzer Ghidra Plugin (opened from a "CERT" menu), which reads the JSON that OOAnalyzer (from the Pharos framework) writes about recovered C++ classes. The plugin applies that data to a Ghidra project in several ways. It adds constructors, destructors and virtual functions to the symbol tree. It changes calling conventions from __fastcall to __thiscall and sets the return and `this` parameter types. It creates class structs and vftable structs in the data type manager under an "OOAnalyzer" folder. It merges Ghidra's own RTTI-derived types with the Pharos results instead of discarding them. The post is dated in one way: the plugin it describes was removed from Pharos and moved into CERT Kaiju, where the menu is now "Kaiju > OOAnalyzer Importer". The blog shows the workflow and the ideas but is not current install guidance.
license: The blog post is SEI copyright and should only be cited, not copied. The tools are open source: cmu-sei/pharos is "BSD (SEI)", a BSD-3-style license with a CMU/SEI naming restriction (LICENSE.md, Copyright 2021 CMU). CERTCC/kaiju uses the same "BSD (SEI)" license (LICENSE.md/LICENSE.txt). Neither is an exact SPDX match; the closest is BSD-3-Clause with an extra no-endorsement/naming clause.
how_to_use: Treat this as reference-only documentation for the internal reverse-engineering toolchain. Do not ship it and do not depend on it at runtime. It is useful only if the project analyses the original LOTRO client binary, and that work must be kept apart from the reimplementation. Under a clean-room process, only the "dirty" analyst team would run OOAnalyzer and Kaiju on a legally obtained lotroclient.exe. That team writes behavioural and format specifications (class hierarchies, struct layouts, packet and DAT handling described in prose). The implementing team works only from those specs, and no decompiled code or Ghidra output goes into the repo. Watch the platform limit: OOAnalyzer officially supports only 32-bit x86 MSVC executables, and 64-bit support is "may work somewhat, untested". The legacy 32-bit lotroclient.exe fits. The newer 64-bit lotroclient64.exe probably won't give reliable results. For installs, follow the Kaiju README and docs/OOAnalyzerImporter.md, not the 2019 blog. Kaiju is actively maintained; its latest commit adds Ghidra 12.1.3 support. Both tools are BSD (SEI), so using them as internal tools raises no licence concern. Do not put "CMU" or "SEI" in the names of any derived tool.
key_facts:
- Blog checked: HTTP 200. Author Jeff Gennari (SEI CERT), 2019-07-15, filed under "Reverse Engineering for Malware Analysis". It points to the CCS 2018 paper "Using Logic Programming to Recover C++ Classes and Methods from Compiled Executables" (https://edmcman.github.io/papers/ccs18.pdf).
- How OOAnalyzer works: it generates constraints from the binary and solves them with XSB Prolog. It recovers class definitions, virtual call information, and inheritance and composition relationships, then writes them to a JSON file. That JSON is the exchange format the Ghidra/IDA importers read.
- What the Ghidra importer does: it adds ctors, dtors and virtual functions (named like VIRT_FUN_xxxxxxxx) to the symbol tree. It fixes method signatures (__fastcall to __thiscall, return type to Cls*, param_1 to `Cls *this`). It creates two kinds of struct per class: a class struct, with parents embedded as implicit members, and vftable structs whose members are the virtual functions. Ghidra's decompiler then resolves virtual calls on its own. Ghidra RTTI types are merged by member count and size. Everything goes under an "OOAnalyzer" namespace and type folder.
- Current location: the pharos README (cloned; HEAD 782492fe, last commit 2026-08-03) says the Ghidra plugin was removed from Pharos and its functionality now ships in CERT Kaiju. Pharos still ships an IDA plugin under tools/ooanalyzer/ida.
- Kaiju (cloned; HEAD 208cec47, last commit 2026-09-10, "Add Ghidra 12.1.3 support (#111)"): docs are in docs/OOAnalyzerImporter.md, tests in src/test/java/kaiju/ooanalyzer, and test samples are ooex_vs2008 and ooex_vs2010. Kaiju's README still links the blog's old insights.sei.cmu.edu URL.
- Limitation: OOAnalyzer targets 32-bit x86 MSVC binaries. ooanalyzer.pod says 64-bit "may work somewhat, but have not been tested". Large executables need the tuning notes in share/prolog/oorules/README.md, which matters for a binary the size of the LOTRO client.
language: Blog: English prose. Pharos/OOAnalyzer: C++ with XSB Prolog rules. Kaiju (the Ghidra importer): Java.
last_activity: Blog published 2019-07-15. The plugin it describes has moved: cmu-sei/pharos last commit 2026-08-03, CERTCC/kaiju last commit 2026-09-10.

label: verify:themissingdocs DatOptimize.exe / LOTRODefrag.exe / Da
actual_description: The "LOTRO Software" page on themissingdocs.net is live. It links three small Windows .NET (MSIL) executables by "Missing Docs". DatOptimize.exe (v0.7.9.0, (c) Missing Docs 2010, 53.5 KB) reorders the files inside a LOTRO .dat to match usage patterns. LOTRODefrag.exe (v1.1.0.0, 36.5 KB) is a GUI that defragments the .dat files on the NTFS disk and inside the archive. The page says to use v1.1 because of a format change for files over 4 GB. DatHash.exe (v0.1.0.0, (c) Missing Docs 2011, 34.5 KB) checks dat integrity by MD5-hashing the files inside a dat, so two installs can be compared or corruption found. All three download URLs (themissingdocs.net/downloads/<Name>.exe) still work. The page gives no dates. The assembly copyright strings date the tools to 2010-2011.
license: none/unknown. There is no SPDX license. The page's exact terms are: "It is all free to use, read, disassemble/reflect. But if you redistribute it you must not claim you wrote it."
language: C# / .NET (managed MSIL PE). All three binaries import mscoree.dll/_CorExeMain and carry #Strings, #US, #Blob and #GUID metadata streams.
last_activity: Assembly copyrights are 2010 (DatOptimize, LOTRODefrag) and 2011 (DatHash). The page shows no update dates. Binaries were still downloadable on 2026-10-03.
key_facts:
Checked by fetching the page and all three binaries with WebFetch. WebFetch's helper model pulled readable metadata out of each binary.

Not checked: the claim's low-level details (header fields at 0x1A0/0x1A4, a free-extent chain with a low-bit tag, an exact field order). Those need an IL disassembly. Bash failed with ENOSPC (device full) in this session, so I could not run ilspycmd/monodis. Treat those details as unconfirmed until someone decompiles the binaries.

Confirmed identifiers in DatOptimize.exe:
- Classes: DatFile2, DirectoryEntry, FileEntry, DatFileRewriter, PatternFinder, PatternTree, DatProfileEntry, DatProfileSave.
- FileEntry fields: CompressionMode, Version, Id, FileLoc, Length, BitField, Iteration, StorageLength, Reserved. This matches the entry fields in the claim, plus BitField, which the claim did not list.
- Other members: Parent, Children, Files, Name, Fragmented, FragLength, DirectoryEntrySize.
- Methods: CheckFileStart, PopFreeSpace, UpdateMap, WriteDirectory, WriteFile, CopyHeader.
- Assembly GUID: dda0e801-a2ce-44ba-8d24-2adc1200e85f.
- It parses and rewrites dats itself in managed code. It does not go through datexport.

DatHash.exe contains the same DatFile2/DirectoryEntry/FileEntry/DatFileRewriter code plus CheckJumpTables, PopFreeSpace, CreateMap, GetFileIdEnumeration, TryMapToId and DirectoryEntryStatus. It hashes with System.Security.Cryptography.MD5.

LOTRODefrag.exe:
- P/Invokes DatExport.dll (Turbine's DLL). Per the claim it calls CalculateFragmentation through it; the extracted strings include a CalculateFragmentation identifier but do not show it is the DatExport entry point.
- P/Invokes kernel32 (CreateFile, DeviceIoControl with FSCTL_GET_VOLUME_BITMAP, FSCTL_GET_RETRIEVAL_POINTERS and FSCTL_MOVE_FILE) for NTFS-level defragmentation.
- Classes: DefragHelper, FileDefrag, FullDefrag, ValidateFreeSpace.
- Its assembly copyright is a template default ("Microsoft 2010").

Corrections to the claim:
- The licence is not "redistribution restricted". Redistribution is allowed as long as authorship is not misrepresented.
- The page itself does not say the tools are .NET. The binaries are.
- "verified-by-fetch" holds for the page and the binaries existing and for the field names. It does not hold for the 0x1A0/0x1A4 and low-bit-tag specifics.
how_to_use:
Use these tools as reference only, to extract a clean-room spec. Do not depend on them or port them.

The author explicitly permits reading and disassembling/reflecting the binaries, and the tools are third-party community work, not Turbine/SSG code. So decompiling DatOptimize/DatHash with ILSpy is a legitimate way to confirm the LOTRO .dat container layout: header fields, directory-tree entry size, FileEntry field order and the free-space chain. Write the results into our own format spec.

No licence grants rights to copy or adapt the code, so do not paste decompiled C# into the project. Write down facts (offsets, field meanings) and reimplement from that spec, ideally checked against independent sources such as LotroCompanion/lotro-dat-utils or other dat readers.

LOTRODefrag adds little. It relies on Turbine's DatExport.dll, which we must not depend on or ship, and on Windows NTFS defrag IOCTLs.

DatHash's MD5-per-subfile approach is a handy idea for our own test harness, for checking that our dat reader matches across installs.

Next action: once disk space is freed, run ilspycmd on DatOptimize.exe to confirm or reject the 0x1A0/0x1A4 header claim and the free-chain low-bit tag claim.
